sections.title: 📘 What this guide covers
sections.text: 📘 What this guide covers Wick Hunter is a self-hosted trading server: it runs on your own box, places real orders with your own exchange key, and never holds your funds. Every bot you can create is one of the five below. Each section covers one bot completely — what it is for, every field on its form, what each field costs you when it is wrong, and a worked example. Read the section for the bot you are about to run; you do not need the other four. The honest warning. This is live trading with real money. Trade only capital you can afford to lose — a bot does exactly what you configured it to do, including when what you configured was a mistake. How long a deal has been open. The Deals page, its phone cards and the dashboard’s Active deals table carry an Open for column, counted from the moment the position opened as the exchange or this app recorded it, and it keeps counting while the page is open. A deal whose open moment was never recorded — a position adopted from the exchange that the exchange did not date — shows a dash rather than a made-up number. Running more than one account. You can add and run as many as you like — each with its own keys, its own book and its own markets. One thing to know before you do: every running account’s API keys are decrypted together and held in memory for the life of the process , so accounts you keep separate on the exchange are not separate here — one compromised host yields all of them. Which markets an account runs is set on the account itself, and those changes apply immediately with no restart. Removing an account. Remove on the account card deletes its stored API keys, stops its markets, and clears its run plan and market caps. If the account still holds anything — open deals, armed hedge stops, or order submissions whose outcome this app could not confirm — you are shown exactly what, on which market , and asked once more. You can always go ahead: it is your account and your decision. What it does not do is close anything. Removing the key does not cancel an order, does not close a position and does not fire a take-profit or a stop — it only removes this app’s ability to reach any of them, and after that only the exchange’s own screens can act on them. An override is written to Activity and sent to your notifications , naming the account, the market and precisely what was left behind, so it can still be explained a week later. On your phone. Add this to your home screen and it opens full-screen with its own icon, like an app. On iPhone that is Safari’s Share button, then Add to Home Screen — Chrome and Firefox on iOS cannot do it. On Android Chrome offers an Install button. A banner offers this the first time; dismissing it with the × keeps it away for a week. Nothing is installed on the phone and nothing runs there — it is the same page, in its own window, still talking to your own server. Connecting an account on a phone. Open More → Accounts → Add account . Exchange buttons wrap into rows. If the dialog is taller than the available screen, scroll inside it to reach the remaining fields and the Add account and Cancel buttons. A new bot\u2019s form is empty on purpose. Create any bot except the Hedge Bot and every box on its form is blank . That is not a loading state and there is nothing to wait for \u2014 a number you did not choose is not a default, it is a trade someone else sized, so the form asks you rather than guessing. You cannot save a form with an empty box: the save is refused and the message names every box you left empty , in the words on its own label. The same applies to a box you clear on a bot you already run \u2014 emptying a field and saving is refused rather than quietly putting yesterday\u2019s number back. Bots you already have are untouched: they open showing exactly what they were storing before. The Hedge Bot is the exception and ships pre-filled from the Moderate Hedge template, which you can change or replace with Slow or Aggressive at any time. The guided setup is a read-through. Guided setup in the sidebar walks the six screens in order and points at what matters on each. It never waits for you to do anything — not saving a bot, not adding a key — so Next always moves you on whether or not you did the thing the step describes. Skip the tour , the ✕ and the Esc key all close it immediately, from any step, and it reopens from the same place. If a step cannot point at its control — the page it lives on is not open, or that control is not on screen — it says so on the panel instead of going quiet.

sections.title: 📣 Notices you may see, and what they mean
sections.text: 📣 Notices you may see, and what they mean Some of what the app reports looks like a fault and is not. These are the ones worth recognising before you go looking for a problem, or open the exchange to check. Aster closed P&L reads slightly higher than your wallet. Aster has no closed-position endpoint, so a trade is rebuilt from the account ledger: its exit fee is tied to the trade and deducted, its entry fee is a separate row nothing can tie back, so that one is left out rather than guessed at. Expect about one fee per trade, more after several DCAs. Funding is unaffected. Timed DCAs are not on the exchange, and that is normal. A DCA ladder built with timed DCAs shows two sections on a deal: the ones resting on the exchange as real limit orders, and the ones held by this bot . An exchange has no concept of “12 hours after my entry”, so nothing is placed for a timed DCA and you will not find it on the venue — the bot checks it every few seconds instead. Three things follow, and each has surprised somebody. They only fire while the bot is running : one that came due during an outage fires as soon as the bot is back, not at the moment it was due. Pausing a bot does not stop them — pausing stops NEW deals, and a deal that is already open keeps its timed DCAs, which the deal says on its own screen while it is paused. And on a position the bot adopted rather than opened, the clock starts when it took the position over, because the exchange does not always report when a position opened; the deal names which clock it is using. An adopted deal carried over from an older build may have had no clock at all , and its timed DCAs could never come due — they counted down for ever. This build starts a clock the first time it sees such a deal, writes a line in Activity, and the deal says so on its own screen: those delays then run from that moment, not from whenever the position really opened. A bot left behind by a removed account. Removing an account does not remove the bots you created on it — those bots simply have nowhere to run any more, so they get no card on any market. My Bots lists them at the top instead, with a Retire button. Retiring one takes it off this install and stops it counting against your bot limits (ten TV Signal bots, ten Optimized Liq bots, ten Hedge Bots), which is what frees you to create a replacement. Two things it deliberately does not do: it changes nothing on any exchange — no order is cancelled and no position is closed — and it keeps the bot’s name , so trades it already closed still say “Sniper” on the P&L page rather than falling back to a bare id. A bot that never placed a real order says so on its row and is the safe one to clear; a bot that did keeps a full warning, because this app can no longer see what it left on the exchange and only you can check. Retiring is written to Activity and sent to your notifications . Bots on an account you still have are not retirable at all — delete those from their own card, which still refuses while they hold open deals. Sharing on Community, and who may delete a share. A Strat you publish is signed to your licence — an identity nobody else can present — and only you can delete it again. Strats published before this build were not signed to anyone. The old scheme took the publisher’s name from the request itself, which meant anyone could have claimed it, so those entries now have no verified owner and can no longer be deleted by anyone , their author included. They still show, and they are still copyable. If one of them is yours, publish it again — the new entry is signed to you and is yours to remove. “Unattributed add / unattributed reduce” in your notifications. A bot compares the exchange’s position against its own book every few seconds. When the two disagree by more than rounding and no order the bot has working can account for the difference , it adopts the exchange’s figures — size, average and the take profit that follows them — and tells you, naming the pair and the amount. It does not tell you who did it, because it cannot know: your own trade on the exchange, a liquidation, an auto-deleverage and a venue action all look identical from here. Earlier builds called this a manual DCA or a manual reduce , which asserted something the bot had no way to establish — and it fired on the bot’s own ladder orders as they partially filled. A change the bot can attribute to one of its own resting orders is now silent : it waits for the exchange’s answer on that exact order id and reports it as the DCA or take-profit fill it is. If you did not trade, an unattributed notice is worth opening the exchange for.

sections.title: 🏦 Notices only one exchange can raise
sections.text: 🏦 Notices only one exchange can raise Each note below names its exchange. If you do not trade there, nothing on this card applies to you. Bitunix reports several positions for one pair. Bitunix has a per-pair Multi-Trade setting, switched only on its website (the pair’s Cross/Isolated panel), that opens every order as a separate position instead of adding to the one you hold. Its API offers no way to read or switch it, so this app cannot turn it off for you. When the venue reports more than one open position for one pair and side, this app treats them as one combined position, refuses any further opening order on that leg (closes still go through), and sends one notice. Turn Multi-Trade off for the pair on bitunix.com and let the positions merge or close down to one; the bot resumes on its own.

sections.title: 🔔 Notifications — what you get, and what you can add
sections.text: 🔔 Notifications — what you get, and what you can add Everything on this card is set in one place: Settings → Notifications , beside the Discord webhook address. Which webhook is in use is now printed under the scope control — Using: custom webhook for this account · …/1234567890123/••••ab12 · saved 2 Sep 2026 — resolved by the same code that sends the message, so it names the destination the next card will land in. Only the webhook’s id and the last four characters of its token are shown; the saved URL is still never returned to this browser. A webhook saved before this build shows no date, and an account set to a custom webhook with nothing saved says so instead. Which messages you get. Five toggles under Which messages — Deal opened , DCA filled , Deal closed , Hedge events and System alerts . All five are on unless you turn them off, and each covers every bot on every account and market this install runs. Turning Deal closed off is the only thing that stops a close alert, including the “Closed — reconciling” card that is later edited into the settled one. Adding your balance to a close card. Three more toggles under Include on close cards — Wallet , Daily P&L and Total P&L . They are independent: turn on one, two or all three. All three ship off , so nothing about your messages changes until you ask for it. What they add is one extra line at the bottom of the close card, reading something like Wallet: $4,210.50 · Daily P&L: +$123.40 · Total P&L: +$67.89 . Daily P&L is realised profit for the current UTC day, counting each position on the day it fully closed, and Total P&L is the account’s realised total — the same two figures as the Day P&L tile in the header and the Net (synced) tile on the dashboard. Every figure is the account the card is about , on the exchange and market named in the card’s own footer — never another account you happen to be looking at. Sync cards are held back until they are worth reading. exchange sync DEGRADED is sent only once the account read has been failing for over a minute, RESTORED only once it has held for two passes, and brief sync failures that recover inside that window are recorded only in the service journal for debugging, without notifications or Activity entries. When the cause is this app’s own polling budget rather than the exchange, the card says local sync DELAYED and that nothing was sent to the exchange. A price-feed card ( PRICE FEED MISSING , RESTORED , FLAPPING , and the Hedge Bot’s equivalents) names every pair that went dark together in one card — 23 pairs (COAIUSDT, QUSDT, … +17 more) — because on these venues one request prices them all, so one refusal is one event. It waits five minutes before it reaches you — longer than the sync card above, on purpose: a socket that redials, or a request that is briefly refused, usually heals on its own within a minute or two, and a card for that is not worth reading. Activity and the service log still note a gap once it passes 75 seconds, so the record is never blank — you just are not interrupted for it unless it is still going five minutes later, at which point the card gives its real age, not a rounded one.For the first ten minutes after an account starts, these sync and price-feed cards are held back altogether: a start-up wobble that clears on its own sends nothing, and one that is still there when the ten minutes are up is reported then, with its real age. A figure this app has not read is left off, not printed as zero. A wallet balance it has not fetched yet, or an account whose closed-trade books have not been read since the app started, produces no line for that figure rather than $0.00 — a zero would be this app telling you your wallet is empty. If one of the three is missing from a card and the other two are there, that is what happened, and it fills itself in within a minute or two. An account that genuinely has no closes today does print +$0.00 , because that one is a fact. The wallet figure is read when the card is sent , so a card that is later updated with its settled profit shows the balance as it is at that moment. “NATIVE CORE DEGRADED / RESTORED / FLAPPING” only appears on an install running the compiled decision core in authoritative mode — an operator-enabled build option, off by default. While it is on and answering, hedge and deal decisions run through it; if it stops answering for a hedge or a deal, that hedge holds its last recorded stop and Paired TP levels and that deal keeps its resting orders exactly as placed, and neither opens anything new until it answers again. The card follows the same five-minute dwell and quarter-hour FLAPPING fold as the price-feed cards above, and is held back for the same first ten minutes after an account starts.

sections.title: Updates & returning to a previous version
sections.text: Updates & returning to a previous version Open Settings → Updates to see your installed version and any approved previous Go version. Select Return to previous version and review the version shown before confirming. If no compatible release is approved, the control stays disabled and explains why. Versions before 0.90.128 cannot be used as recovery targets. All accounts restart. Local stop-loss and hedge logic pause during the restart. Your current settings, history and trading data are kept; reverting does not close positions for you. If the previous version fails its startup checks, the installer attempts to restore the original Go version. If recovery needs attention, submit a bug report: release diagnostics are included automatically. After a successful revert, the rejected version stays out of update offers. A newer corrective release can still be offered. Allow the rejected update again removes that hold without installing anything.

sections.title: 🐛 Sending a useful bug report
sections.text: 🐛 Sending a useful bug report Open Report a bug from Help, describe what you expected and what happened, and send it while the problem is still visible. An optional PNG, JPEG or WebP picture can now travel with the report. A source image may be up to 20 MB; when it is larger than the 2 MB evidence limit the browser resizes and recompresses it on this device before sending. The useful context is attached automatically. The report includes a bounded tail of recent Activity with ISO time, account context, bot, event kind and symbol where known, plus this page, browser/viewport, selected account and market, and counts and summaries for managed deals and read-only Hedge Bot attachments. The oldest rows are dropped when the fixed evidence budget is full; the report says the exact time range and number that were included. Credentials and secret-shaped fields are redacted before anything leaves WickHunter. Report text and diagnostic values are scrubbed again by the Hub, and screenshots are accepted only as genuine raster images. A report carrying the new evidence is accepted only when the Hub confirms that it understands evidence format v2, so an older Hub cannot say success while silently losing the picture or diagnostic state. On this install's own Feedback board (✉️ New feedback / the Feedback page), ticking Attach diagnostics builds a fuller bundle in the background — this box's own health, recent console output (including the previous boot's, if this process is still young), the running bots' scrubbed settings, and everything the general debug export already covers — and attaches it to that one report. Each row's ⬇ Export button downloads that ONE report as a single file; the general Export debug log button elsewhere in Settings still exports the whole install.

sections.title: 🔗 Sharing a bot's configuration
sections.text: 🔗 Sharing a bot's configuration Every bot's card on My Bots carries a Share button. It hands over that one bot's settings — its entry rules, its DCA ladder and its exits — as JSON, or as a link, so someone else can open it on their own install. A share never carries a key, a secret or a webhook address. Not an exchange API key, not a TradingView webhook secret, not a Discord webhook URL — none of those live in the settings a share reads, so there is nothing to leave out by mistake. What travels is the trading configuration only, and nothing on your account changes because you pressed Share. Three ways to hand it over. Copy JSON puts the raw configuration on your clipboard. Download saves it as a file. Copy link puts the whole thing inside a web address — paste that address into anyone's own install and its Import box opens with everything already in it, with no server or account involved on either side. A configuration too large for a link still copies and downloads; only the link itself is refused, and it says so. Importing changes nothing until you say so. Paste a link, its code, or raw JSON into Import (beside Create Bot on My Bots) and press Preview to see what is inside — each bot's type, its name if it has one, and a few headline numbers. From there each bot has its own button: most open that bot's own form already filled in, and nothing is saved until you press that form's own Save. A shared hedge configuration instead creates a new one of its own, paused and with no pairs, after asking you to confirm — your own hedge bot and everything it is already protecting are left exactly as they are.

sections.title: 🚚 Moving to a new install
sections.text: 🚚 Moving to a new install Settings → Move existing setup exports every bot and setting on this install as one file, for a fresh install of Wick Hunter running somewhere else. Press Export setup on the OLD install to download it, then choose that file under Import setup on the NEW one. A brand-new install applies it right away. One that already has an account connected, or a bot configured, refuses first and shows the reason; confirming asks it to go ahead anyway and overwrite what is already there. Either way the app reboots once the import lands, and it tells you exactly what still needs your hands — each account to reconnect with its key, the Discord webhook, and any TradingView bot's webhook secret — because none of those ever leave the exported file. Stop the old install before the new one starts trading. Nothing here fences two running installs on one license from trading the same account at the same time — that is on you to prevent, by stopping the old box first.

sections.title: 📊 Whose candles WickHunter uses
sections.text: 📊 Whose candles WickHunter uses A price decision always belongs to the exchange and product being traded. Bybit USDT and USDC perpetuals use its linear book, Spot uses its Spot book, and coin-margined contracts use its inverse book. Bitunix, Bitget, Binance and Aster USDT-futures decisions use that venue's own candles. A selected Bybit, Binance or OKX liquidation feed may contribute the event that wakes a bot, but it contributes only the coin and side; it never supplies another exchange's price, VWMA, volatility window or order price. The Liq Scalper's VWMA is the period and timeframe you selected, not a one-minute approximation. Choose 2–199 bars and 1m, 3m, 5m, 15m, 30m or 1h. Bybit reads that exact interval from the correct product book. On Bitunix, Bitget, Binance and Aster, one exact-venue one-minute live tail is folded into clock-aligned candles at your selected width after an exact native-width history seed. Open, high, low, close and base volume are combined; a gap makes the value unavailable instead of manufacturing a bar. One-minute VWMA uses completed candles only, while slower widths include their exact forming bucket. Period and timeframe are fixed when that account context starts. If you save a different value while it is running, new Liq entries fail closed until the context restarts. Pair Info and Activity name both the requested and currently running value; the old indicator is never shown under the new label. Open positions keep being managed during that refusal. Volatility Filters are separate direct exchange reads. 1d / 10% / 10 inspects ten completed daily candles one by one; any single candle over 10% refuses new exposure, ten days are not added together, and exactly 10.0% passes. Demand is kept by pair, timeframe and depth for the bot that owns it, so another bot's deeper rule cannot invalidate a usable shallow one. Every account context sharing one public endpoint also shares the same bounded request allowance. A broad short-timeframe scope may therefore warm gradually or be refused with the required and available read rates; WickHunter will not burst the venue or call permanently stale data current. Missing data stays visible and heals itself. An empty candle reply or a page that stops before the venue's current bucket does not make old data look fresh: the last measured values and timestamp remain as evidence. They can still support an entry while they are inside the existing 90-second freshness limit; once that expires, Pair Info and Activity say unavailable, warming or stale and no new entry is allowed. On a broad pair roster WickHunter retries the failed pair before finishing another full pass, using only request time the roster has earned; one unpinned pair on its own can still take about a minute to earn its next ordinary try. Fresh live candles cancel a retry only after they supply the history the indicator still needs; a missing minute keeps repair active, an older or forming update cannot replace a newer confirmed close, and pairs attached to open positions keep their separate 20-second candle refresh. ATR take profit and Scaled ATR DCA can use different timeframes. A 1m ATR take profit works alongside 3m DCA and entry candles. Supported venues reuse the account's shared one-minute candle store and exact-timeframe history seed; the entry VWMA keeps its own selected interval. Missing or stale candles still pause ATR pricing until they recover. The Scaled ATR preview says which of the two it is looking at. A DCA row reading not priced yet means nothing has measured that pair on that timeframe yet — the panel prints the exchange’s own refusal where there is one, and otherwise those three words rather than pretending a floor or a cap was applied. If a fetch runs past twenty seconds the panel keeps the last priced ladder and says the venue did not answer; press Refresh to ask again. Liquidation sizes after a restart. The Screener restores saved Hub and local percentile tables while refreshing them in the background. A first installation still needs a valid Hub table or enough recorded liquidation history. The Optimized Hub download has one narrow job: accelerate deep band history. It is an optional signed one-minute prefill and is accepted only after an exact overlap matches a live page from the same exchange the Optimized bot trades. Bad, absent or mismatched Hub data is discarded and same-venue paging continues. It is a different download from the volatility-window snapshot described under Pair filters , which warms those rules and is separately confirmed against this exchange.

sections.title: 🛒 The Strategy Marketplace
sections.text: 🛒 The Strategy Marketplace The Marketplace is alpha-only. Customer beta builds omit its UI and API. Alpha also requires the Marketplace licence feature; an unavailable or unreadable licence fails closed without changing existing bots. Marketplace shows approved strategies to copy and, for approved providers, a publishing console. Your API keys never leave your server. This install verifies the Hub’s signed, sequenced intents and applies its normal risk gates. You must acknowledge the versioned disclaimer before browsing, following, publishing or paying. Cancel returns to the previous page. Changed wording requires a new acknowledgement. Each track record comes from the strategy’s permanently linked, WickHunter-owned Bybit Demo account. The Hub derives every metric from authenticated account history. It is not a backtest, projection, follower result or provider-entered number; an unmeasured figure is an em dash . The provider application is the only human approval. Approved providers create strategies and bots with the normal forms. Enabling the first bot provisions and permanently links an isolated $10,000 USDT Demo account. Publishing requires authenticated Demo execution evidence. Subscriptions buy alerts, never a share of trading profit. Payment uses Stripe’s hosted checkout and the provider’s displayed recurring price. WickHunter activates access only after Stripe’s signed paid webhook is durably recorded. This creates no provider revenue share, performance fee, payout balance or claim on follower profit. Pending activation survives refresh; if payment is recorded while entitlement is reviewed, do not pay again . A lapsed subscription stops new entries, while existing exits keep flowing. Status, payment, pause and entitlement never withhold an open copied deal’s close, stop, take-profit or cancel. During a Hub outage new copying pauses while local management continues. Your size is yours. Provider percentages pass through your multiplier and caps, so your absolute ladder differs . Following lets you edit account, market and risk limits; a live deal blocks unsafe account/version rebinding but permits risk tightening. Your exchange shows your pairs and fills while strategy logic stays private. The Demo account and each copier consume one ordered strategy stream independently. Each account can fill or refuse under its own gates. Durable sequence, replay, receipts and reconciliation recover without duplicating an action; risk reductions remain fail-safe. A strategy may have several bots. Each keeps its type, settings and percentage risk envelope. Providers pause, resume or edit them in the workspace; they execute in the dedicated Demo account. Provider positions appear in Open Deals. Their drawer offers Add to position and Close as exact percentages of that lifecycle. A failure stays in the dialog with the same safe-retry identity. Submitted means the durable instruction was accepted, not filled. Copier settings start with account and size multiplier. More copy settings contains pair filters and protections. Close if provider entry fails closes the matching copy only after a confirmed provider-entry refusal, never a slow connection. It defaults on for new follows; existing follows keep their saved choice. Armed Exit Protection is visible. After the provider’s exact position closes, an open copy shows “Provider closed · closing remainder in N s” . The durable timer continues after the tab closes. Strategy actions match subscription state: Subscribe , Check payment , Create Copy Bot with secondary management, View Copy Bot , or Manage subscription when lapsed. Unpublished open- or closed-trade detail is stated plainly. Deleting a Copy Bot does not cancel its subscription; use Manage subscription . A flat bot deletes immediately. Otherwise choose Stop new trades and delete when flat (management continues) or Close positions and delete .

sections.title: Copier sizing and protection
sections.text: Copier sizing and protection Position value cap means notional, not margin. It limits each copied position's entry and DCA combined, as a percentage of your equity. For example, 5% of 10,000 USDT is 500 USDT of position value; at 5× leverage, that uses about 100 USDT of initial margin before fees. Take profit and stop loss are separate choices. Copy either provider level or enter a local percentage. A local percentage uses your actual average entry and adjusts after DCA. Saved choices apply to new copied trades; existing trades retain their entry-time settings. Search and select pairs from your account's list. The selected-pair dropdown includes Select all. The blacklist excludes only the pairs you select and takes precedence for new entries and DCA.

sections.title: 🟢 Marketplace connection
sections.text: 🟢 Marketplace connection The dot beside a followed subscription or a Copy Bot always carries words, never just a colour. Green (“Connected to Hub”) means this install has heard from the Hub recently; amber (“Reconnecting”) and red (“Not answering”) both name the moment it was last heard from; grey (“Not yet observed”) means nothing has been confirmed yet, which is normal for the first few minutes after a follow is created. Going red does not stop anything already open — closes, stops and take‑profits still come through your own exchange connection, unaffected.

sections.title: 🧬 Subscribing, your Copy Bot, and the provider console
sections.text: 🧬 Subscribing, your Copy Bot, and the provider console Subscribing shows what actually happened, never a guess. While a payment is being confirmed the screen says Opening checkout… and everything else stays usable. Once the Hub durably confirms it — never optimistically on the click — the screen offers Create Copy Bot or View subscriptions ; creating one still lands paused and starting it is a separate step. A payment that failed or could not be confirmed shows the server’s own sentence with Check again , which re-checks the exact same attempt rather than starting a second purchase. View Copy Bot opens a dedicated detail screen for that one bot: its name, strategy, account/market and current phase read straight from the server — never an invented “starting”. Pause/Resume there is the same safe compare-and-swap the card’s own toggle uses; if the setting moved elsewhere first, the screen reloads the real current state and says so rather than retrying blind. Its Positions table and Exit Protection countdown read the same live feed every other screen does, its Delivery health strip shows when this account last heard from the Hub, and its Settings section is the one shared editor — not a second copy of it. A close that Exit Protection makes says what it left standing, too — if a copied Hedge leg was still open for the mirror the instant the close went through, the row names it once, as a plain closed fact, never a warning. A retired Copy Bot keeps a History button on its card — a read-only screen with its exact retirement record (status, the mode you asked for, and every fact recorded at the moment it was removed) plus a link to the deals it left behind, read straight from the server on open; nothing on it is guessed from a possibly-stale card. Approved providers get a Subscribers tab and an Earnings tab on their own strategy. Subscribers lists who has paid, who has paused, who is pending and since when — never your copiers’ exchange keys, account IDs, wallet, equity, order sizes or private positions. Its Runtime phase column shows what that copier’s own agent last reported, with its age; Not reported means exactly that, never a guessed “copying”. Earnings lists your own payable ledger by period — each statement’s gross and your share of it, pending/available/paid/voided — exact figures from that ledger, never a computed subscription-revenue chart. On an install with neither configured, both tabs say so plainly instead of showing a fabricated zero. Running your own strategy is a normal Wick Hunter account. Create Bot, DCA, Pause/Resume and Delete on your source bot are the same account controls every other account has — there is no separate remote-control console for a provider. Publishing is a different, deliberately separate step: a strategy moves to a demo account, warms up, then reviews and lists itself automatically once your Bybit Demo evidence and price are in place, so Submit for review only appears once that step is legally reachable. Unlist hides a live strategy from new subscribers — the ones you already have keep their subscription, and closes, stop‑losses and take‑profits are never affected. Plan service end stops it for good: if the source account still shows open positions it asks you to confirm once, in the server’s own words, before moving the listing through its real states — never a shortcut that takes a strategy off the shelf in the same instant it stops trading. A strategy whose accepted version contains Hedge Bot keeps its copied hedge ownership. Its Copy Bot and local Hedge Bot screens do not offer a handoff. For a strategy positively proven to contain no Hedge Bot, an explicitly listed local Hedge Bot may still take the next tranche after the existing side is flat and every resting stop is proven closed. Unknown capability stays blocked until the Hub confirms the accepted immutable version.

sections.title: 📈 The Terminal
sections.text: 📈 The Terminal Terminal in the sidebar opens a second page: one open deal at a time, drawn on its own exchange’s candles , with everything that deal is waiting on marked on the price axis — original entry, blended average, the stop, every DCA and every take‑profit step. You can drag the take profit and the stop on the chart, or type them, and change how many DCAs rest on the exchange. Nothing is changed until you commit it, and you are told what it will do first. Dragging a line or typing a number stages the change: a bar appears under the chart showing the price it moves from and to , and the literal count of orders that will be cancelled and placed on the exchange — for example “1 change · 1 cancel · 1 place” . Discard throws it away; Review & commit applies it to that one deal only , exactly like the Edit button on the deal card, and never to the bot’s settings. Switching to another deal drops anything you had staged rather than carrying it across. Some edits are refused, and the reason is written out. A take profit or a stop dragged through the current price is not a target — committing it would close the position at market, worse than the price on offer — so it is refused with both numbers named and nothing is changed. A single take‑profit percentage cannot be applied to a deal on a take‑profit ladder , and a resting‑DCA cap means nothing on a venue that cannot rest DCA orders at all; both say so. When an edit is refused the Commit button is disabled and the sentence stays on screen. The stop is drawn where it actually lives. A stop resting on the exchange is drawn solid, like any other exchange order; one WickHunter is only watching is drawn dashed, and the row says which in the venue’s own words. A deal opened before v0.88.0 reads not reported rather than being guessed. Notices explains what decides it. The lines are drawn differently on purpose, and the difference is not decoration. A solid line is an order resting on the exchange : it fills whether or not this app is running. A dashed line is held by WickHunter — a timed DCA, which no exchange can hold, and which therefore does not fire while the bot is stopped. A dotted line is a plan : the ladder intends it, but nothing is placed until a nearer DCA fills, so there is no order on the venue to find. A faint line has already filled . The same shapes appear as small swatches beside every row of the Orders table and in the legend under the chart, and the sentence spelling out what each one costs you is on the row itself. Shape, not colour — green and red already mean long, short and profit here, and a difference this expensive to misread must survive being printed, dimmed, or seen by someone who does not separate those two colours. The one number to read before you close the laptop. Under the chart is a single line counting this deal’s orders by where they live — for example “3 resting on the exchange · 1 held by this app · 1 not placed yet” . The middle figure is the one that matters when you stop the bot or the machine reboots: those are the DCAs that will not fire until it is back. No chart makes that readable by eye, which is why it is written out. The order book, and what it will not pretend. A small book sits beside the chart — five levels a side and the spread — and it refreshes about once a second. It is deliberately plain: the numbers are the point. What matters is that it never draws a dead feed as a thin market . If depth has stopped arriving it says how long ago; if the best bid is at or above the best ask it says the book is corrupted, not tight , because that is a book this app has mis-assembled rather than a market; and if no depth has arrived at all it says so in words instead of showing you an empty table, which would read as a pair with nothing in it. One caveat belongs here rather than on the panel, where it would sit on every venue on every load: each venue’s depth format is read from that venue’s documentation and none has yet been confirmed against a live socket, so real-looking numbers are worth a second thought. Whose candles you are looking at. The chart is fetched for the deal’s own account and market , named above it, so a position on Bitget is drawn on Bitget’s price action and never on someone else’s. If a venue does not publish the timeframe you picked, the terminal says which venue and which timeframe and draws nothing — it will not quietly substitute a different interval or another exchange’s bars, because a chart that is wrong about whose market it shows is worse than no chart. A stale mark price is labelled too, on the header and on the notice strip.

sections.title: 📈 Reading the chart
sections.text: 📈 Reading the chart The price axis carries prices. The names sit on the chart. Every line the terminal draws has a small tag at the left of the chart giving its name — Avg Price , DCA 2 , Paired TP — while the axis on the right shows only the number. That split is the whole reason the axis is readable: a tag as wide as its own name, five of them stacked, hides the axis’s own price ticks underneath. When two lines sit close enough that their tags would overlap, the tags are nudged apart; the lines never move, because a line that is not at its price is the one thing this screen must never do. The average entry says what the position is. Its tag reads Avg Price with your size and what it cost beside it — for example 12.4 HYPE / $813 . That is the number the take profit and the hedge ladder both measure from, and the one that moves when a DCA fills. If your size has not been reported the bracket is simply absent rather than showing a zero, because a zero there would be a claim that the position holds nothing. The original entry is drawn quietly, and that is deliberate. It is where the deal started and what the DCA distances are measured from, so the chart cannot be read against the ladder table without it — but it is not something you are waiting for or can act on. It keeps its place and loses its voice: dimmed, and with no tag on the axis at all. The mark price is not drawn: it is already the largest number in the header, the last candle an inch to its right, and the chart’s own axis label — three statements of one fact, one of them cutting through every line that is a decision. Panning and zooming does not rebuild the chart. Moving a line — dragging the take profit, the stop or the order ticket — moves that one line and leaves every other one alone. Before v0.88.7 a drag tore the whole ladder down and re-drew it on every frame, which is what made the price scale jump while you were holding it. If you want the whole picture back, Fit in the bottom-right corner returns the candles and the full ladder to view; nothing else re-fits it, so a view you panned to stays where you put it. Every order row tells you where it is edited. The Orders table under the chart has an Edit button on each row that can still be changed: a DCA takes you to that DCA’s own distance and size boxes, the take profit and the stop to their boxes in Manage this deal , and the panel is un-hidden first if you had it hidden. It is a shortcut, not a second way to send an order — everything still goes through the staged bar and Review & commit . A DCA that has already filled shows a dash instead: that is money already spent. So does a timed DCA , which belongs to the bot’s own ladder settings rather than to this deal, and is edited on the bot’s DCA form. Hiding a panel, and getting it back. Every panel with a small × in its corner can be closed, and Panels at the top of the terminal is where it comes back — the same menu also switches between Default , Chart focus and Dense layouts, and has a Reset to default . While anything is hidden that button counts it, so it reads “Panels · 2 hidden” rather than leaving you to remember. Your layout is remembered on this browser and is not part of any bot’s settings, so it changes nothing about how a deal is traded. One thing hiding a panel does not do is hide its warnings: anything the panel would have told you — a hedge that is not protected, orders this app is holding rather than the exchange — is moved up to the notice strip under the header instead, because switching off a panel must change where you read a warning and never whether you read it. The deal list is the account in the header, and dragging a line moves that line. Open deals shows only the positions on the account and market named at the top of the page — switch accounts and the list, the count and the selection all move with it, and an account with nothing open says so by name rather than going blank. Everything else on the page has always acted on the deal’s own venue; the list was the one place that showed you all of them at once. And the small grab handles on the left of each line — the take profit, the stop, each unfilled DCA and an order-ticket price — are draggable with a mouse or a finger: they sit on top of the in-chart labels now rather than underneath them, and each one moves its own order, so dragging DCA 3 changes DCA 3. As always the drag only stages the change: nothing reaches the exchange until Review & commit . On a phone the terminal is tabbed. Below about 600 pixels wide — a phone in portrait — the three columns become one: the chart stays pinned at the top and everything else moves behind a row of tabs under it, Deals · Position · Orders · Ladder · Manage · Hedge · Book · Ticket . Only one panel is on screen at a time and it scrolls on its own, so the chart never gets pushed off the top. Deals is where you pick the pair or the position, and tapping a deal takes you straight to its Position with the chart already showing it. The tabs are the same panels as on a desktop, so a panel you hid has no tab either — bring it back with Panels in the header — and a tab only appears when there is something behind it: no Hedge tab until a hedge is attached. Dragging the take profit and the stop works with a finger , exactly as it does with a mouse. Nothing changes on a wider screen. Two small things on the chart. On a hedged deal only the hedge’s Paired TP line is drawn, because that is the exit that closes both legs; the deal’s own TP line is not shown beside it. The TradingView mark in the bottom-left corner opens the pair you are looking at on TradingView, on the same timeframe.

sections.title: ✋ Moving a line, and committing it
sections.text: ✋ Moving a line, and committing it A drag stages; it never sends. The grab handles on the take profit, the stop, each unfilled DCA and the order-ticket price move with a mouse, a finger or the arrow keys, and each moves its own order — dragging DCA 3 changes DCA 3. Nothing reaches the exchange until Review & commit . Escape abandons a drag without asking the server anything at all, and the line goes back where it was. A line turns red before you let go. While you are dragging, a handle goes red the moment the price under it is somewhere the order cannot go — a take profit dragged through your average entry, a DCA dragged above the entry it is measured from, a stop on the wrong side, anything already through the current market price , or a DCA dragged past its neighbour so the ladder would fill out of order. The chip says which of those it is, beside the price and the distance, so you can see where to put it instead. It is a warning rather than a veto: the real answer still comes from the staged bar when you release, and Review & commit stays switched off while anything is refused. A line already resting at the market is never marked red — that is an order about to fill, not a mistake. Two kinds of line are locked, and they say why. A position that is being closed is having its orders cancelled as you look at it, so none of its lines can be dragged: moving one would ask the app to place an order on a position it is getting rid of. And a line whose residency is not reported — this view cannot say whether it is resting on the exchange, held here, or nowhere — is locked for the plainer reason that nobody could tell you what moving it would do. Both stay drawn, dimmed, and refuse a finger and an arrow key alike with the reason on the action line. Avg Price is not a handle at all: it is what the position cost, not an order, so there is nothing there to move. Committing is one instruction, and a refusal puts the line back. While a commit is in flight its handles are drawn dashed — this page’s own word for “not resting anywhere yet” — and the moment the exchange answers, the chart is re-read from it rather than assumed. If it is refused , the line returns to the price that is actually resting and the exchange’s own sentence appears on the action line: a chart showing an order at a price the venue has just rejected is exactly what this screen exists not to do. If you make a second change to the same order before the first answer lands, the second one wins and the older reply is discarded rather than allowed to overwrite it. No resting order is edited in place. No exchange here offers that, so committing a moved distance or a retyped size cancels each resting order and re-places it — which is why the staged bar counts the cancels and the places before you press the button, and why a ladder edit is never free. The cancel is confirmed before the replacement goes in. A change you commit belongs to this deal only : it does not touch the bot’s own settings, and a deal that has been edited here keeps its own numbers across a restart rather than going back to the bot’s. An uncommitted drag is the opposite — it lives in this browser tab and nowhere else, so a reload puts the line back at the price the exchange is actually holding.

sections.title: 🛡 The hedge, on the deal’s own screen
sections.text: 🛡 The hedge, on the deal’s own screen When a hedge is open, the paired take profit logically owns the exit. Its displayed price is a projected, WickHunter-watched combined target , not a TP order placed at that price on the exchange. WickHunter watches both legs, realised hedge P&L and funding, then closes both sides at market when the target is reached. The main position’s own TP is a separate physical order: Terminal reports it as confirmed absent, resting, cancellation pending, restoration pending or unverified . Only confirmed absent proves there is no separate main TP on the venue; while cancellation is pending it may still be there. A different TP value shown by Bybit is therefore not the paired target. Bybit’s Full / TP Entire is a conditional main-position TP: WickHunter now removes it through Bybit’s one-sided position operation so a bound Stop Loss stays in place, and restores that exact Full trigger recipe when the hedge closes. A Hedge Bot attachment is not always a WickHunter-managed deal. A hand-opened main position can be attached and hedged while no deal bot owns its TP, stop or DCA ladder. Deals and Terminal show that position as Hedge Bot only · read-only , with its venue candles, average entry, both leg sizes, hedge lines and projected paired target, but they do not invent deal controls or a close action. If you want full deal management, enable and configure Manual Bot adoption for the main position; until it adopts, the read-only row is the truthful state. The Hedge panel, and the toggle beside it. A Hedge section appears in the right-hand column whenever a hedge is open, and its On chart button also draws the hedge on the price axis. It is on by default : an open hedge is not something you should have to switch on to notice. Turning it off leaves the deal’s own lines exactly as they were, and the choice is remembered. When there is no hedge the whole section is absent rather than shown empty. And the deals list on the left says so too. A hedged deal wears a HEDGED chip with the hedge’s share of the main beside it, and a combined figure under the row. That second number is the one to read: the dollar amount beside the pair name is the main leg alone , so a pair sitting at −$40 on the main and +$38 on the hedge looks like a $40 loser there while the pair is nearly flat — and it is the combined figure, not the main one, that the paired take profit fires on. Both come from the same calculation this panel uses, so the chip and the panel can never disagree. The percentage is by size , the same unit ratio named above. A hedge whose legs cannot yet be sized shows the chip with no percentage, and a combined figure that has not resolved shows nothing rather than a zero. Four numbers that add up, on purpose. The panel shows Realized + funding (what the hedge has already banked this cycle, funding included), Unrealized · main , Unrealized · hedge , and their total as Combined . Those first three sum to Combined exactly , because all four come from the same calculation the paired take profit itself fires on — not from four separate sums that could quietly disagree. Beside them: both leg sizes, and the hedge as a percentage of the main by size — which is what the hedge ladder itself works in. Note that is a unit ratio: the builder’s hedge-skip rule is measured on the notional share instead, and the two differ whenever the hedge’s average entry differs from your deal’s. The deal card prints both, each named. Where the hedge grows next, and the switch that hides it. The ladder is listed as prices — “60% of the main at 88.00” — and a second button, Ranges , draws those unreached levels on the chart. It is off by default , the opposite of On chart beside it, and for the opposite reason: an open hedge is a fact you should not have to switch on, while a range is a price the ladder might grow to — nothing is placed there and it may never happen. Four of them across one chart is the single busiest thing this screen draws, so you ask for them. The list in this panel is always there either way. Note the anchor: hedge distances are measured from your deal’s blended average , not its original entry, so they move every time a DCA fills . That is the opposite of the DCA ladder on the same screen, and it is deliberate on both sides. A level the hedge has already grown past is not drawn: nothing is waiting there. The one thing on this panel worth reading twice. Each hedge tranche gets a stop, and the stop lives in one of two places. On the exchange it fires whether or not this app is running. In memory it does not — it only fires while the bot is up. That happens when the pair’s conditional-order slots are full (exchanges cap them; Bybit allows ten), and the panel says how many of each you have, warns you by name when any are in memory, and draws them differently on the chart: solid for the exchange, dashed for held by WickHunter , the same shapes used everywhere else here. It tells you why a stop is in memory only when the exchange actually said so — there is more than one reason, and this app does not guess at which. A stop whose location has not been reported at all is counted separately and named as unknown rather than assumed. A tranche with no stop at all yet is called out separately, because that is a different and worse thing than one held in memory. A paused Hedge Bot is flagged too: open tranches are still managed, but the ladder will not grow however far the deal goes.

sections.title: 🧭 Editing a deal’s DCAs
sections.text: 🧭 Editing a deal’s DCAs You can move the DCAs too, and that deal then stops following the bot. Every DCA that has not filled has its own handle. Drag one and the staged bar shows the whole ladder before and after, plus how many resting orders are cancelled and re-placed — all of them , because every DCA is priced off the ladder you just changed and no exchange lets a resting order’s price be edited in place. Distances are measured from the original entry , not the average, which is the same anchor the bot uses. Two things it refuses: a DCA dragged through the current price (it would fill the instant it was placed, at a price you did not choose) and DCAs dragged out of order , which would fill back to front. A DCA that has already filled has no handle at all — that is where money already went. After this, that deal keeps your ladder across restarts and no longer follows the bot’s DCA settings ; every other deal is unaffected. And each DCA has its own size box, which is where the money is. Beside every unfilled DCA is a Size box in dollars. Leave it blank and that DCA follows the bot’s own rule — First DCA multiplied by the volume scale for each step out — and the grey figure in the empty box is what that rule spends, so you can see it without working it out. Type a number and that DCA becomes that many dollars instead. A blank box is not zero and zero is not blank : typing 0 means add nothing at this DCA , so the ladder steps straight over it and carries on to the next one. That is a real instruction rather than a mistake, and the deal says “adds nothing” beside it so it cannot be read as an empty box. A DCA that has already filled shows what it actually cost and cannot be resized — that is money already spent. These controls need a deal, and they say so when there is not one. Manage this deal and the DCA ladder both act on an open deal . If you have typed a pair you do not hold — which is what you do when you want the order ticket — there is no deal to manage, so both panels grey out, empty their boxes and tell you so, and + Add DCA does nothing. That is the point: a DCA belongs to a position, so open one with the ticket first and the ladder appears with it. Previously those boxes kept the last deal’s numbers, which read as though a deal were still selected. Changing a size cancels and re-places, exactly as moving one does. A DCA resting on the exchange carries its quantity there, and no venue here lets that be edited in place — so the staged bar counts every resting DCA as cancelled and re-placed at the new sizes, and shows you that count before you commit. On a venue that cannot rest DCA orders at all nothing is cancelled or placed; the new sizes simply apply as WickHunter fires each one. Sizes and distances travel together : adding or removing a DCA moves the sizes with it, so a size can never end up attached to the DCA next door. As with the distances, once you have typed a size this deal keeps it across restarts and those DCAs no longer follow the bot’s sizing rule. The two-second background refresh does not interrupt a number you are typing. While a Distance or Size box has focus, Terminal keeps that exact field, its value and its caret through passive polling; the number stages when you change or leave the field. A blank Distance is invalid, not zero , so clearing it restores the server-backed ladder instead of quietly staging a DCA at the entry price.

sections.title: 🧾 The order ticket
sections.text: 🧾 The order ticket The order ticket — the one place in this app you place an order yourself. Everything else here is a bot acting on a signal; this is a number you type. It is a separate switch from the rest of the Terminal, so it stays off until it is turned on for you. Pick Buy/Sell , Market or Limit , and a size in dollars, contracts or a percent of balance , and the terminal shows you the exact order first: the quantity after the exchange’s own rounding, the price after its tick, and roughly what it is worth. Send is disabled until that preview succeeds , and sending asks you to confirm the order in words. What it refuses, and why each refusal is money. An order that rounds down below the exchange’s minimum is refused, never rounded up — rounding up would spend more than you asked for — and the refusal names both the floor and what you typed. An order above the exchange’s single-order cap is refused and never split , because the pieces would be orders nothing here can follow. A percent-of-balance size is refused outright when the balance has not been read yet, rather than treated as zero. A reduce-only order is refused when nothing is open, and trimmed to the position when it is larger. And if the price moves between the preview and the press, the order is refused rather than sent at numbers you never saw. You choose which bot looks after the position — and you can give it settings of its own. Managed by lists every bot on that market. The one you pick is the bot the order is placed under, the bot the position lands with, and the bot whose take profit, stop and DCA ladder then run it — so the trade reads as that bot’s on the P&L page afterwards. Bots that cannot take on a new position are still listed, greyed out, each with its own reason (“paused — resume it in My Bots”, “not created on this market”), so you can see what to fix without leaving the ticket. Tick Give this position its own take profit, stop and DCA ladder and you can type them right there: it applies to this position only , it creates no bot, and it never appears in My Bots. Anything you leave blank follows the chosen bot’s own settings — blank is not zero — and how much each DCA spends follows that bot’s ladder rule. Some bot has to be available before you can open — and none is needed to close. A position opened by hand with nothing watching it has no take profit, no stop and no ladder, so if no bot on that market can take one on, the ticket refuses before sending anything and names what each bot needs. It says so on the form before you fill it in, not after you press Send. A reduce-only order is never gated this way: it closes a position rather than opening one, so there is nothing to look after and no bot has to be running for it. You can drag the order onto the chart instead of typing its price. Give the ticket a limit price and a line appears on the chart where that order would sit — against the market, your entry, your DCAs and the book, all of which are right there. Drag that line and the price follows; the number in the box and the line on the chart are always the same thing. It is drawn dotted , like every other plan here, because nothing is resting until you press Send and the exchange accepts it . A market order has no price, so there is no line and nothing to drag, and the ticket says so. Dragging changes where the order is and nothing else: the preview is rebuilt when you let go, Send stays disabled until that preview comes back clean , and if the market moves between the preview and your click the order is still refused rather than sent at a size or price you did not approve. The handle is offered even when you have no open deal , which is the case it is most useful in. If the ticket is not on your screen, it is switched off, and the page now says so. Opening a position by hand is a separate switch from the rest of the Terminal — everything else (managing, closing, re‑laddering) works without it. Where the ticket would be you will see “not enabled on this install” rather than nothing at all, which is what it used to show. Two other things must also be true before an order that opens can be sent: at least one bot on that market has to be able to take the position on (see Managed by above), and for a market order the pair must be one this account is actively pricing. A limit order works either way, and a reduce-only order needs no bot at all. Each of those refusals is written out in the ticket in full.

sections.title: 🛑 Your stop loss
sections.text: 🛑 Your stop loss Your stop is now a real order on the exchange, where the venue can hold one. Until v0.88.0 the stop was a monitor and nothing else: the bot watched the price and closed at market on touch, so a stopped bot meant no stop at all — a deploy, a crash or an outage left the position unprotected. It now rests a genuine reduce‑only stop order on Bybit, Bitget, Bitunix and AsterDex, which fires whether or not this app is running. Three things still fall back to the old monitor, and the deal names which on its card and on your notifier: a venue that cannot hold one, a venue that refuses this position’s size, and a pair where the Hedge Bot is using every conditional slot the exchange allows (Bybit permits ten). The hedge always wins that contest — taking a slot from it would demote a hedge stop on every symbol on the box — and while a hedge is open it owns the exit anyway, so the deal’s own stop is suspended exactly as it always was. The monitor is never switched off just because an order is resting: if the exchange were to drop that order silently, the bot is still watching. Where to see which you have. Every deal shows its stop on its own card, and the Terminal draws it on the price axis: solid when it is resting on the exchange, dashed when WickHunter is only watching. A change either way is sent to your notifications once, in both directions — the first time a stop simply lands where it should, nothing is said, because that is the normal state and announcing it would be one message per open deal. Every loss of protection, and every recovery, is still loud. The size unit names the coin. The three size modes are $ , the coin itself and % balance . The middle one is labelled with the pair’s own base asset — BTC on BTCUSDT, SOL on SOLUSDT — so what you are about to buy is named rather than left as the word “contracts”. On a pair whose base coin cannot be read it stays Contracts instead of guessing: a wrong unit on an order ticket is a wrong order.

sections.title: 🔌 Connecting an exchange account
sections.text: 🔌 Connecting an exchange account Every venue asks for a slightly different credential, and one of them recently changed what it will issue. These are the differences worth knowing before you stand at the Connect screen. Aster asks for three things, and they are all on one page. Aster stopped issuing V1 API keys on 25 March 2026 and Wick Hunter no longer speaks V1 at all, so there is nothing left to choose: the only credential is an API wallet , created at asterdex.com → API wallet on the “Pro API” tab. The form asks for it in the venue’s own words: the API wallet address (0x…, 40 hex characters), the API wallet private key (0x…, 64 hex, and it is shown once — if it was not saved, make a new API wallet, because it cannot be re-read), and your master account wallet address — the wallet you log in to Aster with. If you are looking for an “API key” or an “API secret” on that page, you will not find one; those were V1’s words. The master wallet address is required, and it is not bookkeeping. Aster counts its order limit per account , and one master wallet can hold several API wallets. That address is the only thing that says which account a given API wallet belongs to, so it is what lets Wick Hunter pace all of your Aster wallets together instead of letting each one aim at the whole allowance. It is never sent with a trading request — it is used to group your own wallets and nothing else. Pasting the API wallet address into this box by mistake is refused by name: both are valid addresses and the private key still matches the signer, so nothing else could catch it, and the cost would be silent. Rotating an Aster key, and filling the master wallet in later. If you connected Aster before the master wallet address became a required field, that box is empty on your account — and until v0.88.26 rotating the key pair was refused for it, from a screen that had nowhere to type one. That is fixed in two ways. Edit account now shows the master account wallet address for Aster, prefilled with whatever is stored, and you can fill it in on its own — no key rotation needed, nothing else touched. And a rotation is no longer refused when the box is empty: the address is never sent with a trading request, so the key still works without it. What you lose is the shared order lane — Aster counts its order limit per account, so without that address this API wallet is paced on its own rather than alongside your other Aster wallets. The save tells you so in as many words. What is still refused, because it is wrong rather than missing: an address that is not 40 hex characters, and your API wallet address pasted into the master box. Both now point at the box to fix. What connecting actually checks. Each market you tick is validated separately against the venue, and a market that fails is left out of the run plan until you fix its permission and save again. On Aster the check goes further than reading a balance: it reads the venue’s own canTrade flag, so a read-only credential is stored with a plain ⛔ TRADING IS BLOCKED line on the account instead of validating green and refusing your first order hours later, on a live position. Nothing places a test order to find out. It also reports whether the account is in Hedge Mode , which every bot here needs before its first exposure on a pair. If any of that comes back with a ⚠, the account still saves; the warning is on the card so you can fix it on the exchange and revalidate. On Bybit, a key’s READ-ONLY flag outranks its permission boxes. A Bybit API key can show every permission ticked — ContractTrade , Spot , Derivatives — and still be marked read-only , and that one flag switches all of them off. The venue then answers every read perfectly normally, so balances, positions and prices all look right, while it refuses every order , leverage change and account setting with 10005 Permission denied . Before v0.89.12 Wick Hunter reported such a key as “ContractTrade permission verified” and the bots ran for hours accepting entries without ever placing one — which looks exactly like a quiet market. It is now refused when you add it , by name, and no account is created. Create a new API key on Bybit with read-only not selected and connect that one; ticking the permission boxes on a read-only key does not help. Demo accounts. Bybit (Demo Trading) and Bitget (paper trading) can be connected as a demo account instead of your real one — pick Demo on the Environment control when adding the account; it only appears for a venue that has one. The key must be created inside that venue’s own demo environment , not your live account — a real key will not authenticate against it. Market data, klines and the liquidation feed always come from the real, live exchange ; only orders, positions and P&L stay on the demo account. A demo account is a separate account in the picker, labelled DEMO , and never mixes with your real one. Licence extensions install themselves. When the hub extends your licence, the bot picks the new key up at its next check-in, verifies it, and shows the new expiry under Settings → License . There is nothing to paste and nothing to reinstall.

sections.title: Wallet and equity history
sections.text: Wallet and equity history The Home chart can show Equity or Wallet balance for the selected account, with the same USDT / USD and 3h / Week controls. The choice is remembered in this browser. Hover the line, or tap it on a phone, to read the value and time of the nearest real sample. The small CSV button exports the series currently selected; a missing wallet reading stays an empty cell. Each account keeps its own seven-day history across restarts. Week samples are saved every five minutes; wallet history begins when this build first records a real wallet reading, and missing readings remain gaps rather than being replaced with equity or zero. A new series needs two adjacent real samples before a line appears.

sections.title: 💵 Reading the P&L page
sections.text: 💵 Reading the P&L page Exchanges do not all publish the same things about a trade they have settled. Where one of them publishes less, this page shows less rather than filling the gap in for you. Every day on this page is a UTC day — the same day the header’s Day P&L tile and the exchange count. USDT / USD — the equity basis switch. The Wallet and Equity tiles can read the exchange’s actual USDT coin balance or its unified-account USD value , and the two differ on an account holding other collateral. The USDT side is offered only where the exchange publishes an exact USDT figure; where it does not, the button is disabled and says so rather than converting one into the other. Dashes in Recently closed , and where the figures come from. The caption beside Recently closed names the exchange the numbers were settled by — the one your header is on. Some exchanges publish a closed trade as a position (quantity, entry price, exit price and profit on one record) and some publish only the money . Aster is the second kind: its account-wide history carries the realised profit and the pair, and no size, no entry and no exit at all. Where a figure was never published this app now prints — rather than 0 : a zero would be the app telling you the trade had no size and both its prices were zero, which is not true. The profit column is unaffected — that figure is real and is the exchange’s own. On Aster those dashes now fill in by themselves. This app reads that account’s individual fills and rebuilds each position from them: from flat, through every DCA and partial close, back to flat. A position it can rebuild becomes one row with a real side, size, average entry, average exit, DCA count, opened time and duration — and the several ledger lines it was built from stop appearing as separate trades. Its profit also becomes the wallet’s figure rather than the ledger’s: the ledger cannot attach an opening order’s fee to anything, so it reads slightly more profitable than your balance did. A position it cannot yet rebuild is left exactly as it was — the ledger line, with its dashes — because a half-guessed trade row is worse than an honest one. That happens while a pair still has a position open, while its fill history has not been walked back far enough, or when a fee could not be read; the coverage note below says which. Nothing here is invented : an opened time is the moment of the first fill that opened the position, or the cell keeps saying not reported . A close whose exact figure has to be rebuilt, and the Discord message that waits for it. After a deal closes, this app checks its own record against the exchange’s and reconciles the two — and it does not announce a close until it has a figure the exchange published. On an exchange whose closed record does not say which side the trade was ( Aster ), that match can never be made against that record; earlier builds gave up there, which meant an Aster close could be real, visible on the venue, and produce no Discord message at all . It is now rebuilt instead, from the account’s own fill history , which does carry the side, the exit price and every fee — so the close is reported with a figure that is still entirely the exchange’s. Nothing is invented either way. “Closed — reconciling” is one message, not the first of two. If the fill history proves the position went flat before its fees and funding have finished settling, Discord gets a card that says Closed — reconciling and carries no number — because there is not yet an honest one to print. That same card is then edited in place the moment the exact figure lands. You will not get a second message, and you do not need to go looking for one. Discord alerts are also delivered rather than fired and forgotten now: if Discord is rate-limiting, down, or the app restarts mid-send, the message is retried until Discord acknowledges it, and a webhook Discord refuses outright (deleted, or its token revoked) is recorded as undelivered rather than retried silently for ever. Turning Deal closed off in Notifications is still the only thing that stops a close alert. ⚠ “History incomplete”, and why the warning exists. On most exchanges this app downloads the account’s whole closed-trade history in the background, and while that sync is unfinished a one-line amber note says how far back the table reaches. Some exchanges publish only a recent ledger and no way to page back through the account’s past — on those the table can only ever hold the trades this app has seen since it started watching, and the note says “recent ledger only” with the date of the oldest row it holds. Aster is the special case, and it now reads differently. Its closed-trade endpoint really is only a ledger, so instead this app walks each traded pair’s own fill history backwards until it reaches the pair’s first ever trade. Until that walk joins up, the note says how many of your traded pairs are done — and those pairs’ trades are already whole. When every pair is walked the note disappears , because at that point the table really is the account. It appears above the trade table, beside the range buttons whenever the selected range (including All , which then reads “all synced history”) reaches further back than the rows do, and as a final # coverage line in the CSV export. WEEX has a bounded import instead ; see WEEX P&L history below.

sections.title: ⏪ Replay — walk back through one deal
sections.text: ⏪ Replay — walk back through one deal Every closed trade on the P&L page has a Replay button (an open deal is replayed once it closes). It opens the deal on its own chart with a slider above it: drag it and the tiles beside the chart (under it on a phone) show what the deal looked like at that minute — position size, average entry, take-profit and stop, the hedge (if one acted), and the unrealized and realized P&L for the main leg, the hedge, and both combined. Play steps through on its own; the arrow keys step one minute; the event buttons beside the slider jump straight to the next DCA, hedge action or close instead of stepping through every quiet minute between them, and the Entry / TP & SL / DCA / Hedge / What-if chips above the chart hide any of those lines and markers, remembered for next time. A row of dots under the transport marks every event at a glance — click one to jump straight to it — and All events , collapsed below the chart, lists every event with its exact time; open it and click a row to jump the same way. The replay is built from what this app recorded for this exact deal: the open, every DCA and partial-close fill, every take-profit and stop placement or move at its own exact price, the hedge opening and closing, and the close — each with its own price, quantity and time. A deal opened before this recording started, or older than 30 days, reads “Replay unavailable” instead of a button. Anything the replay could not recover is listed under the chart rather than guessed. What if… The card under the figures keeps its result and Apply at the top; the Exit group is open, and the DCA and Hedge groups sit collapsed behind one line that shows their current values — open one to edit it. Press Apply and the same deal is re-run against the same candles, the result is drawn over the chart in a muted colour, the What-if chip switches on and the slider rewinds to the start, with one line saying whether it would have closed earlier or later and for how much. Slippage is applied against you on stops, hedge fills and market closes, never on take-profit or DCA orders that rest at their price. Under the result, the line names the worst drawdown along the way, how big the hedge got, the fees, and, for a what-if still open at the end, how close it came to its take-profit. The starting numbers are the dials the deal opened with , closed deals included — every deal now keeps its own recorded config. A DCA size is shown in the unit the bot uses (dollars, % of balance or % of entry) with its dollar value beside it, and a hedge level carries its own optional Max w/o stop cap. A cleared stop box means no stop, and only the boxes you actually change are sent — everything else keeps running on the bot’s own numbers. Hedge on turns the hedge off for the run, or back on with whatever dials you set; it is disabled when no Hedge Bot manages this pair. A deal that ran the DCA builder ladder shows an editable table instead of the dial boxes — add, edit or remove a level and Apply re-runs the ladder exactly as edited; an ATR-priced level is re-priced against this deal’s own candles at the moment it opened, so changing its multiplier changes where it rests.

sections.title: WEEX P&L history
sections.text: WEEX P&L history WEEX lets the app request up to 365 days of fills. The import starts automatically, saves its progress across restarts, and retries unavailable reads after five minutes. Downloaded older records stay on this installation even after they leave the exchange’s API window. The history note states how far the import has reached. Completing the available window does not prove an account’s entire lifetime. A position is reconstructed from its opening fills, DCA fills and closes; missing boundaries or funding evidence remain unresolved rather than being guessed. Private position, order and fill events appear in Activity → WebSocket stream. A close event triggers a fresh account check before cleanup; it cannot retire a reopened position by itself. Background history yields to live account reads , and API budget shows WEEX’s shared counters .

sections.title: ⚡ The Liq Scalper — what it is
sections.text: ⚡ The Liq Scalper — what it is A forced liquidation dumps someone's contracts onto the market at whatever price it can get, and the print shows up on a public feed.
