The Liq Scalper takes the other side — buying the panic sell, selling the panic buy — but only while price is already stretched an unusual distance from its own recent volume-weighted average, so it fades an overshoot rather than stepping in front of a trend. A DCA ladder, a take-profit and an optional stop loss then manage the deal to its exit. Run it if you believe forced selling overshoots and snaps back, and you can fund a ladder that averages down while you wait. Do not run it if you need every trade to have a tight, known maximum loss — its default shape is a deep ladder and no stop, and a trending market keeps filling that ladder. The two gates Both must be true at the same instant. Neither alone opens anything. A liquidation printed , big enough to clear your minimum, on the side you want to fade. Longs liquidated = forced selling , which a long entry wants. Shorts liquidated = forced buying , which a short entry wants. Price is outside the band — far enough from the fair-value line to look like an overshoot. A liquidation that prints while price is inside the band does nothing at all. Where the numbers come from. A liquidation print tells this bot one thing only: which coin . The price, the fair-value line, the band edges, the order size and the order itself all come from the real listing on the exchange and market this bot trades. Example: a Binance print about SOL can wake the bot, but the bot then reads its own venue's SOL contract and trades that. If its market has no live listing for that coin, the print is dropped.

sections.title: 🧩 Main — name, side, and how many deals
sections.text: 🧩 Main — name, side, and how many deals The top block of the form: which direction this bot may trade, and how many deals it may hold at once. Name — a label on the My Bots card and in Activity, with no effect on any trading decision. Example: "Alt shorts — slow band". Get it wrong: blank, and the form refuses to save and jumps you back to the top. Exchange · account — read-only; it follows the header at the top of the app. Get it wrong: editing a bot while the header points at a different account edits the bot you were looking at, not the one running elsewhere — check the form title before you save. Market — also from the header. A USDT-futures Liq Scalper reads only USDT perpetual listings, a USDC one only USDC perpetuals, a coin-margined one only coin-margined perpetuals. There is no Liq Scalper on Spot: Spot has no perpetual contract to execute against. Get it wrong: a bot cannot move between markets — delete it and create a new one. Direction — Long fades dumps, Short fades pumps, Both takes either. It is a hard filter: a short-only bot ignores every long setup and does not even log a "considered it" row. It also changes the form — a short-only bot hides the Long band and Max longs boxes. Get it wrong: picking the single side the market then trends against is the most expensive mistake on this form. Both with small caps is the safer start if you have no view. Max longs — the most long deals held at once; visible when Direction is Long or Both. Example: at 2, a third qualifying signal is skipped and logged "Max longs open" until one closes. Get it wrong: too high and one market-wide flush opens six correlated alt longs that go offside together, each with a full ladder under it. At 1 you sit out most of what the bot exists to take. Max shorts — the same ceiling for shorts; visible when Direction is Short or Both. Example: 2 with Direction Short means two short deals is the whole budget. Max both — the combined ceiling, shown only when Direction is Both . Example: Max longs 2, Max shorts 2, Max both 3 → 2 longs and 1 short, or 1 long and 2 shorts, never 4 deals. Get it wrong: above Max longs + Max shorts it is dead weight, because the per-side caps bind first; at 1 you have a one-deal-at-a-time bot whatever the per-side numbers say. These count deals, not pairs, and a deal still being placed already holds its slot. Five signals in the same second cannot all sneak through a cap of two. The ceiling actually in force is the LOWER of two numbers — the account's own open-deal cap and the total of the enabled bots' caps on that account — and the form now names which of the two is binding. Get it wrong: raising a bot's cap changes nothing while the account cap is the smaller one, and the line under the box is what tells you so. Two more ceilings live outside this form. The Accounts page has a per-market deal cap shared by every bot on that market, and an Isolation mode percentage that blocks new entries once used margin reaches it. The lowest ceiling is the one that stops you. Isolation mode never closes anything and never stops an existing ladder filling — it refuses new deals only.

sections.title: 🎯 Pairs — which coins this bot is allowed to trade
sections.text: 🎯 Pairs — which coins this bot is allowed to trade Pair criteria are grouped into Volume , Funding , Volatility and Market limits . Groups with active or incomplete rules open when you load a bot; groups whose rules are off start collapsed. The summary shows active and incomplete counts. Open a group to edit its controls or read its help. Collapsing a group never disables a rule or changes its saved value; use the rule’s switch or documented off value. The watch set. A liquidation on a coin outside it is ignored completely — no decision, no log row. This section is the most common reason a bot looks "asleep". Pair selection: Auto — by filters / Manual list — Auto builds the watch set from the rules below and keeps rebuilding it; Manual list discards every rule and trades exactly the coins you name. Get it wrong: in Manual you own every judgement the filters were making — a delisting-bound coin, or one whose exchange maximum leverage is below yours, sits in your list until you remove it. Manual also hides the filter panel, so a filter you spent an hour tuning is no longer running. Blacklist — coins this bot never touches, in both Auto and Manual mode. Separate them with commas or spaces; they are stored in capitals. Example: LUNAUSDT, HMSTRUSDT — the two the app ships with. Get it wrong: empty is a real choice, not a neutral one — the filters below judge liquidity and volatility, not whether a coin is a rug you distrust. A second, platform-wide blacklist under Settings applies to every bot at once. Volatility Filters — optional rows combining a candle timeframe, a maximum low-to-high move, and how many closed candles to inspect. The forming candle is never judged. Example: 1d / 10% / 10 inspects ten completed daily candles separately and excludes a coin if any one moved more than 10%; it is not the coin's cumulative ten-day move. 1d / 60% / 30 applies the former 30-day rule. Every row runs and any one can exclude; delete every row to turn volatility filtering off. Existing 4-hour and 30-day settings are converted into these visible, removable rows automatically when you upgrade. Min max limit order · pair's cap on ONE order — drops pairs whose ceiling for a single limit order , on the exchange this bot trades , is below your figure. It measures one order, not a position. A laddered deal is many orders, and the venue's ceiling on a whole position is a different number (its risk-limit tier) that this app does not read — so this box cannot promise your full deal will fit. Example: at 15,000 USDT, a pair capped at $8,000 an order is excluded. Min max market order · pair's cap on ONE order — the same for a market order. Example: at 5,000 USDT, a pair that only accepts $2,000 market orders is excluded. Get it wrong: too low and a pair passes that cannot swallow your biggest DCA level or your exit in one go. Max funding rate · absolute, either direction — the rent for holding a perpetual, measured per 8-hour funding interval . "Absolute" because a rate against you costs the same whichever sign it carries. Example: at 0.10% with funding every 8 hours, the worst case is three charges a day — about 0.3% of notional per day, or 9% a month; on a $1,000 position, $3 a day for as long as you hold it. Not every coin funds every 8 hours: a coin charging 0.09% every four hours costs twice what one charging 0.09% every eight does. Every pair is converted to its 8-hour equivalent before being compared, so the 4-hour coin above is judged as 0.18% and excluded — the "Filtered out" panel shows the raw rate, its real interval and the converted figure. Get it wrong: too generous and a slow-recovering deal bleeds more in funding than the 1.2% take-profit would ever make. Too tight and you exclude the volatile coins that pay you to be on the right side. Which exchange these numbers come from — every rule in this section is judged against the exchange this bot trades on , and nothing else. Leverage ceilings, order-size caps and funding rates all differ between venues; a "Filtered out" row names the exchange whose number excluded it wherever a number was involved. Where an exchange does not publish something a filter needs — Bitunix and Bitget carry no usable listing date, and the ST badge and delisting feed are Bybit's own — that filter does not run there and its box is not shown at all , chips included; your stored setting is untouched and returns if you connect an exchange that can serve it. A grey line above the filters names what is running here, what is on last-known data, and what is not available. The one thing that is still Bybit's everywhere is the liquidation signal itself, which is deliberate: Bybit has the only unsampled public liquidation feed, and price, VWMA and every order still come from the exchange you trade. Which pairs are even considered — the list starts as your exchange's own catalogue , filtered by the rules above on its own numbers. A coin Bybit lists and your exchange does not is not part of your universe and appears nowhere on this page. Off switches — Min leverage, Min max limit order, Min max market order, Max funding rate, Min 24h rolling volume and Minimum coin market cap each carry their own small on/off switch beside the label. Off greys the box and stops that one rule judging any pair, whatever number is still sitting in it — the figure is kept, not cleared, so switching back on restores exactly what you had typed. Every install ships with all six on, matching every stored config today.

sections.title: 🌪 Pairs — Volatility Filters
sections.text: 🌪 Pairs — Volatility Filters One optional list covers every timeframe, including 4h and 1d. Existing 4-hour and 30-day settings appear as ordinary removable rows. Empty means off. What one row means — a row is a timeframe , a Max move and an Over last count. Each of the last N closed candles is judged on its own, and the coin is excluded if any single one swung more than your percent from its low to its high. Exact example: 1d / 10% / 10 inspects ten completed daily candles separately. One 10.1% candle excludes; ten quiet candles whose combined change is 10.1% do not, and an exact 10.0% candle does not because the test is more than . Direction never matters: a collapse and a squeeze are both measured by their candle range. Every rule runs, and any one of them can exclude — the rows are independent and are never ranked, which is why they carry no numbers. A coin has to clear all of them plus every other filter on this page. Adding a row can only shrink the watch set; deleting a row disables that test. Timeframes — 1m, 3m, 5m, 15m, 30m, 1h, 2h, 3h, 4h, 6h, 8h, 12h and 1d. Minute rows cost more public candle reads, so they are paced behind trading requests and may visibly warm across a broad pair universe. The former Max 4h rule is represented as a 4h row. The former Max 30d rule is represented exactly as 1d / your limit / 30 . Those migrated rows can be deleted like any other row. A blank box is not a zero, and here that matters more than anywhere else on the form — on Max move , 0% would exclude every candle with any range at all and therefore every coin on the exchange. Typing 0 is refused with those words. Delete the row to switch that rule off. A box you have simply not filled in yet is inert and refuses nothing. A half-finished row is refused when you save, by what you typed — Volatility filter "1h / 25%" , never "row 2", because deleting a row above would renumber it. A row with nothing in it is fine and is simply dropped when you save: you are allowed to press ＋ Add filter and then save something else. The dangerous shape is the one that reads as configured and can never fire, and that is the one you are stopped on. Four rows, and one shared request budget — each pair pays only for the exact timeframe and deepest usable candle count required by the automatic bot that owns it; the app does not multiply every bot's rules across every bot's pairs. Accounts using the same public endpoint share one bounded lane, including cold-start credit, so creating another context cannot mint another burst. If a broad short-timeframe roster needs more reads per minute than that lane can sustain, the excess pair/timeframe rows fail closed and name the required and available rates. The ＋ Add filter button still stops at four configured rows. Cold, warming or stale means no new exposure — a rule asking for 30 candles of a 12-hour timeframe needs fifteen days of history before it can answer honestly, and judging it on six would understate the move. On a fresh boot or newly admitted pair it says warming up — 6/30 candles ; a window past its closed-candle boundary stays usable for one more candle while its refresh is queued, then says the candles are stale. A pair that has not measured an exclusion stays eligible while it warms. A pair already excluded keeps its last measured candles and reason while direct reads continue, then re-enters automatically when it passes or you delete the rule instead of restarting cold. Neither missing nor old data is treated as a pass. An already-held position keeps being managed. Warming pairs are counted, not listed — a daily row's boundary is the same instant for every coin at once, so on the pass after a daily close the whole list is warming together. Closest to trigger would then be a page of pairs reading refused for the one reason that is about to fix itself, so those rows are left out and one line under the rail says how many there are, at which timeframe, how much of the list is already measured, and when the next candle closes. The same line sits on the bot's own card in My Bots . A pair an actual rule excluded keeps its row and its reason — that is the filter working, and it is what explains a coin you expected to trade. Warm-up and recovery remain visible in Activity and on the bot card, without sending Discord notifications. It never touches a position you already hold — an open deal keeps its DCA ladder, its take-profit and its stop whatever the price does. Only new exposure is refused, a second stacked deal on a coin you already hold included. And if you list your pairs by hand this list is not applied : an allowlist is your scope, and the whole criteria panel is hidden beside one. The filter candles come directly from the exchange this bot trades on — at that exchange's own timeframes; where it does not publish one, the app folds exact finer candles and never substitutes a different timeframe or another venue. Depth is part of the cache key: an unsupported 500-candle request cannot make another bot's valid 10-candle rule at the same timeframe look unsupported. The Hub can warm a window, and the exchange still confirms it. Where a signed Hub snapshot covers this exchange at your rule's timeframe and depth, it fills the windows that have none — which is what stops a daily rule leaving every pair unjudged for minutes after a rollover or a restart. Those windows are marked awaiting venue confirmation in the browser console, and each one is re-read from this exchange within about a minute; if the two ever disagree, the exchange's own candles win and the disagreement is recorded. A Hub that is absent, unreachable or unsigned changes nothing at all: the windows warm from the exchange exactly as they did before. On an exchange that cannot serve the rule, the block is hidden while the stored rows remain. The Optimized Liquidation bot has its own copy of this list , on its own form, judged on its own pairs. Setting a row here does not set one there.

sections.title: Volatility windows — Hub retries
sections.text: Volatility windows — Hub retries While requested volatility windows remain missing or stale, the app retries the Hub every five minutes, including when a snapshot supplied only some pairs. Retries stop once the exchange has filled those windows. Keep the Hub updated so incomplete snapshots can refresh within that interval. Warm-up and recovery stay visible in Activity and on the bot card without Discord notifications. Missing data still blocks new exposure; existing positions keep being managed.

sections.title: 📊 Pairs — the 24-hour rolling volume floor
sections.text: 📊 Pairs — the 24-hour rolling volume floor Min 24h rolling volume · blank or 0 = off; ships off — a liquidity floor, in USDT, read from the exchange you actually trade . “Rolling” is the point: it is the last 24 hours counted backwards from now, not a figure that resets at midnight UTC — five minutes after a UTC reset those two numbers differ by roughly 288x, and a filter that quietly meant one on one exchange and the other elsewhere would be worthless. Every figure is checked three ways before it is used: the pair’s quote asset must really be USDT (read from the exchange’s own instrument record, never guessed from the symbol), the volume divided by the coins traded must land inside that pair’s own 24-hour high and low (which is what catches a venue publishing coins where we expected dollars), and the window must be the rolling 24 hours. Where the number comes from: Bybit turnover24h , Bitunix quoteVol , Bitget usdtVolume , Aster quoteVolume — Pair info shows the field, how old it is, and whether the exchange states the rolling window in its own documentation or we inferred it. On BloFin the box is not shown at all: it publishes no exact USDT volume, and multiplying coins traded by the current price would be a made-up number on a screen you are about to risk money on. This is the one filter that refuses rather than steps aside: switch it on and a pair whose volume this app cannot read is refused a NEW entry, by name, instead of being entered blind. It is asked twice: when the pair list is rebuilt, and again at the moment of the trade. The pair list is rebuilt on the schedule you set (an hour by default, and never at all if you set it to 0), so between rebuilds a pair can fall below your floor and still be on the list — and a pair you are holding stays on it deliberately, so the deal keeps being managed. Asking again at the trade is what stops a NEW deal opening on one. It never touches a position you already hold — an open deal keeps its DCA ladder, its take-profit and its stop whatever the volume does; only new exposure is refused, including a second stacked deal on a pair you already hold. If you list your pairs by hand, this box is not applied — an allowlist is your scope, and the whole criteria panel is hidden beside one, so nothing here is judging a pair you typed yourself. Refused for thin volume and refused because the figure could not be read look different on screen: the closest-to-trigger list prints the pair’s own number against your floor in the first case, and says the figure is unavailable or stale — with its age — in the second. A starting point, not a recommendation: many operators use the larger of $250,000 and 100x their biggest planned deal. Nothing is filled in for you.

sections.title: 🪙 Pairs — the coin market cap floor
sections.text: 🪙 Pairs — the coin market cap floor Minimum coin market cap · blank or 0 = off; ships blank — trade only coins at or above a size. The box is a plain USD figure and takes the same shorthand as Min 24h rolling volume above it : 250M , 0.25B , 250000000 and 250,000,000 all mean the same thing, the line underneath reads back = $250,000,000 USD , and that is what gets saved. Anything this app cannot read is refused by name rather than guessed at. (It was denominated in millions until 24 Aug 2026, which is why it had to refuse a k/M/B suffix — in a box already meaning millions, 1.5M could be $1.5 million or $1.5 trillion. In plain USD there is only one reading, so the shorthand is safe and the box beside it no longer parses the same text a different way. Your saved figure did not change; only how it is written on screen.) There is no maximum any more. It is the COIN’s market cap, not the exchange’s — nothing to do with the position and order limits on the Accounts page, which are about how much of your own money one order may commit. Where it comes from: a signed snapshot that names, for every contract on every exchange, which coin it tracks, that coin’s id at the data provider, the figure, the provider and the time it was measured. Nothing is guessed from the symbol; a contract quoted in thousands of a coin is matched to that coin explicitly, and its market cap is the coin’s either way. With the box blank nothing is judged and your pair list is exactly what it was — no request is even made. When a floor is set this rule refuses rather than steps aside , and that is deliberate: an older version of this filter failed open and quietly stopped filtering, which is worse than no filter. A pair is refused a NEW entry, by name, when the coin cannot be identified, when two contracts could be the same ticker, when the provider does not track the coin at all, when two providers disagree, when the figure is more than fifteen minutes old, or when the contract is not a coin (an index, a commodity, a tokenised stock). A figure this app does not have reads “unknown”, never $0 — a made-up zero would sort as the smallest coin in the market and read as a fact. CoinGecko fallback figures are never used: a fallback is not the primary provider’s number, and a pair whose only figure is one is refused like any other unverified pair. The tick-box that used to admit them is gone — which provider is good enough is decided by the hub that publishes the figures, not per bot. It never touches a position you already hold — an open deal keeps its DCA ladder, its take-profit and its stop whatever the market cap does; only new exposure is refused, including a second stacked deal on a pair you already hold. It is asked twice , when the pair list is rebuilt and again at the moment of the trade, so a pair that drifts out of your band between rebuilds cannot open a new deal. If you list your pairs by hand this box is not applied — an allowlist is your scope. Nothing is filled in for you.

sections.title: ⚖️ Pairs — the leverage floor, and what it means per exchange
sections.text: ⚖️ Pairs — the leverage floor, and what it means per exchange One rule, and the one most likely to cost you margin quietly if it is set below your own leverage. Min leverage · pair must support — the pair's maximum leverage on the exchange this bot trades must be at least this, as a proxy for a listing that exchange takes seriously. Example: at 12, a coin the venue caps at 10× is excluded; one it allows to 50× is fine. Get it wrong: set this at or above your own Leverage. Run 25× against a Min leverage of 12 and the bot enters pairs the exchange caps at 12× — the exchange keeps its lower number, so you use twice the margin you planned. At 50 the watch set narrows to a handful of majors. On Aster this ceiling is an account figure, not a public one; until your own leverage-bracket read lands the rule steps aside rather than guess. It is also a figure about a position size there: Aster publishes a ladder of notional bands, and the leverage it allows falls as the position grows. So the number this rule judges a pair on is the one that applies at the largest this bot’s deal can get — your base order plus the whole DCA ladder, not the first entry. Get it wrong: read it at the smallest band and a pair passes on a ceiling the exchange withdraws the moment your ladder fills, which is the same lost margin as running above the cap in the first place. If nothing on the market states a readable order size and ladder, the rule says so and stops judging rather than fall back to the smallest band.

sections.title: 🗂️ Pairs — refreshing the list, the category switches and the read-only panels
sections.text: 🗂️ Pairs — refreshing the list, the category switches and the read-only panels The rest of the Pairs section: how often the watch set is rebuilt, the classes of listing you can exclude in one tick, and the panels that report what the rules did. Auto-refresh — how often the pair list is rebuilt from scratch, in minutes. Example: 60 re-runs the filters hourly; a coin that just breached a volatility row drops out at the next pass and a newly qualifying coin joins. 0 turns rebuilding off; 1–9 is raised to the minimum of 10. Get it wrong: at 0 the watch set goes stale and you trade yesterday's verdicts. Very short intervals only add exchange requests — these are slow-moving facts. Refresh now — a button, not a setting: rebuilds immediately and reports how many pairs came out. Use it after changing a filter to see the effect before you save. Exclude categories — tick to remove a whole class of listing: Main (regular crypto) , Innovation Zone , Stock , Commodity , Forex , Pre-Market , New listing (≤30d) . None are excluded by default. Example: ticking New listing (≤30d) keeps the bot off freshly listed coins with no price history. Get it wrong: ticking Main (regular crypto) removes almost everything you wanted — that is the category the majors live in. The six tier chips are Bybit accounts only — no other exchange here publishes a tier, so they are hidden elsewhere rather than lit and enforcing nothing. New listing (≤30d) needs a listing date , not a tier, and also runs on Aster . Two of the seven are worth knowing about even on Bybit: Pre-Market contracts are excluded unconditionally whatever you tick, because they are not yet trading; and a listing tier Bybit adds in future is not swept into an exclusion you never chose. Delisted — excludes contracts the exchange has announced it is retiring. On by default, with little reason to change it: a delisting coin is force-closed at the exchange's chosen moment, not yours. Bybit accounts only — no other exchange this app supports publishes a delisting feed, so the chip is not shown there. ST-tagged — excludes coins the exchange flags special-treatment, its own warning label for a troubled listing. On by default. It is read from the same feed Bybit's own futures screen reads , so the verdict matches the ST badge you see there. That is a change: the app used to take Bybit's spot ST flag and match it across to the perpetual by base coin, which could not see a perpetual whose coin has no Bybit spot listing at all, and disagreed with the futures badge in both directions. The spot join survives only as a fallback for a contract the futures feed does not mention. Bybit accounts only — ST is a Bybit designation with no equivalent elsewhere, so the chip is not shown on other exchanges. Pairs to trade · Manual list only — the picker that replaces the filter panel in Manual mode; search and click to add. Pairs whose maximum leverage on the exchange this bot trades is below your Leverage setting are dimmed, skipped by Select all, and block the save with a message naming the exchange, the pairs and their real maximum there. A pair that exchange publishes no maximum for shows ?× and does not block: the app invents no limit, and the entry itself is refused at order time rather than opened at a leverage nobody could confirm. Get it wrong: an empty list means the bot watches nothing and never trades. Filtered out — read-only: every pair one of your rules rejected, with the rule named. Only rules appear here: a pair your exchange does not list is not in the universe at all, and a pair with no Bybit liquidation feed has its own panel. The first place to look when a coin you expected never appears. Why pairs are being filtered while every criteria box is empty — a bot nobody has configured on this account opens with every number blank, on purpose: a blank box is sent as "clear this" and the save names it, so a value you did not choose can never be frozen as if you had typed it. The universe is still carved in the meantime, on the numbers stored for this account — so an amber line above the criteria (and above Filtered out ) states exactly which ones, rather than leaving you to guess from the rejection rows. Type your own and save to make them yours; the amber line then goes. No liquidation coverage — pairs your exchange lists that Bybit does not. Bybit runs the only unsampled public liquidation feed and this bot enters on a liquidation print, so those pairs have no trigger whatever their numbers look like. It is not a filter verdict — none of your criteria touched them, and no filter change will admit them — which is why they are kept out of "Filtered out". A TradingView bot can still trade them, because it does not wait for a liquidation. The panel is absent on a Bybit account, where it is always empty. Not subscribed — read-only and normally empty. Every pair passing your filters gets a live price feed automatically; rows appear only if this installation was given a deliberately smaller watch limit, which loosening your filters will not change. Pair info — a lookup box for any coin on the exchange you trade, watched or not: funding rate and interval, maximum leverage, exchange order caps, snapshot price, and why it is or is not in the watch set. Every figure is that exchange's own; a field it does not publish says so instead of borrowing another exchange's number. Data that genuinely needs a live subscription reads as unavailable rather than as a misleading zero. A pair you are already in is never dropped mid-deal. If a coin stops passing your filters while you hold a position, the deal keeps its ladder, take-profit and stop until it closes normally. The filter governs new entries only.

sections.title: 🎚️ Signal — the liquidation trigger and the entry band
sections.text: 🎚️ Signal — the liquidation trigger and the entry band The Signal — liquidation trigger block inside Entry orders. These decide when the bot fires, not how much it bets. Change one at a time and give it real market hours before you judge it. Min liquidation size · USD — how many dollars of forced liquidation counts as an event worth fading. Example: at 300, a $299 print is ignored and a $300 print is not. With more than one feed selected, prints on the same coin and the same side inside a one-second window are added together and checked once: $180 from one feed plus $140 from another is a single $320 event that clears a 300 minimum where neither would alone. Prints on opposite sides are never mixed. With exactly one feed selected there is no waiting and no summing — each print is judged as it arrives. Get it wrong: too low and you enter constantly on liquidations too small to have moved anything. Too high and you wait days between entries; the largest cascades are rare by definition. Dollar floor / Pair percentile — the segment above the box switches the whole rule: Dollar floor is the fixed figure above; Pair percentile compares each print to that pair's own recent liquidation-size history instead, computed from every liquidation on that pair in the last 30 days, or its newest 1,000 when 30 days holds fewer, long and short separately, so a print counts on a thin pair at a much smaller dollar figure than it would on a busy one. Set the percentile (50–99.9; 90 is a reasonable start) and the bot refuses a pair with no history yet rather than falling back to any dollar figure — a quiet pair stays quiet until it has one. The figures come from a shared community hub when one is linked (most installs have no cold start), with this install's own recorded history filling in anything the hub does not yet cover. See the table itself, every pair at once, on Screener → Liq sizes . Long band · % below VWMA — how far below fair value price must fall before a long may open; shown when Direction is Long or Both. Example: fair value $100.00 with a 2% band puts the lower edge at $98.00, and a long opens only strictly below $98.00 — at exactly $98.00 price is still inside the band and nothing happens. Get it wrong: at 0.2% you buy every small dip at prices barely better than fair value and the ladder does all the work. At 10% you fade only genuine catastrophes, which are rare and do not always bounce. Short band · % above VWMA — the mirror: how far above fair value price must rise before a short may open; shown when Direction is Short or Both. Example: fair value $100.00 with a 0.5% band puts the upper edge at $100.50, and a short opens only strictly above it. The two sides are independent — a tight 0.5% short band against a wide 3% long band is a valid way to say pumps mean-revert faster than dumps.

sections.title: 📐 Signal — the fair-value line the bands hang off, and the feeds that trigger it
sections.text: 📐 Signal — the fair-value line the bands hang off, and the feeds that trigger it The bands are measured against a fair-value line, and the trigger arrives from a liquidation feed. These are the settings for both. VWMA period · bars — how many candles build the fair-value line. VWMA is a volume-weighted moving average : each candle's close is weighted by how much traded in it, so a heavy bar pulls the line towards itself and a quiet one barely counts. Example: five 1-minute bars closing at $100.00 (2,000 traded), $100.50 (1,000), $101.00 (1,000), $99.50 (4,000) and $100.00 (2,000). A plain average is $100.20; the volume-weighted average is $999,500 ÷ 10,000 = $99.95 , pulled down because the big volume happened at the low price. That $99.95 is what the bands measure from. Choose 2–199 whole bars; values outside that common exchange-safe window are refused rather than silently shortened. Get it wrong: at 2 or 3 the line races along behind price, so price is almost never "far" from it and entries dry up. At 60 it becomes a slow trend average — band edges miles away, entries rare and much deeper, and in a steady trend price sits permanently outside the band on one side. VWMA timeframe — the size of each candle: 1m, 3m, 5m, 15m, 30m or 1h. Period and timeframe multiply. Example: 5 bars on 1m is a five-minute reference; the same 5 bars on 1h is a five-hour reference, and the band sits somewhere completely different. The forming candle: on 1m the line uses closed candles only , so a candle still being built cannot move your band edge underneath you mid-move. On every slower timeframe the forming candle is included — at 12:59 on an hourly setting, excluding it would blind fair value to everything since 12:00. The timeframe decides this; there is no switch. Get it wrong: the candle feed is built for both the period and timeframe at app start. A saved change fails closed until that account context restarts; Pair Info names the requested and running values instead of showing the old window under the new label. Change either, restart, then judge it. Liquidation sources — which feeds may trigger this bot: Bybit USDT / USDC / Inverse, Binance USDT / Inverse, and OKX USDT / USDC / Inverse perpetuals. Each button's dot is green live, amber connecting, red errored, grey off. One source always stays selected — the last button re-ticks itself, since a bot that can hear nothing is not a valid configuration. Changes apply live, no restart. Example: Bybit USDT plus Binance USDT roughly doubles the events you see and turns on the one-second summing described under Min liquidation size. Get it wrong: more feeds means more triggers, so the same Min liquidation size becomes a looser filter — expect to raise it when you add a source. Two feeds are known to be incomplete: Binance publishes at most one sampled liquidation per coin per second and can be blocked outright depending on where your server is; OKX states plainly that its feed does not represent the full set of liquidations. Neither is a fault in the bot and neither can be worked around — treat them as extra hints, not as a complete picture. Every feed is recorded whether or not it is selected; selecting one only controls whether it may open a trade. Why did nothing open? Activity → Liq Scalper → Skipped — why? names the first gate that failed in the bot's own words: "Inside band", "Liq side ≠ band side", "Below min size", "Max shorts open", the volatility filter, Isolation mode, a deal cap, or a venue rejection. If Activity is silent while the Screener's liquidation stream is busy, the coin is not in this bot's watch set, or its price and fair-value line have not warmed up.

sections.title: 💵 Base order — how big the first bet is
sections.text: 💵 Base order — how big the first bet is The Base order block inside Entry orders. This is the opening trade only. The DCA ladder and the exits do not start until this order has actually filled on the exchange. Size type: Dollar / Percent — a fixed dollar amount, or a share of your wallet resolved into dollars once when the deal opens and then frozen for that deal's life. Example: Percent 12 on a $2,500 wallet commits $300 of contracts; if the wallet grows to $4,000 that open deal still works with its original $300, but the next deal opens at $480. Get it wrong: Percent compounds both ways — a losing run shrinks every later bet, so the bot gets quietly smaller exactly when you may not be watching. If the wallet balance cannot be read at that instant, the entry is refused rather than guessed at. Size — the number: dollars in Dollar mode, percent of wallet in Percent mode, with a grey estimate beside the box. Example: Dollar 200 buys $200 of contracts; Percent 12 on a $2,500 wallet buys $300. Get it wrong: this is the seed of the whole deal — a ladder set in "% of entry" multiplies off it, so doubling the entry doubles the worst case. Below the exchange's minimum order value for a coin, the entry simply fails on that pair. This number is position size, not margin. $200 at 10× is a $200 position tying up about $20 of margin. Raising leverage does not buy a bigger position — it buys the same position with less money locked up and a liquidation price much closer to you. Entry order type: Market — crosses the spread and takes what the book offers, paying taker fees and some slippage to actually get in during the cascade. Nothing is recorded as a deal until the exchange confirms a real filled quantity; an order merely accepted, rejected, or unreadable is never treated as a fill. Get it wrong: in a violent flush your fill can be much worse than the price that triggered you, which moves your whole ladder and take-profit with it. Entry order type: Aggressive limit — posts a maker limit at the touch and re-prices as the market moves, banking partial fills. Maker fees, no slippage, and it never converts to market and has no deadline. Get it wrong: a price running hard away leaves the order chasing or partly filled, so you miss the move or end up much smaller than configured. Repeated rejections abort the attempt and write it into Activity. Leverage — the margin the exchange demands, set on the coin just before entry; 1× to 50× by slider or box. It changes your margin and liquidation price, not your position size, profit per percent moved, or dollar risk. Example: a $300 position locks about $25 of margin at 12× and about $12.50 at 24×. Both make or lose $3 per 1% move; the 24× version is simply force-closed much sooner. Get it wrong: high leverage plus a deep ladder is the classic way to be liquidated at level 3 of a ladder that would have worked at level 4. Keep Min leverage in Pairs at least this high, or the bot enters coins whose exchange maximum is lower and you use more margin than planned.

sections.title: 📉 Dollar Cost Averaging Orders — the ladder
sections.text: 📉 Dollar Cost Averaging Orders — the ladder If the trade goes against you, the bot buys more at worse prices to pull the average entry towards current price, so a smaller bounce exits in profit. This section decides how much a losing trade can cost you. Read this before you touch the numbers. The ladder is static : every level's distance is measured from the price the deal originally opened at and never re-measured, so after two fills have moved the average a long way, level three still sits exactly where it was placed. Levels fill the instant price touches them — no bounce required, no minimum time between fills, no cooldown, and one fast candle can fill several on its way through. And nothing anywhere caps the total size of a deal . The ladder you configure here is the only limit that exists. DCA style: Static / Scaled ATR · how the FIRST level's distance is chosen — everything else on this page is shared by both. Static puts the first level at the Deviation you type, the same percentage on every pair. Scaled ATR derives it from each pair's own recent volatility instead — ATR multiplier × ATR ÷ price , held between your minimum and maximum deviation — and then grows the gaps with Step scale exactly as the static ladder does. Example: ATR multiplier 1 on a pair whose ATR is 3% of price gives a first level 3% away, while a calmer pair the same day might get 0.9% and a violent one 7%. It is worked out once, when the deal opens , and frozen for that deal's life — a pair getting wilder afterwards does not move levels that are already resting. Get it wrong: this is not a free upgrade. If ATR cannot be worked out for a pair, that entry is refused — the bot does not quietly fall back to your static Deviation, because a deal opened on distances you did not choose is worse than a deal not opened. So a broken candle feed is a bot that stops trading; the pair's row on Closest to trigger says refused with the reason, and you get an alert if every watched pair is unpriceable. ATR multiplier / ATR timeframe / ATR length · Scaled ATR only — the three inputs behind that first gap. The timeframe and length are this ladder's own , deliberately not borrowed from your VWMA settings: those time an entry, these size a ladder. Example: multiplier 1.5, timeframe 5m, length 14 reads Wilder's ATR over the last fourteen 5-minute candles and asks for one and a half of it. A 1m ATR can run beside a coarser VWMA timeframe : ATR reuses this account's shared exact-venue 1-minute store and its own exact-timeframe history while VWMA stays on the interval you selected. If the required ATR history or current closed tail is missing, stale or unsupported, the entry is refused by name rather than given a static fallback. Minimum / Maximum deviation · Scaled ATR only — the floor and ceiling on that first gap, and the floor is the one that protects you. Example: minimum 2 means a very quiet pair still places its first level 2% away rather than 0.3% away. Get it wrong: with no floor, ATR on a sleepy pair puts level one inside its ordinary noise, so the ladder fills on wiggles and is spent before the move it exists for. With no ceiling (0), ATR on a violent pair can put level one so far out that nothing ever fills and the ladder quietly does nothing. Set the maximum below the minimum and the save is refused, here and on a builder ATR DCA — that combination is a typo, not a strategy. Scaled ATR preview · the panel under the ATR dials — pick a pair and see what it would actually get, re-priced as you type. Get it wrong: a row marked Preview only is a real calculation, but on candles downloaded for this screen so you need not wait for a long ATR timeframe to warm up — it is not a ladder this bot can place yet, and the line beneath says why. Expect it to shift slightly once the bot has warmed that pair. Size type: Dollar / % of balance / % of entry — a flat amount, a share of your wallet, or a share of what the opening trade committed. The last two resolve into dollars once when the deal opens, then freeze for that deal's life; the unit label and the grey estimate beside the box both follow your choice. Example: $2,500 wallet, entry resolved to $300 — Dollar 200 gives a $200 first DCA, % of balance 12 gives $300, % of entry 100 gives $300, the same size as the entry. Get it wrong: in % of entry mode, 100 does not mean $100 — it means "the same as the entry". Read the unit before you save. First DCA — the first ladder order's size in the unit you chose; every later order is this multiplied by the Volume scale. Example: First DCA 200 dollars with Volume scale 2 and 3 orders gives $200, $400, $800 — $1,400 of extra exposure on top of the entry. Get it wrong: this is the multiplier on your worst case, so doubling it doubles every level. Set far larger than the entry, the first DCA fill immediately dominates your average entry — the take-profit comes close, but you are very large very early. Deviation · first level, % from entry — how far the trade must move against you before the first ladder order fills. Example: a short entered at $205.00 with Deviation 5 places its first level at $205.00 × 1.05 = $215.25 ; a long at $205.00 places it at $194.75. Get it wrong: at 0.5% the ladder spends immediately on ordinary noise and you are fully loaded before the move develops. At 25% it never engages on a normal adverse move — a losing trade with a lifeline out of reach. Number of orders · 0 = no DCA — how many ladder levels exist. Example: 3 gives three orders beyond the entry and then nothing; the position stops growing. At 0 the entry, take-profit and stop loss are the entire deal. Note: the − button stops at 1 — type 0 to switch the ladder off. Get it wrong: levels are not free. With any Volume scale above 1 each new level is the largest yet, so 4 levels to 5 can add more exposure than the first four combined. At 0 you have no defence unless a stop loss is armed.

sections.title: 📐 DCA — the scaling multipliers and the generated ladder
sections.text: 📐 DCA — the scaling multipliers and the generated ladder The three settings that turn the numbers above into a ladder, and the table that shows you the result before you save. Volume scale · size × per order — the multiplier on each successive order's size . Example: First DCA $50 at Volume scale 2 gives $50, $100, $200, $400; at 1 every level stays $50; at 1.5 you get $50, $75, $112.50, $168.75. Get it wrong: this is the number that turns a ladder into a martingale — at 2 the fourth level alone is eight times the first and the ladder totals fifteen times it. At 1 the ladder barely moves your average entry, so the take-profit stays far away. Most people land between 1.2 and 1.8. Step scale · level step × per order — the multiplier on the gap between levels, so the ladder spreads as it deepens. The first gap is your Deviation; each next gap is the previous times this, and the distances add up. Example: Deviation 4, Step scale 2, 3 orders puts levels at 4% , then 4+8 = 12% , then 12+16 = 28% from entry. Step scale 1 gives even levels at 4%, 8% and 12%. Get it wrong: below 1 the levels bunch together and the whole ladder is spent inside a small move. Well above 2 the deep levels fly out of reach — level 4 at 160% from entry is decoration, not a safety order. DCA style: Builder · one row per DCA — for a ladder no formula produces: you write each DCA, and the three kinds mix in one ladder. Every DCA states its own size, so this tab hides First DCA, Deviation, Number of orders, Volume scale and Step scale — they describe nothing here. Static DCAs sit at the percent you type; ATR DCAs at their own multiplier × the pair's ATR (timeframe and length come from the Scaled ATR tab), priced once when the deal opens and frozen. Both measure from the entry price and both rest on the exchange. Time DCAs fire a set period after open, and only once price is also far enough offside; if the time passes first the DCA waits, it does not expire. The two anchors differ: a timed DCA measures from your current average entry , not the original — it is a drawdown tool, so it follows what the position now costs. Get it wrong: a timed DCA cannot rest on the exchange , so it is checked on this bot's own clock and only fires while the bot is running — a restart or a stopped bot means it waits. Static and ATR DCAs are unaffected. Every DCA needs a size, in whatever Size type reads (see below), and if ATR cannot be computed an ATR DCA refuses the entry rather than placing a shorter ladder. Skip if hedge ≥ · timed DCAs only — do not fire this DCA while the Hedge Bot is already carrying at least this much. Measured as the hedge's notional as a percentage of this position — not its profit, not its distance. Example: 60 means "if the hedge is already 60% the size of this trade, we have enough protection; do not add more". Get it wrong: at a low number the DCA almost never fires and the ladder you designed quietly has one fewer step; at 0 (off) a deep hedge and a fresh add can both be working at once, which is exactly the position size you were trying to avoid. Size · per DCA — every DCA carries its own, read as USDT , % of balance or % of entry , resolved to dollars once at open or pickup and then frozen. Each row prints the dollars it comes to, live as you type. Example: a DCA of 10 on "% of balance" with a $5,000 wallet shows ≈ $500 . Blank and 0 differ: blank is refused on save, 0 means "add nothing here". Get it wrong: these were plain USDT before this release, so an older percent ladder now commits far more — read the ≈ $ on each row. A typed size also ignores Volume scale, so check the total is what you meant. Orders on exchange · resting at once — how many levels sit on the exchange as real limit orders; as one fills the next is placed, and all are cancelled the moment the deal closes. Example: a 6-level ladder set to 3 shows three orders; when level 1 fills, level 4 is placed, keeping three live. At 6 all six rest at once. Get it wrong: at 1 a fast candle can blow through three levels while the bot is still placing the second, filling you worse than the ladder describes. High across many deals eats the exchange's per-account open-order allowance. The count is of real orders — if the exchange briefly cannot describe one it keeps its slot and deeper levels wait, rather than the bot over-placing. Generated DCA ladder — a live table of exactly what your numbers produce: each level's size, distance from entry and running total, updating as you type. Always read it before saving. It is also what actually gets saved — if the boxes and your existing deals' ladder disagree, saving adopts the table. "Stored DCA ladder" — when the table changes title — Deviation, Step scale and Number of orders generate a ladder; they are not the ladder. The two can differ: the shipped Liq Scalper preset carries a hand-tuned 12 / 26 / 45 / 70% that no step scale reproduces (its own generator gives 12 / 34.8 / 78.1 / 160.4%). When they differ the table is titled Stored DCA ladder and shows what your deals really use, and saving leaves it alone — so you can rename the bot or change the take-profit without touching your distances. Edit Deviation, Step scale or Number of orders and you have asked for a new ladder: the title flips back to Generated DCA ladder and that is what the save writes. Get it wrong: nudging Deviation just to see the effect and then saving really does replace your ladder — the title is the tell. The static ladder, shown. A short opens at $1.0000 with Deviation 4, Step scale 2, 3 orders — levels at $1.0400, $1.1200 and $1.2800. The first two fill, blending the average entry to about $1.0603 . Level 3 still rests at $1.2800 , 28% above the original $1.0000, not 28% above the new average ($1.3572). This is deliberate, and it is the biggest difference from other DCA bots: as the deal deepens, the remaining ladder sits closer to you in percentage terms than it would elsewhere.

sections.title: 🎯 Exit orders — take profit and stop loss
sections.text: 🎯 Exit orders — take profit and stop loss How the deal ends. The take-profit is always on; the stop loss is a switch and ships off. Take profit Take-profit source: Fixed % / Trailing / ATR · pick the source first, single-target mode only — Fixed % rests one reduce-only limit at the Target profit box below, cancelled and re-placed on every DCA fill; it does not follow price up. Trailing rests nothing on the exchange — it arms at Activation % profit from the average entry, then rides this deal's own stop, tightening to Trail % behind the best price since and never loosening. ATR derives a Fixed-%-style distance from the pair's own recent volatility instead: ATR multiplier × ATR ÷ price , held between a minimum and maximum deviation you set. Example: min 1%, max 5%, the multiplier × ATR ÷ price works out to 3.5% — the exit rests 3.5% away; work out to 10% and it is capped at 5%. Worked out once, when the deal opens , and frozen for that deal's life. Get it wrong: if ATR cannot be worked out for a pair, that entry is refused rather than quietly falling back to Fixed % — an exit resting on a distance you did not choose is worse than a deal not opened. An adopted position manages on Fixed % until candles arrive, then moves to ATR on its own. Target profit · % — Fixed % only — how far in your favour from the average entry the exit sits. Example: a short averaging $210.00 with Target profit 1.2 rests a buy-back at $210.00 × 0.988 = $207.48 ; after a DCA fill lifts the average to $222.13 it re-places at $219.46 . Get it wrong: at 0.1% fees and funding eat the whole profit — you can close hundreds of "winners" and be down. At 10% deals sit open for days paying funding and holding a deal-cap slot. Take profit type: Ladder (multiple TPs) — several targets, each closing a slice, so you bank early and let the rest run. It replaces the Target profit box AND the source seg above with a table — ladder mode is always Fixed % ; only the ladder's own last step may switch to trailing. TP ladder — Profit % — one row per step, each a distance in your favour from the average entry, increasing down the table or the form refuses to save. Example: 1%, 2% and 3% on a short averaging $1.0000 rest buy-backs at $0.9900, $0.9800 and $0.9700. TP ladder — Close % of deal — the share each step closes; they must total exactly 100 unless the last step is trailing (below), and the running total stays red until they do. Example: 50 / 25 / 25 closes half at 1%, a quarter at 2%, the last quarter at 3%. Get it wrong: 90 / 5 / 5 is one small profit plus a token position; 5 / 5 / 90 leaves most of the deal depending on the furthest target. Last step: Trailing · a toggle beside the last row — swaps that row's two boxes to Activation % and Trail % : it rests nothing and closes whatever is left of the deal once the fixed steps above it have filled and it arms — the same mechanism as the Trailing source above, riding in behind the fixed steps rather than instead of them. The fixed steps must total less than 100 so there is a remainder for it to protect, and Add step is disabled while it is on. + Add step / Even split / ✕ — Add step appends a fixed row one percent beyond the last (disabled while the last row is trailing); Even split equalises the close percentages of the fixed rows only; ✕ removes a row down to a minimum of two. Ten steps maximum. Every ladder step rests as a reduce-only limit anchored to the average entry, and any DCA fill resets and re-places the entire ladder — including already-filled steps, which re-arm at the new average. Steps below the exchange's minimum order size merge into the nearest earlier step, so the position always stays covered. Ladder SL · ladder mode only — an On/Off chip that turns the TP ladder into a ratchet: once profit is banked, a stop moves up behind the remaining position so a reversal cannot take the deal back to nothing. Off by default; turning it on reveals three controls. SL mode: Level based trails a fixed number of ladder levels behind the last filled TP step and keeps moving. SL mode: Average entry jumps to breakeven when the step you nominate fills, then stays. Get it wrong: Level based protects more but stops you out of shallow pullbacks more often; Average entry only guarantees breakeven, so a deal that reached step 2 and reversed gives back everything above your entry. Arm after · TP fills (N) — how many TP steps must fill before the ladder stop exists, 1 to 10. Example: at 1 it arms on the first fill; at 2 you bank two steps first. Get it wrong: at 1 on a tight first step, an ordinary wiggle arms it and then hits it for a near-nothing gain. Beyond the number of steps you have, it can never arm. SL buffer · % past breakeven, toward profit — nudges the armed stop past breakeven so being stopped out leaves you slightly ahead. Example: a short averaging $210.00 with a 0.2 buffer stops at $210.00 × 0.998 = $209.58 ; 0 is exactly breakeven. Get it wrong: too large and normal noise triggers it, ending deals early. A position too small for a resting take profit is watched instead, and you are told. Every venue has a minimum order size, and on a cheap coin with a coarse lot it can be larger than a small position — BEATUSDT on Bitunix takes whole units with a ten-unit minimum, so a $20 position cannot rest anything. Rather than leave the deal with no exit, the bot switches that one deal to a monitored exit : it watches price and sends a market close at your take-profit target, exactly the way the stop loss has always worked. The difference matters: a resting order sits on the exchange and fills whether or not this app is running; a monitored exit only fires while the bot is running, so a restart or an outage leaves the position with no exit until it is back. You get a TAKE PROFIT NOT RESTING notice naming the pair and the venue's own arithmetic, and the resting take profit comes back by itself if a DCA fill grows the position past the minimum.

sections.title: 🛑 Exit orders — stop loss
sections.text: 🛑 Exit orders — stop loss The other half of Exit orders. What the percentage MEANS depends entirely on the offset you pick. Stop loss Stop loss · the switch beside the heading — off by default, and off means nothing closes a losing deal automatically: the DCA ladder, plus a separately enabled Hedge Bot, are your whole drawdown management. On reveals the settings below and arms a hard exit for the entire position. Get it wrong: no stop plus a deep ladder puts your true worst case in the hands of the exchange's liquidation engine rather than yours — legitimate for some people, catastrophic for others, so make it deliberately. Offset from: Initial entry price — measured from the opening price and never moved, which pairs naturally with the static ladder off the same anchor. Example: a short opened at $1.0000 with Stop loss 35 stops at $1.3500 , however many DCA levels fill. Offset from: Current entry price (avg) — measured from the blended average , so it retreats with every DCA fill. Example: the same short, after two fills lift the average to $1.0603, stops at $1.0603 × 1.35 = $1.4315 instead of $1.3500. Get it wrong: it gives the loss more room exactly as the trade goes worst — the stop stays outside the ladder automatically, but the dollars it permits grow every time. Offset from: Account balance — the percentage is not a price distance but the share of your wallet you will lose on this deal , and the bot puts the stop at the price where the loss equals that. Example: $2,500 wallet, Stop loss 5 = $125 at risk; 990.25 coins short at an average $1.0603, so $125 ÷ 990.25 = $0.1262 of price and the stop sits at $1.1866 . As the position grows, that same $125 buys less price distance — the stop marches towards you as the ladder fills. Get it wrong: this is the only mode where the stop lands inside your own ladder without you changing a number — above, level 3 at $1.2800 would never be reached. Pick it when the dollar loss is what you care about, then re-check the ladder. Stop loss · % — the number, slider 5 to 150 or typed, meaning whatever the Offset from mode says; the grey hint restates it as you switch. Get it wrong: too tight and it fires before the ladder meant to save the deal has finished — the form warns when your stop sits inside the ladder, and you should believe it. Too loose and it is never hit, which is no stop plus the false comfort of a number. Stop loss and ladder must be read together. With levels at 4%, 12% and 28%, a 20% stop from the initial entry means level 3 can never fill — you have paid for a three-level ladder and configured a two-level one. Put the stop beyond the deepest level, or shorten the ladder. Cooldown after Stop Loss Pair Cooldown (minutes) — after this bot's stop loss fires on an instrument, new entries on that instrument (both long and short) are skipped for this many minutes. 0 = off. Bot Cooldown (minutes) — after a stop loss on any instrument, new entries anywhere for this bot are skipped for this many minutes. 0 = off. The two timers run at the same time, not one after the other, and a pair only reopens once both have cleared. Requires Stop loss to be switched on — a duration typed while the switch is off is a saved preference only, and the save is refused until either the switch is on or the boxes are set back to 0. Only a confirmed stop-loss fill starts the clock: a threshold merely touched, a rejected order, a manual close or a take-profit never do, and a trailing take-profit never does either even though it can use the same exchange stop order. Existing deals are never touched: the DCA ladder, take-profit and stop loss on a position that is already open keep running exactly as configured. A cooldown only blocks a new trade — the terminal's manual order ticket is gated too, but a reduce-only order is never blocked. Every other deal form (TV Signal, Optimized Liq, Manual Bot) has the identical two boxes in its own Stop loss section.

sections.title: 🧮 The Summary panel — check this before you save
sections.text: 🧮 The Summary panel — check this before you save Live arithmetic on the numbers you typed. None of it is a setting and none of it limits anything — it is the fastest way to find out that a configuration which looked reasonable in the boxes is not. Balance — the wallet figure every percentage on the form resolves against. Base order — your entry in dollars, with the percentage alongside if you sized it that way. Max ladder spend — entry plus every level: one deal's full position size if the whole ladder fills. Example: a $200 entry with a $200 / $400 / $800 ladder shows $1,600. % of balance used · if every DCA fills — the headline number: worst-case margin across every deal your caps allow, as (entry + full ladder) ÷ leverage × max concurrent deals ÷ balance. Example: $1,600 at 10× is $160 of margin per deal; at a cap of 2 deals on a $2,000 wallet that is $320, or 16% . Over 100% it turns red and warns — that means the exchange's own margin checks are all that stands between you and a forced close. · at entry only — the same before any DCA fills: above, $200 ÷ 10 × 2 ÷ $2,000 = 2% . The gap between the two lines is the commitment you make without noticing. The small line beneath states the assumptions — "margin at 10× × 2 deals (Max both)" — and names which ceiling produced the deal count, so you can see whether this form's caps or the Accounts page's market cap binds. It also notes that the exchange can force lower leverage on individual coins, which raises the margin above the figure shown. Pairs — how many coins this bot watches, and whether that came from the filters or your manual list. Take profit and Stop loss — your exit settings restated, with "off" spelled out when the stop is not armed. Hedge — whether a deal from this bot could actually receive hedge protection now, naming the reason when it could not: the market has no hedge mode, the Hedge Bot is not enabled, or auto-attach is off. It never echoes a saved setting back at you. Hedge parameters live on the Hedge Bot page; this bot owns no hedge engine. DCA ladder — a bar chart of level distances, so a badly spread ladder is obvious at a glance. Warnings — shown here when your worst case exceeds your balance, and under the stop loss field when the stop sits inside the ladder. Informational only; nothing clips an order for you. Save & run saves and starts the bot, after validating the name, the TP ladder totals, and leverage against a manual pair list. Anything that fails is spelled out in red rather than silently ignored.

sections.title: 📖 One deal, start to finish, with real numbers
sections.text: 📖 One deal, start to finish, with real numbers A short on SOL, fading a squeeze, with every number worked through. The settings Direction Short · Max shorts 2 · Short band 2% · VWMA 5 bars on 1m · Min liquidation size $300 · Base order Dollar $200 , Market , 10× · DCA Dollar , First DCA $200 , Deviation 5% , Number of orders 3 , Volume scale 2 , Step scale 2 , Orders on exchange 3 · Take profit 1.2% · Stop loss off . Fair value is established. The last five closed 1-minute candles give a volume-weighted average of $200.00 , so a 2% short band puts the upper edge at $204.00 . A liquidation prints. The Bybit USDT feed reports $450 of SOL shorts force-closed — forced buying . It clears the $300 minimum and it is the right side to fade. The band is checked. The mark price on this bot's own SOL contract is $205.00 — above $204.00, on the short side, matching the liquidation. Both gates pass. At $203.90, nothing would have happened. The entry fills. A market sell of $200 at $205.00 → 200 ÷ 205.00 = 0.9756 SOL short, tying up about $20 of margin at 10×. The ladder is placed , all three levels resting at once, measured from the original $205.00. Deviation 5 with Step scale 2 gives 5%, then 15%, then 35%: DCA1 · $215.25 · $200  (205.00 × 1.05) DCA2 · $235.75 · $400  (205.00 × 1.15) DCA3 · $276.75 · $800  (205.00 × 1.35) The take-profit goes on at 205.00 × 0.988 = $202.54 . DCA1 fills at $215.25, buying 0.9292 SOL. The position is 1.9048 SOL for $400, so the average entry is 400 ÷ 1.9048 = $210.00 and the take-profit re-places at $207.48 . DCA2 fills at $235.75, buying 1.6967 SOL. The position is 3.6015 SOL for $800, average entry 800 ÷ 3.6015 = $222.13 , take-profit re-anchored to $219.46 . Note where DCA3 is. Still resting at $276.75 — 35% above the original $205.00, not 35% above the new $222.13 average ($299.88). That is the static ladder working as intended. The squeeze breaks and price falls to $219.46. The reduce-only buy limit closes all 3.6015 SOL at 98.8% of what you committed: $800 × 0.988 = $790.40 , so $9.60 gross — 1.2% of the position, as configured. Exchange fees and any funding come out of that. Everything is cleaned up. The resting DCA3 order is cancelled the moment the position closes, and its Max shorts slot is released. Now the other ending. Had price not turned and DCA3 filled, the deal would be $200 + $200 + $400 + $800 = $1,600 of SOL short about 35% offside, needing $160 of margin at 10× — and with Max shorts at 2, a second identical deal takes that to $320 . With no stop armed and no cap anywhere in the bot, the exchange's liquidation engine is the only thing that ends that trade if price keeps going. That is what the Summary panel's "if every DCA fills" line exists to show you.

sections.title: 🎯 What is the Optimized Liquidation Bot?
sections.text: 🎯 What is the Optimized Liquidation Bot? What it does: it fades forced liquidations like the Liq Scalper, but never asks you for an entry band. It measures each pair against its own recent history and gives every pair its own long band and short band , recomputed as the market changes. Everything after the entry is the same shared deal engine: DCA ladder, take profit, stop loss, full P&L attribution. Prefer it over the Liq Scalper when your watch list is wide. One typed band is right when you trade a handful of pairs you know intimately, and wrong for most of a list holding majors and small alts together. What "optimized" actually means A liquidation bot bets on overshoot , so the only question is how far is far enough . Typing 2% asserts that 2% means the same on Bitcoin as on a three-month-old alt. Example: on Bitcoin a 2% dislocation inside five minutes is a once-a-month event and the bot idles for weeks; on the alt, 2% is Tuesday, so it fires constantly — including into trends, which is how a liquidation bot bleeds. The Optimized bot measures instead. For each pair it takes a window of recent candles — the Lookback , in candles sized by VWMA Timeframe — and asks: what is the tightest distance from this pair's volume-weighted average price that price never spent more than N candles in a row outside? N is the Risk Level , the only judgement call left to you. It measures runs rather than a simple maximum because a single candle poking through and snapping back is exactly the trade you want , while a run parked outside is a trend , and fading a trend is the losing trade. Starting from zero, the bot walks the window and widens the band by the smallest amount that breaks any over-long run. Out comes the tightest band that never let a trend through, per pair, per side. So "optimized" here means measured — not predicted, learned, or tuned toward profit. The bot has no opinion about where price is going, only a fact about how far this pair strays before it comes back. The five dials, and which way each one pushes Risk Level — how many candles in a row are allowed outside the band. Higher → tighter band → more entries, and more trend risk. This is the throttle. Minimum band — a hard floor under the measured band. Higher → wider band → fewer entries. It can only widen a band, never tighten one. VWMA Period — how many candles go into the fair-value line the band hangs off. Longer → slower, smoother line that lags a fast move, so entries come slightly later and deeper. VWMA Timeframe — how big each candle is. Bigger candles → a "streak" covers far more clock time → wider bands → fewer, deeper entries. It also sets how often bands recompute. Lookback — how much history the measurement covers. Longer → old shocks stay in the window → wider bands → fewer entries. Shorter reacts faster to a regime change, in both directions. Where it is: Create Bot gallery → Optimized Liquidation Bot. Up to ten can run, each with its own name, pairs, bands and deal settings. It needs a perpetual market — Futures USDT; Spot has no liquidations to fade, so the button is unavailable there. Configure does not create it. Pressing Configure opens the form on a draft — its heading reads "New Optimized Liquidation Bot" and the button at the foot says Create & enable . Nothing exists, and nothing trades, until you press that button. Leaving by Cancel , by ← My Bots , by the back button or by closing the tab throws the draft away and leaves no bot to delete. Which exchanges, and whose candles. It runs on supported USDT perpetual venues: Bybit, Bitunix, Bitget, Binance, Aster and WEEX . On every one of them the bands are measured from that exchange's own candles — a Bitget bot is never priced off Bybit, because a band is only worth anything on the book where the order actually fills. Bybit, Binance, Bitunix and WEEX can supply current confirmed 1-minute candles through the app's public WebSocket writers. Bitget and Aster use the app's venue REST fallback for current closed candles. Venue REST also repairs gaps on every supported venue. Verified Hub history can seed supported startup windows; unavailable or incomplete history is recovered from the venue. A pair stays fail-closed until its required history and current closed tail are complete. It will look idle on day one, and that is correct. A pair does not trade until its bands are computed from real history, which takes a while to load. Read Warming up, stale, and the quiet screen before concluding anything is broken.

sections.title: 🧩 Main — name, direction, caps, pairs
sections.text: 🧩 Main — name, direction, caps, pairs Which way this bot trades, how many deals it holds, and which pairs it may touch. It belongs to the account and market selected in the header when you created it; to trade another, create one there. Bot name · up to 48 characters, required — the label on My Bots, the Screener band table header, and every refusal message. Example: Alt liq reverter beats bot 2 ; creating one mints Optimized Liq 1 for you to type over. Too vague: with three bots running you cannot tell which just refused an entry. Empty: the save is refused. Direction · shipped Both — which side of a liquidation this bot takes. Longs liquidated means force- selling into a lower price, so the bot buys — a Long ; shorts liquidated means force- buying , so it sells — a Short . Example: on Long, an up-spike from a short squeeze is ignored however far outside the short band it prints. Too narrow: one side halves the opportunities and takes a directional bet the bot never made — long-only in a downtrend catches every falling knife and no pumps. Both is the neutral shape; pair it with small caps. Max longs · shipped 2 — the most long deals held at once, with an in-flight entry already holding its slot so a burst cannot overshoot. Example: at 2 a third long setup is refused and logged, even if it is the best of the day. Too big: six correlated alt longs is one position in six costumes, all offside together. Zero is not accepted — the minimum is 1; to stop the bot, pause it. Max shorts · shipped 2 — the same ceiling on the short side. Max both · shipped 2, total — the combined ceiling, shown only on Direction Both, and a real cap rather than the sum. Example: 2 per side with a total of 2 means two deals in any mix — with one long open, one short may open and nothing more. Too big: your margin is committed before the good setup arrives. Pairs — By filters · shipped — every perpetual that clears this bot's own Pair filters section, below. This changed in v0.74.93: it used to be literally the Liq Scalper's filtered list, so this bot could only ever trade a subset of that bot's pairs, and tightening the Liq Scalper narrowed this bot without you touching it. Now the two are independent — set them the same, or differently, as you like. Example: every qualifying perpetual on the market — far more than you would hand-pick, and that breadth is the point of a bot that bands each separately. Cost: every pair holds candle history in memory — see the ceiling card. Pairs — Allowlist — only the pairs you name, and nothing is ever added. Example: six majors you are comfortable holding through a ladder. Too short: you are hand-picking again, which is the Liq Scalper's job. Empty: every signal is refused with Not in this bot's pair list . Allowed pairs · Allowlist mode only — the picker. It flags any pair whose venue maximum leverage is below this form's leverage and refuses the save naming them, rather than letting the bot try an order the venue will reject. Blacklist · this bot; shipped empty — comma-separated pairs this bot never trades. The install-wide blacklist applies on top and cannot be overridden here. Example: LUNAUSDT, HMSTRUSDT . Too aggressive: you quietly shrink the universe the bands were computed for. Empty: normal — the pair filters did most of this already. Direction and Pairs sit under Main, the deal caps under Entry , because the caps are about size rather than signal. They are documented together because they answer one question: how much of this bot can be live at once.

sections.title: 🧮 Pair filters — this bot's own, per exchange
sections.text: 🧮 Pair filters — this bot's own, per exchange The four groups follow the same layout as the Liquidation Bot: active or incomplete groups open on load, inactive groups collapse, and your open/closed choices survive live updates. Collapsing a group preserves every setting and its effect. Shown in By filters mode only; an allowlist already IS the pair list. These are this bot's criteria, stored per exchange, and they are not the Liq Scalper's — changing one bot never moves the other. A new bot starts with a copy of that market's Liq Scalper filters, so it begins exactly where your existing carve already is, and diverges only when you edit it. Min leverage · shipped 12× — the pair must let you use at least this much. Your Entry leverage is a floor on it: setting 25× on the form raises this filter to 25× whatever this box says, because a pair that cannot take your leverage cannot take your order. Get it wrong: a high number quietly deletes the majors, which usually cap lower than alts. Volatility Filters — this Optimized bot's own optional timeframe / maximum-move / closed-candle rows, evaluated over this bot's own automatic pair roster even when that roster differs from the Liq Scalper's. 1d / 10% / 10 means any one of ten completed daily candles moving more than 10%, not a cumulative ten-day move. The rule reads candles directly from the exchange this bot trades; it does not read the Optimized-band Hub seed. A cold, warming or stale row refuses new exposure until current, while an open position remains managed. Deleting every row switches this filter off for this bot. Min max limit order / Min max market order · shipped 15,000 / 5,000 USDT — the exchange's own ceiling on a single order of each kind. A pair whose cap is under your number is dropped, because one DCA of your ladder would hit the venue's wall rather than yours. Neither box checks a position ceiling; that is the venue's risk-limit tier and this app does not read it. Max funding rate · shipped 0.10%, absolute — either direction. A pair paying more than this costs you to hold in the direction you are most likely to be holding it. Auto-refresh · shipped 60 min, minimum 10, 0 = off — how often this bot re-runs its own filter. Independent of the Liq Scalper's cadence. Exclude categories · shipped none — remove a whole class of listing: Main (regular crypto) , Innovation Zone , Stock , Commodity , Forex , Pre-Market , New listing (≤30d) . Get it wrong: ticking Main (regular crypto) removes almost everything you wanted — that is where the majors live. Pre-Market contracts are excluded unconditionally whatever you tick, because they are not trading yet. Exclude — Delisted / ST-tagged · both shipped on — announced delistings, and coins the exchange flags special-treatment. Turning either off puts a bot on coins the exchange itself has warned about. Filtered out — every pair these criteria excluded and which criterion did it, refreshed when the form opens. If the count is surprising, the answer is in this list. A bot that is not running on the selected exchange says so rather than showing zero, and a cold instrument list says that too — neither is a filter verdict. Off switches — Min leverage, Min max limit order, Min max market order, Max funding rate, Min 24h rolling volume and Minimum coin market cap each carry their own on/off switch, this bot's own, independent of the Liq Scalper's. Off greys the box and stops that one rule for THIS bot only, keeping the figure typed in it. Ships with all six on. A looser filter here costs memory, not just breadth. Every pair in scope holds 1-minute candle history for its bands. Widen the criteria far enough and the save is refused with the arithmetic spelled out — see the lookback ceiling card.

sections.title: 📏 Optimized bands — the five dials in detail
sections.text: 📏 Optimized bands — the five dials in detail You set the measurement, never the band. Each dial changes how the bot measures and the bands fall out of that. Changing any of them throws away every pair's bands and recomputes from scratch, so the bot stops entering until they return. Change one at a time.
