Long VWMA Risk Level · candles in a row; shipped 2, range 1–100 — how many consecutive candles may trade below the long band before it must widen; the main throttle on the long side. Example: on 5-minute candles, Risk 2 tolerates a 10-minute excursion and widens beyond that; Risk 3 tolerates 15 minutes, so it widens less and the band comes out tighter — say 1.62% where Risk 2 gave 2.10%. On a pair averaging 2.4000 that moves the long trigger from 2.3496 to 2.3611, closer to spot, so it fires more often. Too high: the band tightens until ordinary drift crosses it and you buy into downtrends. Too low (1): one candle outside forces a widening, the band turns very conservative, and on calm pairs nothing ever triggers. Zero: not accepted; the minimum is 1. Short VWMA Risk Level · shipped 2, range 1–100 — the same dial for candles above the short band, separate on purpose because crypto down-moves are faster and shallower than up-moves. Example: Long 2 / Short 3 fades pumps a little more eagerly than dumps. Get it wrong: a too-high short risk shorts strength. Min Long VWMA · %, floor under the computed long band; shipped 0 = none — the band in force is the larger of the measurement and this floor. Example: a quiet major measures 0.42%; with Min Long at 0.75% the band is 0.75% , moving the trigger on an average of 62,400 from 62,137.92 down to 61,932.00. A pair that measured 2.10% is untouched. Too high: you overwrite the measurement on every pair and re-create the Liq Scalper's one-band-for-everyone problem without being able to see it. What it cannot do: rescue a pair that measured nothing — a history that never breached shows no band and cannot fire, and a floor does not change that. Min Short VWMA · %; shipped 0 = none — the same floor on the short side, same arithmetic, same warning. VWMA Timeframe · 1m to 1d; shipped 5 minutes — the candle size, which sets three things: the unit a Risk Level counts in, how often bands recompute (every candle close, never faster than 5 minutes), and how long a pair may go without fresh data before it stops trading. Example: at 5 minutes, Risk 2 tolerates a 10-minute excursion, bands recompute every 5 minutes and a pair goes stale after 15; at 1 hour the same Risk 2 tolerates a 2-hour excursion, recomputes hourly, and goes stale after 3 hours. Too big: wide slow bands and few deep entries, with fast reversals over before the next recompute. Too small (1m): twitchy bands, and the setting most likely to collide with the 30-day ceiling, since a minute of history costs the most memory per day covered. VWMA Period · candles; shipped 5 — how many candles build the volume-weighted average the bands measure from, each candle's typical price weighted by what traded in it. Example: 5 candles on 5 minutes is a rolling 25-minute average, deliberately a fast reference; at 20 it becomes a 100-minute average that lags a sharp move, so during a flush the line sits above spot and entries come later and deeper. Too long: you are fading a trend against a stale line, not a dislocation. Too short (1): the "average" is the last candle, so price is compared against itself and the bands collapse toward noise. Zero: not accepted; the ceiling also caps it — at a 1-day timeframe the deepest period is 29. Lookback · days; shipped 30, which is also the maximum — how much history each measurement covers. Example: 30 days is 8,640 candles per pair at 5 minutes (30 × 24 × 60 ÷ 5), 2,880 at 15 minutes, 720 at 1 hour, 43,200 at 1 minute. Too long: a shock from four weeks ago keeps a band wide after the market calmed — though every refresh re-measures the whole window, so old spikes age out and bands tighten by themselves. Too short: the window may hold no real dislocation, so the pair returns no band and never trades, and one bad afternoon defines it. Above 30 days: the save is refused — see the next card. Every save on this section restarts the measurement. Timeframe, period, both risk levels, the lookback and both floors are part of the bands' identity, so changing any one marks every pair's bands invalid. The bot keeps managing open deals but opens nothing new until each pair is recomputed — minutes on a short lookback, longer on a deep one. That is the price of a dial-fiddling session.

sections.title: 💾 The memory budget — sized for your server
sections.text: 💾 The memory budget — sized for your server Every pair in scope keeps its 1-minute history in memory , so the bands can be recomputed. At the shipped 1m × 30-day setting that is about 1.7 MB per pair — roughly 1 GB for a 600-pair auto scope . The budget is shared by every Optimized bot on the exchange, and it is sized from your server's actual RAM . Roughly what a scope costs at the shipped settings: 50 pairs ≈ 86 MB · 200 pairs ≈ 350 MB · 600 pairs ≈ 1 GB. Halve the lookback and you halve the memory. A scope that does not fit is refused at save, with the size named — "…needs 25,920,600 candles (~1.0 GB of memory) — over this machine's 18,790,481-candle (~0.7 GB) budget" — so you can decide between a narrower scope and a bigger server before anything runs, rather than finding out hours later. Why this changed. Earlier builds used one fixed budget on every install, chosen for a large machine. On a small server the bot would accept a scope it could not hold and then be killed by the operating system — while holding open positions . It now reads the machine and refuses up front instead. Only Optimized bots pay this. The Liq Scalper, TV Signal, Hedge and Manual bots keep no candle history in memory, so a server running those is unaffected. If you have measured your own box and want a different figure, set LIQHUNTER_OLB_BUDGET_CANDLES in the environment. Your number is used exactly as given, including one larger than the automatic reading — you know something the automatic reading does not. A rough server guide for a bot running an Optimized bot: 2 GB suits a scope of about 400 pairs or fewer; 4 GB comfortably runs a full auto scope; 8 GB if you run several Optimized bots with deep lookbacks. Servers running no Optimized bot are fine on 2 GB.

sections.title: 🧱 The 30-day lookback ceiling
sections.text: 🧱 The 30-day lookback ceiling How much history a pair may hold depends on the timeframe , because the two things you care about pull in opposite directions. Memory is charged on the span of history; band quality depends on the number of candles in it. A 1-minute band over 30 days gets 43,200 samples — far more than it needs — while paying the most memory of any setting. So short timeframes are held to a shorter span, and the ceiling grows as the timeframe does, up to 30 days. Ask for more and the save is refused, with the arithmetic , rather than accepted and quietly run on less. Timeframe Max lookback Candles the optimizer sees Memory per pair 1m 7 days 10,080 0.38 MB 3m 12.1 days 5,819 0.67 MB 5m 15.7 days 4,508 0.86 MB 15m 27.1 days 2,602 1.49 MB 30m and longer 30 days 1,440 and fewer 1.65 MB Asking for more is refused, not trimmed. Example: a 5-minute timeframe with a 60-day lookback answers in the save bar: 5m × period 5 over a 60d lookback needs 86,405 stored 1-minute candles per pair — over the 43,200-candle (30-day, ~1.7 MB per pair) window ceiling … it would run on 30d × period 5 instead, which is not what these settings say. Shorten the lookback to 30 days or less; nothing was saved. Check it yourself: 60 days of 5-minute candles is 17,280 candles, costing 17,281 × 5 = 86,405 minutes of history per pair. A longer timeframe does not buy more history. The ceiling is calendar time, not a candle count: 30 days is 43,200 candles at 1 minute, 8,640 at 5 minutes, 720 at 1 hour, 30 at 1 day. A bot saved before this rule keeps running, clamped, and says so. Example: a bot set to 45 days on 15 minutes runs on 30; the Screener's Optimized Values header reads lookback 30d and every pair row carries CLAMPED: lookback 30d instead of the 45d set … . You always see both numbers. Re-save at 30 days or less and the note goes. The VWMA Period is clamped by the same ceiling , because a period deep enough to blow the window would leave the pair warming forever on candles that will never be held. Example: a period of 500 on a 1-day timeframe becomes 29, since 30 days is 30 daily candles. The lookback can also be RAISED, not only trimmed. Bands need at least period+1 candles, so a period that is large next to a short lookback wins: a 4-hour period of 100 with a 1-day lookback runs on 16.8 days instead, because 1 day is only 6 candles at 4 hours. The save bar and every affected row say so with the arithmetic, the same way a trim does. It matters most on a coarse timeframe: the Short VWMA measurement skips its own first period candles while the long one does not, so a lookback pinned this close to the period can leave the short side very few — sometimes exactly one — candles to find a breach in. A longer lookback or a smaller period gives it real room; the Account stream names the exact count on a short print it touches. A second refusal is scope-wide: the ceiling is per pair, but the install also has a total candle budget. Example: 1-minute candles over 30 days needs 43,201 stored minutes per pair — fine across a 700-pair watched set (~30 million), refused across 1,000 pairs (43.2 million, over the ~40 million budget). The message names per pair, pairs in scope and total; shorten the lookback, choose a bigger candle, or narrow the pair list. That total is shared by every Optimized bot on this market, so a new bot can silence one you did not touch. The candles are one pool per market: a pair two bots both watch is stored once, at the deeper of their two needs, but the refusal above prices only the bot you are saving — as if it were the only claimant. Example: one bot on 1-minute candles over 30 days across a 700-pair watched set is ~30 million and saves fine; add a second, same candles and lookback, over 300 pairs the first one does not hold, and that save is also fine on its own — together they are 1,000 pairs and 43.2 million, over the budget. Whatever does not fit is refused per pair , in a fixed order by bot id and then pair, so the pairs that drop out can belong to either bot; those pairs stop taking entries and show over the candle memory budget on their Screener row. If a bot goes quiet right after you added or deepened another one, look there first. Nothing is ever saved half-applied. Both refusals happen before the write, so a rejected save leaves the bot on exactly the settings it had a moment ago.

sections.title: 🎚️ Signal filters — which liquidations get to speak
sections.text: 🎚️ Signal filters — which liquidations get to speak The bands decide how far . These three decide which prints are even worth looking at . They are checked before the band test, in the order listed. Liquidation sources · shipped Bybit USDT Perps — which feeds may wake this bot. A print contributes only a base coin ; the price, fair-value line, band test and order all come from this bot's own market listing for that coin. Example: a Bitcoin liquidation reported elsewhere wakes this bot's own Bitcoin perpetual, at this bot's own book — never the other venue's symbol or price. Get it wrong: more sources means more triggers describing markets you are not trading, fewer means less of the flow. None: impossible — deselecting the last re-selects it. A feed with a stream error is flagged amber under the picker. Min liquidation size · USD; shipped 0 = any — how big a forced order must be to count as an event. Example: at 300, a $180 print is refused with Below min size and a $340 one goes on to the band test. Get it wrong: too high and you see only cascades, precisely the moves most likely to keep going; at zero every dust liquidation is evaluated and entries are driven by the band alone, losing the "something real happened" confirmation. Min 24h Volume · millions of USD; shipped 0 = off — refuses pairs turning over less than this. Example: at 25, a pair doing $18.4M is refused with 24h volume $18.4M below min $25M . Get it wrong: too high excludes the small volatile pairs whose earned bands are the reason to run this bot. If 24h volume cannot be read at all, the print is refused, not waved through. Max 24h Volume · millions of USD; shipped 0 = off — refuses pairs busier than this. Example: at 500, Bitcoin is excluded and the mid-caps are not. Get it wrong: too low blacklists the majors without saying so, and the Screener shows them warming and never trading. The full gate, in order: not paused → the print's side matches Direction → not blacklisted → in scope → 24h volume inside the window → at least the minimum size → bands exist and are fresh → the fair-value line is fresh → price outside the band on that side. The first failure stops it, and every evaluation reaches the Recent signals rail with its exact reason, near misses included, as Inside band (-0.31% vs 0.42%) . Read that rail before changing a dial.

sections.title: 🕰️ Warming up, stale, and the quiet screen
sections.text: 🕰️ Warming up, stale, and the quiet screen This bot never guesses a band. If it cannot say what a pair's band is right now, it does not trade that pair — it says why, and how far along it is. That contract produces two states that look like failure and are not. Warming. A pair still loading history has no band and does not trade; every liquidation on it is refused as Bands not computed yet (warming 2,140/8640 candles) — no entry until they are , the two numbers being candles loaded against candles needed. How long: a 30-day window at 5 minutes is 8,640 candles per pair, loaded gently across the watch set so the exchange is not hammered; a wide set on a deep window takes a while on first run, and a newly added pair warms alone while everything else keeps trading. Get it wrong: shortening the lookback to make the number go down buys speed with less measurement. The Hub seed only accelerates this band warm-up. On a licensed install the app may download older one-minute candles from the Optimized Hub, but accepts them only after verifying the signed payload and an exact overlap against a live page from the exchange this bot trades. If you deepen a running bot's lookback, the larger history request gets one fresh verified download instead of relying only on slow venue paging. A timeout, bad signature, mismatch or unavailable Hub discards the whole seed and venue paging continues; it never changes the venue source of truth. This is separate from Volatility Filters : those smaller timeframe windows have their own Hub snapshot and their own warming state, and each one is re-read from the traded exchange to confirm it. Stale — catching up. A pair whose bands or candles have fallen behind is also refused, because values that look tradeable while pricing a market that has moved are worse than none. The ceiling is three refresh periods, never less than 15 minutes . Example: on 5 minutes bands refresh every 5 and go stale after 15; on 1 hour, after 3 hours; on 1 day, after 3 days. The refusal names the age — Stale — catching up (candles 22m old); no entry on old data — and clears when the feed is repaired. Cost: during a venue outage this bot trades nothing, on purpose. No band. A pair whose history never breached has nothing to measure, shows no band and cannot fire — normal on a very quiet pair with a short lookback. A floor does not fix it; a longer lookback or a higher Risk Level might. Full history but catching up. The closed-bar history and the current minute tail must both be ready. WEEX subscriptions now stay active independently of REST polling and deliver the previous minute when the exchange starts its successor. Existing candle pages repair startup prefixes and missed minutes. A real gap still blocks new entries until the missing data arrives. Queued or outside live-tail capacity. Optimized-only pairs join the same exact-venue one-minute tail without entering the Liq Scalper's roster. On supported streams, memory-qualified pairs can subscribe before REST admission; fresh candle frames maintain their tails without spending REST polling slots. The Hub supplies verified history while WebSockets keep it current. If a stream becomes stale, its pairs return to the bounded REST recovery budget. A pair outside that capacity has no band and no entry: restore the candle stream or narrow the pair list. Shortening the history window reduces backfill, but does not increase live-tail capacity. A cold or unavailable Hub can make warm-up take longer than five minutes. Where you watch it: Screener → Optimized Values , a tab that appears only while an Optimized bot exists in the market you are viewing. Each bot gets a table headed with the settings actually in force — 5m × 5 · lookback 30d · refresh every 5m — plus a warming count, and one row per pair: long band, short band, when each was last widened and by which candle, the next refresh, and the state. It refreshes every few seconds while keeping the current table in place. Switching account or market clears the old values immediately. A quiet screen is usually the bot working. "Why has nothing opened", in order: the pairs are warming; the bands are wider than today's moves; the deal caps are full; the print was under the minimum size. Warm-up and staleness show on the Optimized Values tab, everything else in the Recent signals rail. These are facts about a running bot, never a suggestion. Nothing on the Optimized Values tab recommends a setting — the bands shown are what the bot is trading this second, and the dials that move them are on the form. Candle readiness: “Preparing candle data” is normal during startup. Recently ready pairs keep their Ready display for up to ten seconds during a minute-boundary handoff; entry checks still require current candle data. Select a row’s status to see progress and diagnostic details. “New Pair with no significant history” means the exchange listing is newer than your lookback. Candles continue collecting automatically; the pair becomes eligible once its full history and current closed-minute data are ready, subject to your other entry filters. Memory limits and unavailable data stay visible, and no incomplete history is used for entries.

sections.title: 💵 Entry, ladder and exits — identical to the Liq Scalper
sections.text: 💵 Entry, ladder and exits — identical to the Liq Scalper Everything below the bands is the shared deal engine, behaving exactly as on the Liq Scalper — full mechanics in the entry section , the DCA section and take profit and stop loss . Worth stating twice: the bands change when you enter, and nothing else. They have no say in how big the deal is or how it ends. Size type · shipped Dollar — a fixed amount, or a percent of your settled wallet resolved to dollars once at open and frozen for the deal's life. Get it wrong: percent sizing grows your bets as the account grows, including during a losing streak that has not closed yet. Base order · shipped 15 USDT — the first order's notional . Example: 15 USDT at 10× commits 15 USDT of position for about 1.50 USDT of margin. Get it wrong: too small and the venue rejects the order under its minimum; too big matters less than the ladder underneath, which is what actually sizes this bot. Leverage · shipped 10× — changes margin, not order size: the same position ties up less collateral and liquidates sooner. Get it wrong: too high and a full ladder reaches the liquidation price before the last level fills. In Allowlist mode, leverage above a listed pair's venue maximum blocks the save and names the pair. Entry order type · shipped Market — Market takes the price and records only what the venue confirms filled. Aggressive limit posts as a maker at the touch and chases the book, keeping partial fills, with no deadline and no market fallback. Get it wrong: Market pays the spread on a fast print, but Aggressive limit can miss the trade entirely — on a liquidation snap-back, usually the more expensive mistake. DCA ladder — On / Off · shipped On — Off makes every deal the base order alone: one entry, one exit, no averaging, and nothing to rescue an entry that was early. DCA size type · shipped "% of entry" — dollars, a percent of wallet, or a percent of the deal's own entry, resolved to dollars once at open. A new bot ships on "% of entry" at 100 , so the first DCA equals the entry. Get it wrong: "% of entry" keeps the ladder proportional so raising the base order raises everything, a fixed dollar amount does not so a bigger entry quietly gets a shallower ladder, and "% of balance" grows the ladder with the account. First DCA · shipped 100 — read in the unit above, so 100 means "100% of the entry". Example: a 15 USDT entry gives a 15 USDT first DCA. Get it wrong: too big and the deal's real size is set by the ladder rather than the base order you thought you chose; at zero there is no averaging at all. Deviation · %, shipped 8 — how far below the entry the first DCA level sits; later gaps are this one grown by the step scale. Example: 8 on a long opened at 100 puts the first level at 92. Get it wrong: too small and the ladder fills on ordinary noise, spending the deep levels before anything went wrong; too big and price reaches your stop or reverses before the first level ever fills. DCA style: Static / Scaled ATR · the tab above Deviation — this bot has the same DCA-style tab the Liq Scalper does. Static uses the Deviation above on every pair; Scaled ATR replaces it with each pair's own volatility (ATR multiplier × ATR ÷ price, held between a minimum and maximum you set), worked out once when the deal opens and frozen for that deal. Get it wrong: on Scaled ATR, a pair whose ATR cannot be worked out is not opened at all — there is no fall back to Deviation — so a stalled candle feed is a bot that quietly stops trading. It tells you: the pair's row says refused with the reason, and an alert fires if nothing at all can be priced. On a position this bot did not open , “when the deal opens” means when the position opened, not when the bot picked it up, so the same position gets the same ladder whether it is adopted now or after a restart. Where the exchange publishes no open time — Bybit and Aster do not — the ATR is dated from the takeover and the bot says so. It never substitutes your Static distances. The full explanation is under Dollar Cost Averaging Orders in the Liq Scalper section above. Orders · shipped 3 — how many DCA levels exist. Example: 3 levels with the shipped scales reach 56% below the entry; a fourth would reach 120%, which is not a price. Get it wrong: each extra level doubles the deal's potential size — five levels on a 15 USDT entry is 480 USDT of notional, not 120. Volume scale · shipped 2 — each level's size is the previous multiplied by this. Example, all defaults on a 15 USDT entry: DCAs of 15, 30 and 60 USDT, so a fully filled deal is 120 USDT of notional — eight times the base order — using about 12 USDT of margin at 10×. Get it wrong: too big and the last level is most of the deal, so the worst price you paid sets your average entry. At 1.0 every level is the same size. Step scale · shipped 2 — each gap is the previous gap multiplied by this. Example, defaults: gaps of 8%, 16% and 32% put levels at 8%, 24% and 56% below the entry, so a long opened at 100 fills at 92, 76 and 44 — 120 USDT for about 2.07 units, an average entry near 57.9 . Get it wrong: too big and the deep levels only fill in a genuine collapse. At 1.0 the levels space evenly at 8%, 16%, 24%. Orders on exchange · shipped 3 — how many DCA limits rest on the venue at once, the rest posted as the near ones fill. Get it wrong: too low and a violent candle passes a level that was not resting yet; too high and you consume order slots for prices days away.

sections.title: 🎯 Exits — take profit, stop loss, and what bounds a deal
sections.text: 🎯 Exits — take profit, stop loss, and what bounds a deal The exit half of the shared deal engine at its shipped values, and what bounds a deal's size. Take profit — On / Off · shipped On — Off means the only exits are the stop loss or your own hand. Get it wrong: Off leaves unattended deals that never close. Take profit type · shipped single / Fixed % — one target for the whole deal ( Fixed % , Trailing or ATR — same three-way source as the Liq Scalper), or a Ladder closing it in pieces at increasing distances, whose own last step can also be switched to trailing. Example: single takes 100% at 0.7%; a ladder might take 50% at 1%, 25% at 2%, 25% at 3%. Get it wrong: a ladder pays more fees and leaves the deal's tail open when the move ends — a liquidation snap-back is often over in minutes, which argues for the single target here unless you have a reason. Take profit · %, shipped 0.7 — the single target, measured from the deal's average entry, resting on the exchange. Example: the 120 USDT ladder above, averaging near 57.9, exits at about 58.34 for roughly 0.84 USDT. Get it wrong: too tight and fees and funding eat it — at 0.01% every eight hours, a month of funding alone is about 0.9% of notional; too wide and the deal that was 0.6% up gives it all back. TP ladder · Ladder type only; at least two steps — a table of steps, each a profit % from average entry and a % of the deal to close, increasing down the table; the last step can be switched to trailing instead. It also carries the optional Ladder SL controls: a switch, a mode (trail a set number of levels behind the last filled take-profit, or move to breakeven once step N fills and stay), how many fills arm it, and a buffer past breakeven. Full behaviour in the take-profit section . Get it wrong: every extra step pays another set of fees. Stop loss — On / Off · shipped Off — off means no automatic loss cut and the DCA ladder is the entire plan for a deal that goes wrong. Switching it on offers 30% as a starting number, not a recommendation. Offset from · shipped Initial entry price — what the percentage measures against: the initial entry (fixed at open, so the ladder cannot walk the stop down), the current average entry (moves with every DCA fill), or account balance (placed where the loss equals that percentage of your balance). Get it wrong: "current average" plus a deep ladder retreats forever; "initial entry" plus a deep ladder gives a stop the ladder may reach before price does. Stop loss · %; meaning depends on the offset above — Example: 30% from an initial entry of 100 stops at 70, well inside the 56% ladder level, so on defaults the last level never fills and the stop cuts first. Get it wrong: too tight and the ladder is decoration; too wide and it is paperwork, not protection. Check the two against each other before saving. Nothing caps a deal's total size but the ladder you configure. There is no hidden ceiling on notional. Read the full-ladder number, not the base order — on shipped defaults that is eight times the Entry box, and it multiplies again by your deal caps. This bot owns no hedge engine. On supported USDT-futures contexts a separately created and enabled Hedge Bot may attach to its deals; otherwise the ladder, take profit and stop loss are the deal's entire protection.

sections.title: 🧮 End to end: two pairs, one set of settings
sections.text: 🧮 End to end: two pairs, one set of settings One bot, one configuration, two very different pairs — the whole argument for the Optimized bot. The settings. Direction Both · Watched set · Long Risk 2, Short Risk 2 · Min Long 0%, Min Short 0% · Timeframe 5 minutes · Period 5 · Lookback 30 days · Min liquidation size 300 USD · volume filters off · base order 15 USDT at 10× · Max both 2. Nothing here is per pair, and there is no band in the list. What loads first. 30 days of 5-minute candles is 8,640 per pair; until a pair has them it reads warming 0/8640 and refuses every liquidation. Both pairs below are past that. What the measurement returned. The quiet major rarely strayed far from its own average, so a tight band already kept every excursion under two candles. The fast alt's band had to widen repeatedly. BTCUSDT — long band 0.42% , short band 0.47% . With its average at 62,400 : a long needs a print at or below 62,400 × (1 − 0.0042) = 62,137.92 ; a short needs 62,400 × 1.0047 = 62,693.28 . WIFUSDT — long band 2.10% , short band 2.35% . With its average at 2.4000 : a long needs 2.4000 × (1 − 0.0210) = 2.3496 ; a short needs 2.4000 × 1.0235 = 2.4564 . The comparison that matters. Had you typed one band into the Liq Scalper instead: One 2% band. Bitcoin's trigger sits at 62,400 × 0.98 = 61,152 , nearly five times further out than its own 30 days justify — it would essentially never fire, and the pair would be dead weight. WIF would land near its measured level by luck alone. One 0.45% band. Bitcoin would be about right; WIF's trigger at 2.4000 × 0.9955 = 2.3892 sits well inside its ordinary five-minute noise, so the bot fades every wobble, including the ones starting a trend. That is the failure mode this bot removes. The optimized answer. Each pair is judged at the distance it earned — 0.42% and 2.10%. Same settings, two bands, because they are two different animals. What BTCUSDT must clear before opening , since crossing the band is the last gate rather than the only one: not paused → the print is a long liquidation and Direction allows longs → in the watched set and not blacklisted → at least $300 → bands computed and under 15 minutes old (three 5-minute refreshes) → fair-value line fresh → the mark at or below 62,137.92. Then the shared engine checks the caps: with Max both at 2 and two deals open, this one is refused and logged to the Recent signals rail. And what happens next. Say the long fills at 62,100. The base order is 15 USDT of notional (about 1.50 USDT of margin), the take profit rests 0.7% above the average entry, and the ladder waits at 8%, 24% and 56% below — 57,132, 47,196 and 27,324 — sized 15, 30 and 60 USDT. Fully filled that is 120 USDT of notional at an average near 36,000, with the take profit moving down with it. Nothing caps that but the ladder you configured. One more turn of the dial. Raising Long Risk from 2 to 3 says a 15-minute excursion is tolerable rather than a 10-minute one. WIF's long band tightens from 2.10% to about 1.62% and its trigger climbs from 2.3496 to 2.3611 — closer to spot, so more entries at shallower dislocations, more of them landing in trends. Saving invalidates and recomputes every band, so the bot goes quiet for a few refreshes first.

sections.title: 📡 What is the TV Signal bot?
sections.text: 📡 What is the TV Signal bot? What it does: it opens and runs a deal when TradingView tells it to. Your alert sends a short message to a private web address belonging to this bot; the bot checks the message is really yours, opens the position, and manages it with the same engine as every other bot — DCA ladder, take profit, stop loss, full P&L accounting. When to use it: you already have something on TradingView you trust to time entries and want it executed properly rather than firing naked market orders through a relay. The one thing that makes this bot different Something else decides WHEN. This bot decides SIZE, DCA and EXIT. It never looks at the market to decide whether to trade — your alert is the entire trigger. This form controls everything after the word "go". There is no second opinion. The bot does not re-check your signal against its own idea of fair value; if the alert arrives and the guards pass, it trades. There is no queue. A signal is judged the instant it lands, and a refusal — paused bot, wrong side, pair not allowed, caps full — is permanent. Nothing is stored and retried. Configure first, alert second. Size, caps, ladder and exits are read as the signal arrives, so whatever is saved when the alert fires is what the deal gets. You can run ten. Each has its own name, web address, secret, pair list and deal settings, so a fast scalping alert and a slow swing alert stop sharing one configuration. Your alert can also manage deals : close one, close everything, add funds, fill the next ladder step, change a deal's take profit or stop, pause or resume the bot. Full list in the message formats . Every signal is logged, accepted or refused , with its exact reason, in the Recent signals panel beside the form. Read it before you blame the strategy.

sections.title: 🧩 Naming, direction, caps and which pairs it may touch
sections.text: 🧩 Naming, direction, caps and which pairs it may touch What this bot is called, what it may trade, and how many deals it may hold. All are checked before anything is ordered, so a signal outside them never reaches the exchange. Identity and where it trades Bot name — up to 48 characters, shown on the My Bots card and the fill messages, and used once at creation to build the tail of the web address. Renaming later is cosmetic: the web address never changes , so existing alerts keep working. Get it wrong: two similar names and you will eventually paste one bot's message into the other bot's alert. The account and market it belongs to — not a field: the bot is created on whatever the header had selected and trades there for life. To trade elsewhere, switch the header and create one there. Get it wrong: the alert is perfect and every signal is refused because the bot lives somewhere this app is not currently running. On a spot market the form changes shape: direction is forced to Long, leverage disappears, and the "open short" template is not offered — you cannot sell a coin you do not own. Get it wrong: half your alerts log a refusal you will spend an evening debugging. Direction Direction — Long / Short / Both · ships as Both — a filter on your alert, not an instruction to it: a Long-only bot refuses an "open short" message and logs bot trades long only . Get it wrong: a two-way strategy silently loses half its trades, and you keep the wrong half. How many deals at once Max longs · ships as 2 — the most long deals held; shown on Long or Both. Get it wrong: set high, a busy day puts you into ten correlated longs that go offside together. Max shorts · ships as 2 — the same ceiling for shorts; shown on Short or Both. Get it wrong: as above, and in a squeeze it happens faster. Max both · total · ships as 2 — the combined ceiling, shown only on Both, and a genuine third limit rather than a sum. Example: at 2/2/2, a bot holding one long and one short refuses the next signal with Max pairs open even though neither side is full. Get it wrong: set it to longs + shorts and the total cap is gone. An entry still being placed reserves its slot , so a burst of alerts cannot overshoot a cap. Two ceilings sit above these: the per-market caps on the Accounts page, counting every deal bot on the account, and Isolation mode, which stops new entries past its margin threshold. The lower limit wins. Which pairs Pairs — Any pair / Allowlist · ships as Any pair — Any pair trades whatever symbol the alert names, if the market has it and the blacklists allow it; Allowlist trades only your listed symbols and refuses the rest with not in this bot's pair list . Get it wrong: on Any pair, one mistyped symbol opens a deal on a coin you have never looked at. Allowed pairs · Allowlist only — the searchable picker. Saving is blocked if a listed pair cannot support your leverage, and the error names the pairs and their exchange maximums. Get it wrong: leave a pair off and its alerts are refused forever, with the reason only in Recent signals. Blacklist — symbols this bot never trades, comma- or space-separated, case-insensitive ( lunausdt = LUNAUSDT ). The universal blacklist in Settings applies on top, and the blacklist always wins , including over an Allowlist entry. Get it wrong: nothing breaks loudly — you keep trading the delisting-risk coin you meant to exclude.

sections.title: ⚙️ The rest of the form, field by field
sections.text: ⚙️ The rest of the form, field by field The webhook panel at the top of the form holds the connection to TradingView; the panel beside it tells you what actually happened. Webhook Webhook URL · read-only, with a Copy button — the private address TradingView sends this bot's messages to, fixed for the bot's life and unchanged by renaming. The catch that gets nearly everyone: the address shown is built from whatever address you are browsing the app on , so if you reach the app locally you must swap the front part for your public address before pasting it into an alert. See the setup walkthrough . Get it wrong: the alert fires, TradingView reports a delivery failure you never look at, and nothing appears in Recent signals. Secret · read-only, with a Copy button — the password proving a message came from you: generated per bot, and required inside every message. Treat it exactly like an exchange API key — reasons in the card below . Get it wrong: anyone holding both this and the address can make this bot trade. Rotate secret — break old alerts · red button — replaces the secret, asking twice and requiring you to type ROTATE ; the old one dies instantly. Get it wrong: press it casually and every alert you built for this bot fails until you edit each one by hand. Alert message templates — ready-made messages underneath, each with a Copy button and already carrying this bot's secret, also reachable from My Bots via ⧉ Payloads . Always copy from here. Get it wrong: a hand-typed message with a smart quote or stray comma is invalid and the bot answers "unauthorized" — a typing problem that reads like a secret problem. Signal handling Duplicate cooldown · seconds, ships as 300 — TradingView cheerfully delivers the same alert twice; this absorbs it. After an open succeeds, an identical open — same direction, same symbol — is refused for this many seconds and logged as duplicate (within 300s cooldown) . It applies to opens only (close, add funds, fill-next-level and the TP/stop overrides are never suppressed), counts per direction and symbol , and the clock starts only on an open that succeeded . Example: at 300, two identical SOLUSDT long alerts twenty seconds apart make one deal; nine minutes apart they make two. 0 switches it off. Get it wrong: at 0 a double-delivered alert opens two deals and eats two slots; far too high silences a strategy that legitimately re-enters the same pair. Saving, and the panel beside the form Save & enable — writes every setting and enables the bot , so it resumes a bot you had paused either in My Bots or by message. Changes apply to the next signal; open deals keep the settings they opened with. Get it wrong: edit the form to "have a look" while the bot is deliberately paused, press Save, and it is live again. Cancel — leaves without saving and returns to My Bots. Get it wrong: a long editing session and one wrong button, and the bot keeps running the old configuration. Recent signals · the panel right of the form — every signal received, newest first, with a tick or cross, the action, symbol, exact reason and time. Rejected messages appear too, bad secrets included. It is the only honest answer to "did my alert arrive?", since TradingView will not show you the reply. Get it wrong: ignore it and you will rewrite a working strategy to fix a blacklisted pair.

sections.title: 💵 How the entry is sized and placed
sections.text: 💵 How the entry is sized and placed How much the bot buys or sells when your alert fires, and how the order reaches the exchange. Everything after this is measured against what actually filled. Size type — Dollar / % of balance · ships as Dollar — a fixed USDT amount, or a share of your wallet converted to an amount once, when the deal opens , then frozen for that deal's life. If the balance cannot be read at that moment, the entry is refused rather than guessed at. Get it wrong: on % of balance every deal grows as the account grows, losing ones included. Base order · ships as 15 USDT — the opening order, in USDT or as a percentage of the wallet. This is position size, not margin. Example: 200 USDT at 10× buys 200 USDT of the pair for about 20 USDT of margin; on % of balance, 2% of a 5,000 USDT wallet is a 100 USDT position. A single alert can override it — a message carrying "size":500 opens that deal at 500 USDT and skips the percentage entirely. Get it wrong: too small and the exchange rejects the order under the pair's minimum, which raising leverage does not fix. Leverage · ships as 10×, hidden where markets have none — set on the pair before the order goes in; it changes the margin tied up, not the position size. Example: the same 200 USDT position uses about 20 USDT of margin at 10× and 10 USDT at 20× — half the margin, and a liquidation price much closer to your entry. On an Allowlist, saving is blocked when a listed pair's exchange maximum is below this. Get it wrong: high leverage plus a deep ladder is the classic way to be liquidated before the ladder finishes. Entry order type — Market / Aggressive limit · ships as Market — Market takes the price that is there, immediately, and records only the quantity and price the exchange confirms as filled. Aggressive limit posts as a maker order at the near touch and follows the book until it is filled, keeping any partial fills — cheaper in fees, but it has no deadline and no fallback to market, so on a fast move it can simply not fill. Get it wrong: choose Aggressive limit for a breakout strategy and you will miss precisely the trades the strategy exists to catch.

sections.title: 📉 The DCA ladder
sections.text: 📉 The DCA ladder The extra orders that buy more as price moves against the deal, pulling the average entry toward current price so a smaller recovery reaches take profit. It is the same engine as the Liq Scalper's, so the full treatment and the warnings live in the DCA ladder section . The four rules, stated plainly The ladder is static. Each step's size is the first step times the volume scale, again and again, worked out when the deal opens and never re-planned. Distances are measured from the original entry , never the moving average. A step at 24% stays 24% from the first fill for the deal's whole life. Steps fill on touch — no bounce, no minimum time between fills, no cooldown. One fast wick can fill the entire ladder in seconds. There is no cap on the total. The ladder you configure is the size ceiling — read the worked example below and multiply it by your deal caps before deciding it is safe. The settings, in form order DCA ladder On / Off · section heading switch, ships On — Off makes each deal the opening order alone, whichever DCA style tab is under it (static, Scaled ATR or the builder), leaving only the deal drawer or an "add funds" / "fill next level" message to average. Get it wrong: off with a tight take profit means the deal has no way back once offside. DCA size type — Dollar / % of balance / % of entry · a new bot starts on % of entry — what "First DCA" means: a fixed USDT amount, a share of wallet frozen at open, or a share of the deal's own opening order, so 100 makes the first step equal to the entry and it scales with a per-alert size override. Get it wrong: switching from Dollar to a percentage without changing the number is how a 10 USDT first step silently becomes 10% of wallet. First DCA · a new bot starts at 100, meaning "% of entry" 100 — the first step's size in the unit above, so a brand-new TV Signal bot's first ladder step equals the entry . It is only a starting value; a bot you have saved keeps what you saved. Get it wrong: leaving 100 with a volume scale of 2 makes the ladder far larger than the entry — the point, but only if you have priced it. Deviation · %, ships as 8 — how far from the original entry the first step sits. Get it wrong: too tight and it fills on ordinary noise, spending your deepest ammunition on nothing. DCA style: Static / Scaled ATR · the tab above Deviation — this bot has the same DCA-style tab the Liq Scalper does. Static uses the Deviation above on every pair; Scaled ATR replaces it with each pair's own volatility (ATR multiplier × ATR ÷ price, held between a minimum and maximum you set), worked out once when the deal opens and frozen for that deal. Get it wrong: on Scaled ATR, a pair whose ATR cannot be worked out is not opened at all — there is no fall back to Deviation — so a stalled candle feed is a bot that quietly stops trading. It tells you: the pair's row says refused with the reason, and an alert fires if nothing at all can be priced. On a position this bot did not open , “when the deal opens” means when the position opened, not when the bot picked it up, so the same position gets the same ladder whether it is adopted now or after a restart. Where the exchange publishes no open time — Bybit and Aster do not — the ATR is dated from the takeover and the bot says so. It never substitutes your Static distances. The full explanation is under Dollar Cost Averaging Orders in the Liq Scalper section above. Orders · ships as 3 — how many steps in total. Get it wrong: each extra step multiplies the money at risk by the volume scale — step eight at a scale of 2 is 128 times step one. Volume scale · ships as 2 — the multiplier on each step's size : at 2, sizes go 100, 200, 400, 800; at 1 every step is equal. Get it wrong: the most dangerous number on the page — raising it from 1.5 to 2 roughly doubles the money committed at the bottom. Step scale · ships as 2 — the multiplier on each step's distance , with the gaps growing and adding up: deviation 8 and step scale 2 give gaps of 8, 16 and 32, so steps at 8%, 24% and 56% . At 1 they space evenly. Get it wrong: at 1 with many orders the whole ladder is spent inside a small move. Orders on exchange · ships as 3, minimum 1 — how many unfilled steps rest on the exchange at once, the rest placed as earlier ones fill. It changes nothing about where or how large the steps are. Get it wrong: at 1 on a fast pair, a wick can pass a step before its order was placed. A worked example, with the shipped numbers Take a long opened by an alert at $100 , base order 200 USDT , DCA size type % of entry at 100 , volume scale 2 , deviation 8% , step scale 2 , 3 orders. Sizes: the first step is 100% of the 200 USDT entry, so 200 USDT; then 400; then 800. Distances: 8%, then 8+16 = 24%, then 24+32 = 56% below $100 — so $92.00, $76.00 and $44.00. Fills: 200 USDT at $100 = 2.0000 units · 200 at $92 = 2.1739 · 400 at $76 = 5.2632 · 800 at $44 = 18.1818. If all four fill: 1,600 USDT committed for 27.6189 units, an average entry of $57.93 , and about 160 USDT of margin at 10× . What that means: a deal you thought of as "200 USDT" is 1,600 USDT after a 56% move, and with a deal cap of 2, two at once is 3,200 USDT. Nothing in the app stops this. Saving regenerates the ladder. The distances are recalculated from deviation, step scale and order count every time you press Save, and the result is written over whatever was stored. Change one of those three and the whole ladder moves.

sections.title: 🎯 Take profit and stop loss
sections.text: 🎯 Take profit and stop loss Both behave as they do on every other bot, so the full treatment is in Exit orders — take profit and stop loss . Here is this form, plus what is specific to a signal-driven bot. The rules, stated plainly Take profit is measured from the average entry and re-anchors every time that average moves — every ladder fill, every manual add. The take profit rests on the exchange as a reduce-only order, so it fills even if this app is offline. The stop loss does not : the app watches it and closes at market. Fixed % is a target; Trailing and ATR are the two alternatives, and the last ladder step can also be switched to trailing — the same three-way source and ladder shown in Exit orders . Fixed % does not follow price up; Trailing does, once armed. A single alert can override one deal's take profit or stop without touching these settings — see the message formats . Take profit Take profit On / Off · section heading switch, ships On — Off leaves only a close message, the stop loss, or your own hand to end the deal, whichever take-profit type (Fixed %, ATR or Trailing) was chosen under it; the switch reads On whenever any of those is running. Get it wrong: off without exit alerts leaves no way out but the stop. Take profit type — Percentage from average price / Ladder (multiple TPs) · ships as Percentage — one target for the whole position, or several partials. Get it wrong: choose the ladder and leave its rows at defaults, and your real targets are not the ones you meant. Take profit · %, ships as 0.7 — the single target, above the average entry for a long and below for a short. Example: the ladder above averaged $57.93 on 1,600 USDT, so 0.7% targets $58.34 , worth about 11.20 USDT before fees. Get it wrong: a target inside the fee spread turns winning trades into losing ones. Take profit — ladder (shown when the type is Ladder) The step rows: Profit % and Close % of deal — 2 to 10 rows, each closing that share of the deal at that profit. Profits must increase down the rows and the closes must total 100 or the form refuses to save; the default offered is 1%×50, 2%×25, 3%×25. Example: on that $57.93 average those become $58.51 for half, $59.09 for a quarter, $59.67 for the last quarter. Get it wrong: weighting the far rows leaves most of the deal exposed for a target it may never reach. + Add step and Even split — add a row, or rewrite every close share equal and totalling 100. Get it wrong: Even split overwrites the weighting you just typed. Ladder SL · On/Off chip, ships Off — on, the stop moves as ladder steps fill, and the three fields below appear. Get it wrong: on a choppy pair a walking stop closes at breakeven just before the move you were waiting for. SL mode — Level based / Average entry — Level based trails a set number of filled targets behind the last; Average entry moves to breakeven when the chosen target fills and stays. The form prints the meaning of whichever you pick. Get it wrong: they behave very differently in a retrace, and only one protects gains you have banked. Arm after · filled targets, ships as 1 — how many TP steps must fill before the walking stop switches on. Get it wrong: at 1 on a jumpy pair, one early partial arms a stop you did not want yet. SL buffer · %, ships as 0 — how far past breakeven, toward profit, the moved stop sits. Get it wrong: at 0 it sits exactly at breakeven, where fees make the "flat" exit a small loss. Stop loss Stop loss On / Off · section heading switch, ships Off — off means a deal that goes wrong keeps averaging down until the ladder is spent, though a "set stop" message can still arm one for a single deal. Get it wrong: with no cap on ladder size, off means the only floor is the exchange's liquidation — a deliberate choice, not a default to leave unread. Offset from — Initial entry price / Current entry price (avg) / Account balance · ships as Initial entry price — what the percentage measures against: a fixed price set at open on the same anchor the ladder uses; the average, which keeps moving away as the ladder fills; or your wallet, closing the deal when its loss reaches that share. Get it wrong: the average-based one retreats every time the deal gets worse, the opposite of what most people expect. Stop loss · %, shows 30 when switched on — the number, meaning whatever the choice above says. Examples on that long opened at $100: Initial entry 30% closes at $70.00 , between ladder steps two and three, so the deal stops out before the last step fills; Current entry (avg) 30% on a $57.93 average closes at $40.55 ; Account balance 30% on a 1,000 USDT wallet closes it 300 USDT down, whatever the price. Get it wrong: a stop inside your own ladder guarantees you pay for every step and exit anyway — check it against the 8 / 24 / 56% distances before saving. This bot has no hedging of its own. On supported markets a separately created Hedge Bot can attach to its deals; otherwise the ladder, take profit and stop are the entire protection.

sections.title: 🔗 Connecting TradingView, start to finish
sections.text: 🔗 Connecting TradingView, start to finish The one bot where part of the setup happens outside the app. Work through it in order — skipping the reachability step is why most first attempts go quiet. Before you start — what TradingView requires A paid TradingView plan. Webhook notifications are not on the free tier. A publicly reachable address. TradingView's servers must open it from the open internet, so a home or office address, anything starting 192.168, and "localhost" are all unreachable. A standard web port — the ones a browser uses when you type an address with no port. On a custom port, put a reverse proxy in front and give TradingView the proxy's address. A certificate a browser trusts. Your secret travels inside the message, so an unencrypted connection publishes your trading credential to every network in the path. Self-signed will not be accepted. Step 1 — create the bot and copy its two values Select the account and market in the header. The bot is created there and trades there for life. Create Bot → TV Signal, name it, configure direction, pairs, size, ladder and exits, then press Save & enable . The webhook panel now shows the Webhook URL and the Secret . Copy the URL. Check the front of that URL , which is built from the address you are browsing on. If it begins with a local address or a port number, replace that part with your public address and keep the path at the end exactly as it is — that ending is unique to this bot. Step 2 — build the alert in TradingView Open the chart of the pair you actually intend to trade — read the warning in the message formats before going further. Create an alert (the alarm-clock icon, or right-click the chart). On the Condition tab, set what triggers it. Set the frequency to Once Per Bar Close unless you have a reason not to. "Once Per Bar" fires on an unclosed candle that can still reverse, which is how a strategy that tested clean opens deals on signals that never printed. Set the expiry open-ended if your plan allows, so the alert does not quietly die in a month. On the Notifications tab, tick Webhook URL and paste the address from step 1. In the Message box, delete TradingView's default and paste one of this bot's templates — from the webhook panel or the ⧉ Payloads button. The message must be the template and nothing else : no greeting, no explanation, no extra line. Fix the symbol in the message if needed — see the message formats . Save the alert. Step 3 — prove it works before you trust it Fire the alert once — wait for a real trigger, or make a throwaway alert whose condition is true immediately. Open the bot's form and read Recent signals . Something must appear within seconds. A green tick means accepted and opened. A red cross means it arrived and was refused, with the reason beside it — the troubleshooting card explains each one. Nothing at all means it never arrived: the address is wrong or unreachable, and nothing inside this app can fix that. Go back to the requirements above. If your signal comes from a Pine strategy script A strategy script sends its own message per order. Put the payload in each order call's alert_message — single quotes around the Pine text so the payload's double quotes survive — and set the alert's Message box to {{strategy.order.alert_message}} : strategy.entry("L", strategy.long, alert_message = '{"secret":"whu_…","action":"open_long","symbol":"SOLUSDT"}') strategy.close("L", alert_message = '{"secret":"whu_…","action":"close","symbol":"SOLUSDT"}') For an indicator rather than a strategy, alert(msg, alert.freq_once_per_bar_close) works the same way. Replace whu_… with your bot's real secret from the webhook panel.

sections.title: ✉️ The message formats this bot accepts
sections.text: ✉️ The message formats this bot accepts The message is a single line of text in the alert's Message box. Every message needs the secret and an action ; everything except "close everything", "pause" and "resume" also needs a symbol . Copy these from the webhook panel — the copies there already contain your bot's real secret, shown below as whu_… . ⚠ The {{ticker}} trap — read this before you build a single alert. {{ticker}} is TradingView's placeholder, and it resolves to the symbol of the chart the alert was created on , saved with the alert. Example: an alert you happened to build while a BTC chart was open sends BTCUSDT forever , whatever pair you meant and whatever chart you look at later. Switching charts afterwards changes nothing. This is the most common way this bot silently trades the wrong pair — it does not error, it opens a perfectly valid deal on the wrong coin. The fix is to write the symbol in literally: replace "symbol":"{{ticker}}" with "symbol":"SOLUSDT" . Keep {{ticker}} only when you are deliberately building one alert per chart. Opening a deal {"secret":"whu_…","action":"open_long","symbol":"{{ticker}}"} {"secret":"whu_…","action":"open_short","symbol":"{{ticker}}"} {"secret":"whu_…","action":"open_long","symbol":"{{ticker}}","size":100} open_long / open_short — opens a deal on everything the form specifies, after every guard: direction, pair list, blacklists, deal caps, account limits, and whether another bot already holds that symbol. The optional size is that one deal's position size in USDT, overriding Base order. Example: with the form set to 15 USDT, "size":100 opens a 100 USDT position — and on a "% of entry" 100 ladder, that deal's first step is 100 USDT too, not 15. On a spot market, "open short" is not offered and would be refused if sent. Optionally name the alert with "name" (or "alert" , "alertName" , "id" , "strategy" ) and the deal's notification says which alert opened it — {"secret":"whu_…","action":"open_long","symbol":"SOLUSDT","name":"EMA cross 15m"} . Without one it just says the deal came from a TradingView alert. Closing {"secret":"whu_…","action":"close","symbol":"{{ticker}}"} {"secret":"whu_…","action":"close_all"} close — closes that symbol's deal at market, cancelling its resting ladder and exit orders in the same move, and names the estimated result. close_all — closes every deal this bot holds and reports how many closed. It takes no symbol and never touches another bot's deals. Get it wrong: these are the only exits a bot with take profit switched off has. If your strategy sends entries but no exits, do not switch take profit off. Managing an open deal {"secret":"whu_…","action":"add_funds","symbol":"{{ticker}}","usd":50} {"secret":"whu_…","action":"dca_now","symbol":"{{ticker}}"} {"secret":"whu_…","action":"set_tp","symbol":"{{ticker}}","value":1.5} {"secret":"whu_…","action":"set_sl","symbol":"{{ticker}}","value":30} add_funds — buys more at market for the USDT amount you name, without using a ladder step, and re-anchors the take profit. The amount is required. dca_now — fills the next ladder step immediately at market rather than waiting for price, using that step up. set_tp — changes that one deal's take profit. Example: "value":1.5 moves its target to 1.5% from its average entry, leaving every other deal and the form untouched. set_sl — the same for the stop, measured as the form's "Offset from" says; 0 disarms that deal's stop. All four act only on a deal this bot holds, and the cooldown never suppresses them. Get it wrong: firing dca_now from a repeating alert walks straight down your ladder in minutes. Pausing the whole bot {"secret":"whu_…","action":"pause"} {"secret":"whu_…","action":"resume"} pause — stops new entries only ; open deals keep their ladder, take profit and stop, and close messages still work. Wire it to a "market conditions are bad" alert. resume — allows new entries again. A pause sent this way does not survive a restart , and pressing Save also undoes it. For a pause that sticks, use the bot's card in My Bots. Get it wrong: assume it is permanent and the bot trades again after the next restart. How the symbol is read The symbol is tidied up before use: capitalised, anything before a colon dropped, a trailing .P removed, and punctuation stripped. So BYBIT:SOLUSDT.P , SOL/USDT and solusdt all become SOLUSDT . It does not translate between quote currencies. A chart of SOL priced in dollars gives SOLUSD , which is not SOLUSDT — the bot will look for a pair by that name, fail to find a price, and refuse the signal. Chart the venue and the quote currency you actually trade.

sections.title: 🔑 The secret is a credential — treat it like one
sections.text: 🔑 The secret is a credential — treat it like one Anyone holding this bot's address and its secret can make it trade — no password, no session, no access to this app, because the address sits outside the login (TradingView cannot log in). They can open and close positions, add money to a deal, move its take profit and stop, and pause the bot. The only limits are the ones you set on this form. It is unique to this bot , so a leak is contained to one bot and a message copied from the wrong bot's panel authorises nothing. It is never rotated for you. No expiry, no renewal — it stays valid until you replace it. Rotating breaks every existing alert for this bot, immediately. The old value dies the moment rotation completes, and every alert carrying it fails on its next trigger with no warning on the TradingView side. This app cannot update your TradingView alerts. After a rotation you must open each affected alert and paste a freshly copied message in by hand. The rotation button asks twice and requires you to type ROTATE — deliberate friction, not a formality. Where it leaks: a screenshot of the form, a pasted alert message in a chat or forum, an exported strategy script with the payload inline, an unencrypted address. Redact it like an API key. If you suspect a leak: rotate first, repair the alerts after. A broken alert costs a missed trade; a live secret in someone else's hands costs the account's positions. A message with a wrong secret is still recorded in Recent signals as a rejection with no symbol. A run of those you did not cause is worth taking seriously.

sections.title: 🧯 The alert fired and nothing happened
sections.text: 🧯 The alert fired and nothing happened Sorted by how often each is the answer. One question splits the list in half, so answer it first: open the bot's form and look at Recent signals. If the alert is there, it arrived and the app has already said why it was refused. If not, it never arrived and no setting in this app is the cause. Nothing appears in Recent signals — it never arrived The address is not reachable from the internet — by far the most common cause. A local address, a home network address or an unusual port cannot be delivered to; check it against the setup walkthrough . The address was copied with the wrong front on it. The box builds it from however you are browsing, so a copy taken locally is a local address. Preserve the path at the end exactly. The webhook box was never ticked. Pasting the address into the alert without enabling the webhook option sends nothing. The plan does not include webhooks , or the alert has expired or was never saved. The certificate is self-signed or expired. Delivery is refused before your bot ever sees it. It appears with a red cross — it arrived and was refused Unauthorised / a rejection with no symbol — the secret did not match, usually because the message is malformed rather than the secret being wrong: a smart quote, a trailing comma, extra text above or below, or a message copied from a different bot. Re-copy the template and paste it as the whole message. Paused — disabled in My Bots, or a pause message got there first. A paused bot actively refuses signals rather than replaying them later, so what arrived while it was paused is gone. Resume it — and note that pressing Save also resumes it. Duplicate within the cooldown — the same direction and symbol opened recently. Expected; lower the cooldown only if your strategy genuinely re-enters that fast. Trades long only / trades short only — the Direction setting is filtering out your alert's side. Not in this bot's pair list / blacklisted — the Allowlist does not contain the symbol, or one of the two blacklists does. Held by another bot — a symbol has exactly one owner at a time and something else already has this one. Close that deal or trade a different pair. Already in position — this bot is already holding that symbol. Max longs / Max shorts / Max pairs open — one of this bot's own deal caps is full. A market cap or Isolation mode — an account-wide limit refused it, not this bot's. The reason names which one. No live price for the symbol — the pair is not in the price feed. Nearly always the wrong symbol: a quote currency this market does not trade, or the trap in the message formats . Spot is long-only — an "open short" reached a bot living on a spot market. Created on another account or market — the reply names the one it was created on and the one this app is currently running, and ends by confirming nothing was traded. Switch the header back to that account and market. No bot at that address — the path at the end of the address is wrong, or that bot was deleted. Nothing is ever redirected to a different bot; a mistyped address simply fails. It shows a green tick but the position is not what you expected The wrong pair opened — the {{ticker}} trap, every time. The alert is sending the symbol of the chart it was built on. See the message formats . The size is not what the form says — the message carried its own size, which overrides the Base order for that deal. It got much bigger than you expected — the ladder filled. Nothing caps its total; re-read the worked example in the DCA ladder . Two deals opened from one alert — the alert was delivered twice and the cooldown is set to 0. The entry never filled — the order type is Aggressive limit, which posts and follows the book but has no deadline and never falls back to market. It never takes profit — take profit is switched off, so only your close messages, the stop, or a manual close will end the deal.

sections.title: ⚙️ Before anything: your exchange account must be in Hedge Mode
sections.text: ⚙️ Before anything: your exchange account must be in Hedge Mode A hedge tranche is the opposite side of the same symbol . Exchanges offer two ways of holding that: Hedge Mode keeps a long and a short on one pair as two separate positions, and One-Way (netting) collapses them into one. So on a One-Way account a hedge tranche does not hedge — it reduces or closes the very position it was opened to protect . The app checks, and refuses rather than guesses. On Bitunix it reads the account's position mode directly — no open position needed — and if the account is not in Hedge Mode it will not open a tranche, naming the mode and the fix instead. If the venue does not report a mode it can recognise, that also refuses: unknown is not treated as hedge . It no longer changes the setting for you. Earlier builds silently switched a Bitunix account to Hedge Mode before the first order. That is an account-wide exchange setting affecting every USDT-M pair — including positions this app does not manage — so it is now yours to set. If you were auto-switched in the past you are already in Hedge Mode and nothing changes. If you change it while the bot is running, you are told. Flip an account to One-Way mid-session and that account's notifications carry HEDGING DISABLED with the reason; switch it back and you get HEDGING RE-ENABLED . The notice goes to the account it happened on, not to whichever account you are looking at. Deal bots are affected too, not just hedging. On a netting account a long and a short on one pair cancel, so opposite-side opens on the same pair are refused there as well. It is not only hedging that stops — on Bitunix, Bitget, BloFin and Aster it is everything. All four require Hedge Mode here, so an account these venues will not confirm as Hedge Mode has every order refused — entries, take-profits and DCAs, not just tranches. The refusal says so in as many words, says that nothing was sent , and repeats the venue's own message; earlier builds called it an “ambiguous outcome” for an order that had never left the app, which read like a network fault and left that order slot stuck until a restart. Bybit is unaffected: it switches per pair and falls back to one-way rather than refusing. Aster is the exception on who sets it. Wick Hunter does set Hedge Mode on Aster — and since v0.88.31 it does so continuously, not just when you connect : every sync pass it checks the account’s mode, and if the account is One-Way and flat it switches it, by itself, with no reconnect and nothing for you to re-save. Aster has no per-pair switch at all: its own manual heads the endpoint “on every symbol ”, so this is one account-wide setting covering every USDT-M pair, including manual positions this app does not manage. If it cannot switch yet, close your exposure — that is the whole fix. The venue will not change position mode while any position or pending order exists anywhere on the account, so that is the one and only reason an Aster account is still One-Way. Wick Hunter never attempts the change while it can see a position open — it waits, tells you once ( HEDGE MODE BLOCKED , naming the account and how many positions it can see), and keeps watching. Flatten and cancel everything on Aster and it switches itself within about a minute ; you get HEDGE MODE RESTORED and orders are admitted again. If the venue still refuses with nothing open — usually a resting order — you get HEDGE MODE STILL BLOCKED with the exchange’s own words, and it retries on its own, backing off from a minute to fifteen so it never hammers the venue. Earlier builds asked once , at connect: one refusal there left the account One-Way for good, with every order refused and the bot looking merely quiet. Bybit sets itself too, pair by pair (v0.89.9). Bybit’s position mode is per pair , not per account — which is why your Bybit Preferences screen shows it under a symbol. Wick Hunter used to switch a pair only at the moment a bot was about to trade it, so a pair you had never traded stayed One-Way and the exchange screen said so. It now sweeps every pair your bots watch or hold on that market in the background, and any pair added later — by a filter refresh, a new bot, or an edited pair list — is switched on the next pass. It is paced (a handful of pairs every fifteen seconds, behind every order you place) and it stops asking about a pair once Bybit confirms it. Pairs it does not touch: ones Bybit does not offer Hedge Mode on, and anything outside USDT perpetuals — USDC, spot and coin-M are one-way by design. Bybit will not switch a pair while THAT pair has something open. A position or a resting order on the pair blocks it — including ones this app did not place — so Wick Hunter does not even ask while it can see one, and simply switches the pair when it goes flat. If pairs stay stuck it tells you once, naming them ( HEDGE MODE BLOCKED ), and once more when they clear ( HEDGE MODE RESTORED ). Nothing else changes: a pair the sweep has not reached yet is still switched and verified before any new position is opened on it, exactly as before. How to set it: in the exchange's own futures settings. The venue refuses the change while any position or pending order is open on that product type, so flatten first.

sections.title: 🛡️ The Hedge Bot — what it is, and what it is not
sections.text: 🛡️ The Hedge Bot — what it is, and what it is not The Hedge Bot attaches to a position you already have. When the market moves against it by an amount you choose, it opens an opposite-side trade — a tranche — on the same pair, which earns while the market keeps going the wrong way and offsets part of the main position's loss. Do that in steps, on a ladder, and a position deep underwater has something working in the other direction while it waits. What it is for Buying time. A hedged position bleeds more slowly, so a deal that needs a week to recover can take a week. Banking the move against you. Each tranche has its own stop, and when the market pulls back that stop fires and the profit is real, realised cash — yours whatever the main position does next. Getting a pair out together. Once a hedge is open the paired take-profit owns the exit, closing the main and every hedge leg in one go on the combined number. What it is not It is not a stop loss. A stop ends the position and caps the loss; a hedge keeps it open and offsets part of the loss with a second position, and your main position can still be liquidated. For a hard floor, use a stop loss — the hedge is not one and cannot become one. It is not free. Two positions means two lots of margin, two lots of fees and funding on both legs. A hedge that never banks anything is pure cost, and on a fast V-shaped recovery it gives back a large slice of the rebound. It is insurance, and insurance has a premium. It is not a guarantee, and it is not always on. Attaching opens nothing; nothing happens until price reaches a DCA. Even then the size that opens can be smaller than the DCA asked for, or nothing at all. It is not a strategy for choosing trades. It never opens a first position and never picks a pair. Read the ladder section before you run this live. The single most expensive misunderstanding in the app is the ladder's Size % column: it is the total hedge you want to be holding at that DCA, not the size of the next order. Setting it as though it were an order size builds a hedge several times larger than you intended.

sections.title: 🔗 Attaching — and what "attached" actually means
sections.text: 🔗 Attaching — and what "attached" actually means The Hedge Bot does not open positions of its own; it adopts ones that exist. Everything in How it runs decides which positions it is allowed to watch. You can have more than one Hedge Bot The selector at the top of the page names the Hedge Bot that everything below it describes — its enabled switch, its auto-attach, its blacklist, its pair list and its whole ladder. Most installs have exactly one, covering All pairs , and never touch the selector. Pairs — All pairs (the default, and what a single Hedge Bot has always been) or a Pair list you pick. A bot on a pair list watches those pairs and nothing else. ＋ New Hedge Bot — a second bot with its own ladder, so a volatile alt can hedge on different distances from a major. It arrives with no pairs and hedges nothing until you give it some. No two Hedge Bots may claim the same pair , and the save is refused by name if you try — two ladders on one position open tranches against each other and each reads the other's legs as size it cannot explain. To split pairs out, put the first bot on a pair list first, then give the rest to the second. Get it wrong: nothing — the refusal names both bots and the pair, and nothing is stored. A pair that is on no Hedge Bot's list has no manager, so nothing new attaches to it. Positions already attached keep being managed. The three controls Bot enabled — the master switch and the only gate on new attachments. Off, it stops taking on anything new; positions already watched stay watched and open hedge legs stay managed and protected. It is "stop taking on more work", not "abandon everything". Get it wrong: on, with auto-attach on, every new position inherits the ladder — trades you opened by hand and never wanted hedged included. Auto-attach — Auto watches every attachable position the moment it appears, from deal bots and from trades you place yourself; Manual only watches nothing until you attach it from Attachable positions . Get it wrong: on Auto, a quick scalp opened by hand on your phone gets a hedge ladder and starts opening tranches if it goes offside. Never attach to — pairs the bot always ignores, spelled as the venue does and comma-separated ( BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT ). This is the escape hatch that makes Auto safe. Get it wrong: a typo protects nothing — the pair is not on the list, so it attaches like any other. When Auto-attach is refused, you are told (v0.88.19). An automatic attach can be refused for reasons that have nothing to do with your ladder — your exchange account is in One-Way mode, the market has no hedge mode, another runtime on this install already owns both sides of that pair's book, or another market's Hedge Bot already manages it. Those refusals used to be silent, so a position simply went unhedged and nothing on any screen said why. Now, when none of the positions this bot was set to hedge could be attached, it writes an Activity row straight away naming the pair and the reason, and — if that is still true a minute later — sends one HEDGE NOT ATTACHING notification, and one HEDGE ATTACHING AGAIN when it clears. Only none of them is reported: if it attached something this pass, it is working. Pairs it skips because you paused the bot, turned Auto-attach off, blacklisted them, or left them off its pair list are your own settings and stay silent. "Attached" means watching — nothing more Attached DOES mean Attached does NOT mean The position's distance from its average entry is being measured every tick against your ladder. That a hedge order has been placed. Until a DCA is reached, no order exists anywhere. The moment a DCA is reached, a tranche will be opened without asking you. That the position is protected. An attached position with no tranche open is exactly as exposed as an unattached one. While any hedge leg is open, the paired take-profit owns the exit. That the position's own stop loss still applies. While a hedge is open, a deal's stop loss is suspended — the deal can pass straight through its configured stop price. What is never attached Markets with no hedge mode — spot, coin-margined contracts and USDC perpetuals. There the exchange holds one side only, so an "opposite" order would shrink your position rather than protect it, and the page says so. A pair already stacked on both sides. With long and short deals from different bots on one symbol, the bot refuses rather than guessing which is "the main". Anything on the Never attach to list , whatever else is true. The three things you can do to a running hedge Close hedge legs — market-closes every tranche but keeps the position attached : the exit returns to the position's own take-profit and the ladder is live again, so tranches re-open if price is still past a DCA. Use it to take the hedge off now while keeping the net armed. Retry exchange stops — asks the venue again for any stop it refused a resting slot. Those stops keep working from the app meanwhile; this only tries to move them onto the exchange. Detach — hands the position back entirely, closing any open hedge legs first , then returning exit ownership: a hand-opened trade gets its own take-profit back exactly as it was, and a deal bot re-places its take-profit from its own settings.

sections.title: Rolling volume range and funding direction
sections.text: Rolling volume range and funding direction Liq Scalper and Optimized Liq Bot can restrict new entries to a minimum and maximum rolling 24-hour USDT volume on the exchange the account trades. The maximum uses the same validated volume data as the minimum and adds no network calls. Blank or 0 turns the maximum off; amounts accept shorthand such as 250k or 50M. The optional Funding direction filter starts off. When enabled, long entries require positive funding and short entries require negative funding. Zero, missing and stale rates refuse new entries; this filter does not reverse your selected side or close existing deals. A shared all-pairs funding batch refreshes at most once per minute per exchange, environment and market while needed. Rates older than two minutes are not used.

sections.title: Minimum DCA to Hedge
