sections.text: Minimum DCA to Hedge Under Hedge settings, open Advanced · Minimum DCA to Hedge . The option starts off. Enable it, choose a catch-all minimum, and enter a different minimum beside any deal bot on this account. The list includes the original Liquidation Bot and other deal bots created on this account. A blank bot row uses the catch-all; 0 allows immediate hedging. Press Save hedge settings to apply the policy to the selected Hedge Bot. Only recorded, confirmed completed DCA orders count. Entry orders, partial or partially cancelled fills, manual position adds and size-only reconciliation do not. Known completion records are restored after a restart. Older fills without such records count as unknown (0); use a 0 minimum if you want those positions to hedge immediately. Positions with no tracked deal use the catch-all with a count of 0. Each open child of a stacked position must reach the minimum. The policy blocks new hedge tranches while all existing hedge stops, trailing and exits keep working. It adds a condition to the usual hedge ladder; reaching the count alone does not open a hedge. Each Hedge Bot keeps its own policy. When a shared Hedge Bot is copied, this option is off and account-specific bot overrides are cleared so you can choose the bots on this account.

sections.title: 💾 Save hedge settings
sections.text: 💾 Save hedge settings Hedge settings save on the Save hedge settings button at the bottom of the form — nothing is written while you type. Editing any box marks the form unsaved ; the status line beside the button is the only place the page tells you what happened, so it always says one of these: The line says What it means (blank) Nothing has been edited since the form was last loaded or saved. unsaved You have changed a box and nothing has been sent yet. Press Save to write it. saving… The write is in flight, right after pressing Save. saved ✓ Stored, and already applied to every attached position — live, without restarting anything. not saved — fix the value above Something in the ladder or the liquidation tiers is not usable, so nothing was written at all . The reason appears in red above the Save button, naming the exact level. Fix the box and press Save again. An empty box is not a zero. Clearing a Distance or Size and pressing Save does not store 0 — the save is refused and told you why. This matters because a DCA at 0% distance would mean "hedge at the entry price", which is immediately and forever. The 3-second refresh stops repainting this form the moment you edit it — same as the per-pair override panel below — so nothing you typed is ever overwritten while the form is unsaved. Live figures elsewhere on the page keep updating as normal. A save never turns the bot on. Saving Hedge settings does not enable the bot and does not attach anything. A save reaches running hedges immediately. There is no "applies to new positions only" here — the ladder you just saved is the ladder every attached position is using one second later. Ladder distances re-price instantly; tranches already open are left exactly as they are.

sections.title: ↔️ One set of settings, or one per direction
sections.text: ↔️ One set of settings, or one per direction Settings mode sits at the top of Hedge settings and has two positions. It ships on One config , which is the single parameter set that governs both directions and is what every install has had until now. Nothing on this page changes while it is there. Split by main side gives you a second column. The left one, LONG MAIN , governs a position that is long — whose hedge tranches therefore open short . The right one, SHORT MAIN , governs a short position, hedged long. The columns are named after the position being protected , not the hedge leg, because the leg is always the opposite one and "short settings" would read two ways. Nothing is linked. Every setting on the right can differ from the one on the left, including the whole ladder, and editing one never moves the other. There is no "shared" state to keep track of and no per-field link switch — the two columns are two complete configs. Turning it on changes nothing. Both columns start as an exact copy of the single config you already had, so the moment you flip the switch your bot is doing precisely what it was doing. Behaviour only changes when you edit something. Which column a position uses is decided once, when the hedge attaches, and it does not move. The main's own direction picks it. If a position later flips direction, that attachment ends and a new one begins — and the new one reads the other column. A restart does not move a live hedge either; the side is remembered with the attachment. Turning it back off is not destructive. The short column stays stored exactly as you left it and is simply not read while the mode is One config . Switch back and your numbers are still there. Per-pair overrides still work, and are still per pair. An override merges on top of whichever column the position is running — it is not itself split by side. Templates fill one column. With the mode on, a template button writes into the column you are currently looking at, and the label beside Templates names which one that is. On a phone you see one column at a time. A Long main / Short main switch appears above the form; two columns of number boxes do not fit a narrow screen and squeezing them is how a Distance box becomes untypable. Why you might want this. A squeeze and a bleed are not the same shape. A short position going wrong tends to go wrong fast and far; a long one more often grinds. If that matches what you see, the ladder distances and tranche sizes are the settings that earn a split — and the arming threshold after them. If it does not, leave the mode on One config ; a second set of numbers you did not mean to diverge is a real cost.

sections.title: 🪜 The hedge ladder — distance, size, and the one column everyone misreads
sections.text: 🪜 The hedge ladder — distance, size, and the one column everyone misreads Each row is one DCA: how far the market must move against you , how much hedge you want to be holding once it does , and optionally how much of that may sit there without a stop . Add rows with ＋ Add level , remove them with the ✕ . Distance % — how far against you the DCA sits A percentage move against your position from its current blended average entry , not from the price you first got in at. For a long, "against" is down; for a short, up. It re-anchors whenever the average moves. Every DCA fill, manual add and partial close changes the average, and every DCA you have not yet reached moves with it — always measured from where you are, never where you started. Get it wrong: too close and the hedge opens on ordinary noise, paying fees both ways and capping your recovery; too far and the position is already in trouble before help arrives. 📐 Worked example — a DCA moves every remaining DCA You are long 10 units at an average of $100 . Your ladder's first three DCAs are at 4%, 7% and 10% . Right now those DCAs sit at $96.00 , $93.00 and $90.00 . Price falls to $90, all three DCAs are reached, and the hedge holds 7 units short . The deal bot DCAs, buying 10 more units at $90 . The main is now 20 units at an average of $95 . Every DCA re-prices off $95: 4% moves from $96.00 to $91.20 , 7% from $93.00 to $88.35 , 10% from $90.00 to $85.50 . At $90 the position is only 5.3% offside from the new average, so the matched DCA drops from the third back to the first. The same 7 units is now 35% coverage of a 20-unit main, not 70%. Nothing opens — the first DCA wants far less than 7 units — and the hedge sits until price reaches $88.35. The lesson: a DCA pushes every remaining DCA further away and dilutes the coverage you already have. A ladder that looks sensible on a single entry can be far too slow on a position that DCAs three times. Size % — TOTAL coverage at that DCA, not the size of the new tranche Size % is the total hedge you want to be holding once price reaches that DCA , as a percentage of your main position. The bot subtracts whatever is already open and orders only the difference , so a ladder reading 25 / 60 / 70 builds coverage up to 25%, then up to 60%, then up to 70% — it does not open three tranches of 25%, 60% and 70%. Worked example. Main: long 10 units at an average of $100 , a $1,000 position. DCAs at 4% / 7% / 10% with sizes 25% / 60% / 70%. DCA Reached at Size % says Hedge that should exist Already open Tranche actually opened L1 · 4% $96.00 25% 2.5 units short 0 2.5 units L2 · 7% $93.00 60% 6.0 units short 2.5 3.5 units L3 · 10% $90.00 70% 7.0 units short 6.0 1.0 unit L4 · 15% $85.00 130% 13.0 units short 7.0 6.0 units Coverage above 100% flips the book. At L4 the hedge is 13 units short against 10 long, so the combined position is net 3 units short — no longer hedged and waiting for a recovery, but positioned for the trend to continue , with a bounce costing you money on the net. That can be exactly what you want on a trending pair; just know it is what you chose. Read the sizes as a running total, not a list of orders. To mean "open 25%, then another 60%, then another 70%", type 25 / 85 / 155. Get it wrong: typing order sizes into this column builds a hedge several times bigger than intended, eats the margin the main position needs, and turns a hedged long into a large net short at the worst moment. Max w/o stop % — the per-DCA version of the unstopped budget Optional, one per row. Blank uses the global Max w/o stop from Arming & stops ; filled in, it replaces the global while price is at that DCA and follows price in real time, shrinking back if price retraces to a shallower DCA. It lets you be cautious about unstopped exposure while barely offside and progressively more willing once deep. How the budget is spent is in the next card. Get it wrong: far below the DCA's own Size % and that DCA can never fill — the ladder asks for 100% coverage and delivers 25%. Generous at every DCA and the budget is effectively off. If a retracement makes the active cap smaller than the hedge already open, nothing is force-closed and nothing is force-armed — the bot refuses to open anything new until price returns to a deeper DCA. What is open stays open. Min tranche — the dust filter A floor on how small a tranche is worth opening, as a percentage of the main position; below it nothing opens and the bot waits quietly, with no message. Example: on a 10-unit main, a 5% minimum will not open a tranche smaller than 0.5 units. Two floors apply on top of yours and cannot be turned off — the exchange's minimum order quantity and its minimum order value in dollars. The highest of the three wins, and on cheap coins the dollar minimum usually bites. Get it wrong: too high and top-ups near the cap never happen, so coverage silently lags the ladder; at 0 a squeezed budget produces a stream of near-worthless tranches that each consume a stop slot and pay fees. It sits in the Paired take profit block on screen, though it governs opening.

sections.title: 🔒 Arming a stop — and the budget for hedge that has none
sections.text: 🔒 Arming a stop — and the budget for hedge that has none A tranche opens with no stop . It has to earn one. Every tranche is in exactly one of two states, and there is nothing in between. State What it means Counts against the unstopped budget? Unprotected No stop exists for it. It is riding. This includes a tranche that is currently in profit but has not yet reached the activation threshold. Yes — every unit of it. Armed A real stop order exists at a real price — either resting on the exchange or held by the app. No. TP activation — the entire arming rule When a tranche's own profit reaches this percentage, its stop is placed. That is the whole condition — no waiting for the market to turn, no requirement that the move has reversed. Profit is measured from that tranche's own entry, not the main's. Get it wrong: too low and stops arm on noise and are taken out for pennies, dropping coverage exactly as the trend resumes; too high and tranches ride deep moves with nothing under them, filling the unstopped budget and blocking every deeper DCA. TP offset — where that stop is placed This far from the tranche's entry , on the profitable side. Example: activation 4% with offset 2% means a tranche reaching 4% profit gets a stop locking in 2%. The offset must be strictly smaller than the activation, and the app refuses to save a pair where it is not. Otherwise the stop would sit on the far side of the price that triggered it — crossed the instant it existed — so the tranche would arm and close on the same tick, bank nothing, and drop coverage while the main was offside. The save is refused rather than one number quietly "fixed", because either could be the one you meant. Get it wrong: an offset near the activation banks almost nothing per scalp and pays two lots of fees for it; a very tight one gives up most of the move you just captured. Once armed, a stop is never pulled — it only ratchets An armed tranche stays armed until it closes. Nothing disarms it — not a new market extreme, not a retracement, not a config change. The stop moves only toward more profit , never away. That movement is the trail, in its own card. Protection is two-state by design: a tranche is protected or it is not, with no "will probably be protected soon" credit.

sections.title: 🧮 Max w/o stop — the size budget for hedge that has no stop
sections.text: 🧮 Max w/o stop — the size budget for hedge that has no stop How much unstopped hedge the bot will carry at once — and the usual answer to "why is my ladder not filling". Max w/o stop — a SIZE BUDGET, not a count The global cap on how much hedge may sit unprotected at once, as a percentage of the main position. A DCA's own Max w/o stop replaces it while price is at that DCA. It is measured in size , not tranches. Every unprotected unit counts, including a tranche in profit but below activation, and including hedge on the pair the bot did not open. When the budget is full it opens a partial tranche that fits , or nothing, and deeper DCAs wait until coverage arms . It gates opening only — it never force-closes or force-arms a tranche. Get it wrong: too tight and the ladder is decorative, the sizes you typed never built and the hedge permanently behind the market; too loose and a fast one-way move leaves you carrying the full ladder with no stops under any of it. 🧮 Worked example — how the budget throttles a ladder, and how arming releases it Same main: long 10 units at an average of $100 , same DCAs — 4% / 7% / 10% at sizes 25% / 60% / 70% — but the per-DCA cap column is blank , so the global Max w/o stop of 45% applies: a budget of 4.5 units . TP activation is 4%. Price What the ladder wants Unprotected now Budget left What actually opens $96.00 Total 2.5 units — needs 2.5 more 0 4.5 2.5 units — the full amount $93.00 Total 6.0 units — needs 3.5 more 2.5 2.0 2.0 units — throttled $92.16 Tranche 1 (entry $96) hits 4% profit and arms 2.0 2.5 nothing — this is the arm $92.16 Total 6.0 units — still needs 1.5 more 2.0 2.5 1.5 units — the DCA completes At $93 the DCA asked for 60% and got 45% . Nothing was broken — the budget was full. When tranche 1 armed, its 2.5 units stopped counting as unprotected, 2.5 units of budget appeared , and the ladder topped up to the 60% it wanted. Had the freed budget been under Min tranche — 0.5 units here — nothing would have opened, with no message. A tight cap plus a high minimum is the usual cause of "my ladder isn't filling". Safe zone — the anti-churn pause after a scalp After a tranche's stop fires, nothing new opens on that pair until price moves this much further against you past the price it exited at . Without it the bot re-buys the same hedge a second after selling it, because the DCA the stop fired at is still a DCA. Example: safe zone 0.4%, main long, a tranche stops out at $94.08 — new tranches are blocked until price falls below $93.70 . The same pause applies after the paired take-profit fires. Get it wrong: at 0 the bot whipsaws in and out of the same tranche paying fees each time; too wide and after one scalp the hedge sits out a large part of the next leg down. Liquidation-tier override — permission to stack faster near the edge An optional escalation table: when the gap between current price and the main position's liquidation price shrinks to this or less, raise the unstopped budget to this . Close to liquidation, more hedge quickly matters more than stops on the hedge you have — an unstopped hedge still offsets the loss and arms its own stop as it becomes profitable. Build a tier in the three boxes below the table and press ＋ Add tier ; the table orders itself widest-to-most-urgent and ✕ deletes a row. Those boxes are a staging area — typing in them changes nothing until you press the button. Name — optional label so the tier is recognisable in the log. Distance ≤ % — how close to liquidation the tier switches on. Get it wrong: too wide and it is always on, so your ordinary cap never applies. Cap raised to % — the unstopped budget while it matches. Get it wrong: a high number is the fastest way to carry a very large hedge with no stops under any of it, at the worst moment. The rules, exactly: when several tiers match, the deepest wins — the smallest threshold, the most urgent. A tier can only raise the cap, never lower what the DCA or the global already allows, and the result is clamped to 100% whatever you type. If the venue reports no liquidation price, no tier applies and the ordinary cap stands. An empty table means the feature is off. Example. Ordinary cap 45%, with tiers caution ≤ 15% → 60% and critical ≤ 8% → 80%. Price $78 against a reported liquidation at $72 is a gap of 7.7% , so both match and the deeper critical sets the budget to 80% . Had that DCA's own Max w/o stop been 90%, the tier would change nothing.

sections.title: 🎯 The paired take-profit — one exit for the whole pair
sections.text: 🎯 The paired take-profit — one exit for the whole pair Once any hedge leg is open, the main position and its hedge are one trade with one exit. The paired take-profit is that exit: when the combined result reaches your target, everything closes at once — the main and every remaining hedge leg. What goes into "combined" The main position's open profit or loss. Every open hedge tranche's profit or loss. Everything the hedge has already banked this cycle — the realised cash from tranches that stopped out earlier. This is what makes the target reachable on a position that is still underwater: each scalp permanently moves the finish line closer. Funding paid or received, and trading fees, on both legs. Paired TP — the target A percentage, not a dollar figure; what it is a percentage of is the next setting. Zero is not "off" — it is the most aggressive setting here , closing both legs the instant the pair stops losing. Get it wrong: too high and the pair never exits, carrying margin and paying funding indefinitely; too low (or zero) and you close a recovering position for a rounding error and give up the rebound. Paired TP basis — what the percentage is measured against Basis Measured against Behaviour Combined notional (main + hedge) Everything you have deployed across both legs The target grows as the hedge grows , so the same percentage needs more dollars as the cycle deepens. Fires later. This is the conservative choice and the one every template uses. Main notional only The main position alone A fixed dollar target that does not move when the hedge grows. Fires sooner , and reads the way an exchange's own percentage column does. Example. Main: 10 units at $100, so $1,000 . Hedge: 4.5 units at an average of $92.33, so $415.50 . A 1.75% target means $17.50 on the main-only basis, or $24.77 on the combined basis — the same setting, 42% more profit required. Get it wrong: switching basis without re-thinking the percentage silently changes your exit by a large amount in one direction or the other. It is watched live by the app — it does not rest on the exchange No paired take-profit order sits on the venue, and none can: the trigger is not a price but an arithmetic result across two positions plus banked cash plus funding, moving whenever any of those do. The app recomputes it every tick and closes both sides at market when the target is met. Plainly: if the server is not running, the paired take-profit cannot fire. Your positions remain and any exchange-resting hedge stops still work — on every supported venue , Bybit, Bitunix, Bitget, Binance, Aster and WEEX alike — but the combined exit waits until the app is back. What does not survive is an app-managed stop: the tranches past the venue's conditional-slot budget. Where each stop actually lives has the split. Two consequences. First , resting nothing on the venue means it consumes none of the limited conditional-order slots — all go to hedge tranche stops. Second , after it fires the bot pauses until it has confirmed both sides are genuinely flat, because a closing fill on one leg can arrive seconds before the other and it will not act on a half-closed picture. Near-perfect coverage can make the target unreachable. When the hedge is almost exactly the size of the main, the legs move together and the combined result barely changes with price. The way out is the tranches' own stops firing and banking, which lifts the combined number — so coverage at or near 100% deserves a paired target you have checked is achievable. When no hedge leg is open, the paired take-profit does not apply at all — the position's own take-profit governs, exactly as it did before the Hedge Bot ever attached.

sections.title: 📈 Trail — letting an armed stop follow the move
sections.text: 📈 Trail — letting an armed stop follow the move A stop at the offset locks in a fixed amount and then stops helping. The trail lets it walk toward the price while the tranche keeps earning, so a big move against your main banks more than the offset alone. A switch plus three numbers, touching only stops that are already armed. Trail on / off — off, every stop stays where the offset put it. Get it wrong: off on a strongly trending pair leaves most of each tranche's profit on the table; on with careless numbers it drags stops close to price and ends scalps early. Gap to stop — how far price must run past that tranche's current stop before the stop moves. Measured against the stop , not profit from the entry, so a stop that has already trailed far needs another full trigger's worth of movement; each tranche is judged on its own gap, so one can advance while another does not. Get it wrong: too small and stops crowd price and end tranches on ordinary wobble; too large and the trail never fires. This box was labelled "Trigger profit" until v0.74.88 and never measured profit — the rename is the field saying what it has always done. Advance per step — how far the stop moves each time, as a percentage of the stop's own price, always toward profit and never backwards. A safety margin keeps it out of touching distance of current price, and a move too small to be worth re-placing is skipped. Get it wrong: large steps jump the stop close to price and cut the run short; tiny steps churn orders for almost no gain. Cooldown — the minimum minutes between two advances of the same tranche , each keeping its own timer. Get it wrong: very short cancels and re-places venue orders repeatedly, costing rate-limit budget and fees; very long means a violent move gets one advance and no more. 🧮 Worked example — one advance, step by step Trail on, trigger 10% , advance 2% , cooldown 60 minutes . A hedge tranche is short (the main is long) and armed with its stop at $94.08 . Nothing happens while price is anywhere above $84.67 — that is where the gap between price and the $94.08 stop first reaches 10%. Price trades at $84.67 . The trail fires and moves the stop 2% in the profitable direction: $94.08 → $92.20 . The tranche now has roughly twice as much locked in as the offset alone gave it. That tranche's timer starts. It cannot advance again for 60 minutes, however far price runs. Sixty minutes later it is eligible again — but only if the gap from the new $92.20 stop has once more reached 10%, which needs price at or below $82.98 . This is also why, in the full worked example at the end of this section, the trail never moves anything: the deepest that hedge's price got was about 5% past its stop — half of the trigger.

sections.title: 🎚 Templates — Slow, Moderate, Aggressive
sections.text: 🎚 Templates — Slow, Moderate, Aggressive Three buttons above the settings. Each one fills the form with a complete starting point — a seven-DCA ladder, the unstopped budgets, arming, paired take-profit and trailing — and then gets out of the way. A brand-new install already sits on Moderate : unlike every other bot, whose form ships blank, the Hedge Bot ships filled in, and the middle template is what it is filled in with. Pressing Moderate Hedge on a fresh install therefore changes nothing. A template is not a mode. Nothing is locked, nothing is remembered, and nothing about the bot's behaviour changes because you pressed one. After pressing it, every field is an ordinary editable field; change any of them and the change stands. Nothing records which button you pressed, so re-opening the page later cannot tell you — the form shows the values, and the values are all there is. Pressing a template marks the form unsaved, exactly like a hand edit — a running hedge sees nothing until you press Save. The liquidation-tier table is yours and no template touches it. How they differ, in trader's terms Slow Hedge — nothing happens until the position is well and truly offside. The first tranche waits for a double-digit adverse move and coverage climbs in patient steps, so it takes a very deep move before the hedge matches the main size. It carries the tightest unstopped budget of the three, so deeper DCAs genuinely wait for earlier tranches to arm, and it arms on a relatively large tranche profit and takes the biggest bite. For positions you expect to grind and recover, on pairs where a 5% move is an ordinary Tuesday. Moderate Hedge — starts a little earlier and accelerates harder once committed. The first tranche comes at a move that is uncomfortable but not unusual, coverage reaches parity at moderate depth, and past that the DCAs step up steeply — built deliberately to go net-opposite if the trend keeps running rather than sitting neutral. The middle setting in every respect, and the shape closest to what has actually been run in the field. Aggressive Hedge — reacts to a move that is barely news. The first tranche opens on an adverse move many pairs make in a normal session, parity arrives quickly, and the deepest DCA targets several times the main size. It arms fastest and takes the smallest bite — a small tranche profit places a stop close to the entry — so it scalps often, and with the loosest unstopped budget and smallest dust filter it builds size quickly. Expect the highest fee and funding bill, the largest margin draw, and the most damage from a whipsaw. Character Slow Moderate Aggressive How far against you before anything opens Furthest Middle Soonest — a normal day's range How deep before the hedge matches the main Deepest Middle Earliest How far past that the ladder keeps building Moderately Steeply Very steeply — well past net-opposite Unstopped budget Tightest Middle Loosest How readily a tranche gets its stop Patient — bigger profit needed, bigger bite taken Same as Slow Quickest — small profit, small bite, frequent scalps Smallest tranche it will bother opening Larger Larger Smaller Paired take-profit, trailing, safe zone Identical across all three — the templates differ in ladder and arming , not in how the pair exits Press one, then read the ladder it produced against your own position size . A template knows nothing about how big your positions are, how much margin you have free, or how volatile your pairs are. It is a starting point in the literal sense: somewhere sane to start editing. Two custom slots, saved under your own name. Beside the three built-in buttons are two slots: type a name, press Save , and the form’s current settings for the side you are looking at are stored there and the button takes that name. Pressing it later fills the form back in, exactly like a built-in. A slot belongs to the Hedge Bot named in the selector , so a second Hedge Bot has its own two — and the highlight on a button means the form matches that template right now, so a hand edit clears it.

sections.title: 🎛 Making one pair behave differently
sections.text: 🎛 Making one pair behave differently Hedge settings are one set for the whole install. Two places let you depart from them for a single symbol, and both are live the moment they are saved. Per-pair overrides — replace one value on one symbol Three boxes and a button: Pair (as the venue spells it, BTCUSDT ), Setting (the unstopped budget, safe zone, paired take-profit and its basis, activation, offset, minimum tranche, and all four trail controls), and Value . Set override stores it; anything not listed keeps the global value. Everything in the panel is in force right now — ✕ removes one value, clear pair returns the symbol to the globals entirely. Get it wrong: an override set months ago and forgotten is still running that pair today, and this panel is the only place it is visible — glance at it whenever a pair behaves unlike the others. An override breaking the offset-below-activation rule is refused for that pair just as it would be globally. The ladder and the liquidation tiers are authored globally in their own editors, not here. A stored ladder override still appears in this panel with its own ✕, so it can always be seen and cleared. Pair configuration — the panel beside an active hedge Select an attached position and this panel shows the settings that position is actually running : its full ladder (distance, size and cap per DCA) plus Max w/o stop, Safe zone, Paired TP, TP activation, TP offset and Paired TP basis, with a badge saying whether they are the global defaults or a pair override . Save for this pair stores only the values that differ from the globals; Revert to global removes every override on the symbol. Like the main settings form above, this panel saves on a button and not while you type: the page keeps your edit — from the moment you change any box the 3-second refresh stops repainting this form — the line beside the buttons reads unsaved until you press one of them — while the live figures, tranches and stops around it keep updating as normal. Pressing Save for this pair either says saved or names the reason the server refused it; nothing is ever stored silently, and nothing snaps back without an explanation. Get it wrong: sitting beside the live position, it is easy to read as "the settings". It is not — it is this pair's departure from them, and edits here affect no other pair.

sections.title: 🌐 Where it runs, and where each stop actually lives
sections.text: 🌐 Where it runs, and where each stop actually lives The Hedge Bot needs a market where the exchange will hold a long and a short on the same symbol at the same time. That is USDT perpetual futures and nothing else. Market Hedge Bot Bybit USDT perpetuals The field-verified home, and where the bot has by far the most live history. Armed stops rest on the exchange , nearest the price first. See below. Bitunix USDT futures Supported, with order execution and the private account stream verified on the live venue. Armed stops rest on the exchange , nearest the price first — the stop path itself was run against a live key and a real position (place, read back, cancel). One thing differs: Bitunix echoes no client order id on a resting stop, so after a restart the bot re-adopts its stops by their size and trigger price rather than by a tag. Start tiny anyway — one drill is one order, not a season of them. Bitget USDT futures Supported. Armed stops rest on the exchange , nearest the price first — the stop path was run against a live key and a real position here too, and Bitget does echo the bot's own order id, so restarts re-adopt stops by tag. Classic accounts only; UTA, hybrid and migrating accounts are refused before any call is made. Private order WebSocket updates are not wired here yet, so position changes are seen on the polling pass rather than instantly. Start tiny. Binance USDⓈ-M USDT perpetuals Supported on live/mainnet accounts only . Spot, USDC-settled, COIN-M and Futures Testnet are refused rather than aliased. The key must have Futures read/trading permission and the account must be in account-wide Hedge Mode . Wick Hunter only attempts the account-wide switch after it has proved both USD-M and COIN-M completely flat and order-free . If either book has exposure, manage or close it on Binance, clear every position and open order in both books, then retry/save. Until Hedge Mode is confirmed, Wick Hunter fails every app order closed — including entries, DCA, take-profit, stop/protection, reduce-only closes and cancels — so do not rely on app exits during that refusal. Armed stops rest on the exchange at Binance as owned mark-price conditional orders and are re-adopted by client id after restart. The private user stream only rings an immediate REST re-read; REST remains the position and money authority. Availability differs by region, so confirm it in your own Binance account and terms. Start tiny. Aster USDT perpetuals Supported. Armed stops rest on the exchange , nearest the price first. It is newer and less field-observed than the established venues; its margin and verification details are in Venue field notes . Start tiny. WEEX USDT perpetuals Supported in this release. Armed stops rest on the exchange as conditional orders, nearest the price first — the stop path is read from WEEX’s own API docs and proved against a loopback replica of the venue, not yet against a live position, so the first live hedge here is the proof. A stop the venue refuses a slot falls back to an app-managed stop. Mainnet credentials, a passphrase and existing hedge mode are required. Start tiny. Spot, coin-margined, USDC perpetuals No hedge mode exists. The exchange holds one side only, so an opposite order would simply reduce your position rather than protect it. Positions on these markets run unhedged, and the page says so rather than implying protection it cannot give. Two kinds of stop, and why you should care Exchange-resting stops. The order sits on the venue and fires whether or not this app is running — a restart, an update, an outage at your end. The venue caps resting conditional orders per symbol (ten on venues with exchange-resting stops, WEEX included since v0.90.25); the bot applies that venue fact and fills those slots nearest-to-price first , since the stop most likely to fire soon is the one that most needs to be out of the app's hands. A stop the venue splits into several orders consumes several slots. App-managed stops. Everything beyond that budget, on every venue. The price is real and the bot checks it every tick and closes the tranche when crossed — but it does that from here . While the server is down, an app-managed stop does not fire , so a market that runs through that price during an outage leaves the tranche open at whatever price you come back to. So a ladder with more armed tranches than the slot budget always has some stops living in the app, and the nearest ones — the ones about to matter — are on the exchange. An outage leaves the deeper tranches unstopped, not the whole hedge — on venues with exchange-resting stops, including WEEX. WEEX's conditional path is covered against a loopback replica rather than a live position; the placement was confirmed against live keys on Bitunix 2026-08-08 and Bitget 2026-08-09, each time placed, read back by id and cancelled on a real position. Restarting picks up armed tranches and their trails where they were. Two further boundaries on Bitget and Bitunix. A take-profit you placed by hand on an attached position is not pulled and parked while a hedge is open — if it fires mid-hedge the main closes and the hedge leg is then closed at market (a deal bot's own take-profit keeps its normal pull-and-restore handoff on every venue). And on Bitget specifically, treat every size as an experiment until you have watched it work. The exit itself rests nothing anywhere, on any venue: the paired take-profit is always watched live by the app.

sections.title: 🧾 Venue field notes
sections.text: 🧾 Venue field notes These notes separate code coverage from facts observed with a live venue account. They do not change which markets the app offers. Binance: the USDⓈ-M REST, order, conditional-order and private-stream paths are covered deterministically, but this release has not placed a Binance order with a live key. Use a mainnet USD-M account in Hedge Mode and start with the smallest permitted size. The app never offers Futures Testnet. Aster: the order, stop and position paths are wired and covered, but no Aster order or private-stream frame has been observed through this app with a live key. Position changes therefore remain safe through REST polling. The app requires CROSS margin per symbol; changing an isolated symbol is a real account mutation and may be refused while a position or order exists. Its funding sign was confirmed on 20 August 2026: a positive rate on a long produced a negative ledger row, matching “the account paid.”

sections.title: Hedge chart size and Daily candles
sections.text: Hedge chart size and Daily candles From Deals → View hedge , press Expand to fill the app window with the chart. Restore or Escape returns to the pair panel. The same chart stays open, keeping its zoom, hedge lines and planned ranges; their buttons remain available while expanded. Choose Daily in the chart timeframe row to view the selected account's daily venue candles. Changing the timeframe keeps the hedge and range choices. Leaving the Hedge view closes the embedded chart and releases the expanded view.

sections.title: 📊 Reading the Active hedge panel
sections.text: 📊 Reading the Active hedge panel Select an attached position and everything the hedge is doing to it is on one screen. Each number on it is a setting from this section, measured live. View hedge on a deal now opens this screen with that pair already selected, and the chart above the panel is the Terminal’s own — the same venue candles, hedge lines and planned ranges — embedded here rather than a second page. You are not taken out of the app, and leaving the Hedge view shuts the chart down again. What it shows What it is telling you Distance How far offside the position is, from its current average entry . This is the number your ladder DCAs are compared against. Total hedge Coverage right now, as a percentage of the main. Compare it with the Size % of the DCA you are at: if it is lower, something is throttling the ladder. Unprotected How much of that coverage has no stop, as a percentage of the main. This is the number weighed against Max w/o stop — when it reaches the cap, no new tranche opens. Safe zone Whether the post-scalp pause is currently blocking new tranches, and the price it is waiting for. Current avg entry · Main liquidation The ladder's anchor, and the price the liquidation tiers measure against. Paired TP target · Combined P&L What the pair needs, and where it is. These two together are the only honest answer to "how is this trade doing". The deal drawer's Position P&L breakdown shows the same three terms the engine actually sums — Realized + funding (the one figure the paired TP uses; on some venues the venue's own realized total already contains funding, so there is deliberately no separate Funding row), Unrealized · main and Unrealized · hedge — and they add up to Combined exactly. Open tranches — the State column Armed · exchange : a real stop resting on the venue; it works even if this app is off. Armed · memory : a real stop, but it needs this server running — that is where the tranches beyond the venue's slot budget sit, and where any stop the venue refused sits until a retry succeeds. Unprotected : no stop yet — its row names the price where the stop will arm and where it will land. An underwater tranche is exactly as unprotected as it looks. If the venue drops an exchange stop on its own, the once-a-minute order audit notices, protects the tranche from memory at once and re-places the venue stop; the Activity feed and your notifier say so. Open tranches — the mark beside the Stop Whether the Trail has actually moved that stop, and if not, why not. ▲4.0% ×2 : the stop has trailed 4% in two advances, measured from where it was when it armed. · : it has not moved — the gap to price is still under the trigger, which is the trail behaving correctly. ⏳ : the gap has cleared the trigger and it is waiting out the cooldown. ⚠ : it is due to advance and the move was refused — hover for which safety refused it. ↺ : a late fill corrected this leg's entry, so the stop that entry implies was re-derived and checked against the stop already in force — if the new one was further from price it was refused and the stop in force kept, and if it was closer to price it was taken. Either way the stop never moves backwards and the figure is still measured from the arm; hover to see which of the two happened. No mark at all means the trail is off, or this stop was armed before the engine began stamping its starting price — the movement is unknown, and an unknown is shown as nothing rather than as zero. Hover any mark for the full detail. Closed this cycle Every tranche already banked. This is the cash that has moved the paired take-profit's finish line closer. Who owns the exit Exactly one mechanism is meant to take profit at any instant. While a hedge leg is open, the paired take-profit takes logical ownership and WickHunter removes the position's own take-profit — a main take-profit filling behind the hedge's back would leave naked hedge legs. The physical status remains cancellation pending or unverified until the venue proves that removal; only then does it say confirmed absent . When the last leg closes, the exact exit recipe is handed straight back. What the screens draw while it is hedged The deal drawer's chart, its marker rail and its card show the paired TP , while the physical-status row separately says whether the deal's own TP is actually off the exchange. If the deal is on a take-profit ladder , the drawer still lists every step, marked off book — the paired TP owns the exit once the handoff is proven rather than as a refused order. They return when the last hedge leg closes; a pending or unverified handoff stays visible instead of pretending that a second exit cannot still fire.

sections.title: 📓 One hedge, start to finish, with every number
sections.text: 📓 One hedge, start to finish, with every number Everything above, on one trade. Read it once and the settings stop being abstract. The setup The position The ladder The rest of the form Long 10 units average entry $100.00 a $1,000 position L1 · 4% → 25% · cap 25% L2 · 7% → 60% · cap 60% L3 · 10% → 70% · cap 70% TP activation 4% , TP offset 2% Safe zone 0.4% , Min tranche 5% Paired TP 1.75% of main notional Trail on: 10% / 2% / 60 min The per-DCA caps here are set equal to each DCA's size on purpose, so the ladder fills exactly as written and the arithmetic stays readable. With a tighter cap the fills would be throttled — that case is worked through in the arming card. The market goes 10% against you Price What happens Hedge after $96.00 4% offside — DCA 1. Target coverage 25% = 2.5 units; nothing open yet. Opens short 2.5 units at $96.00. 2.5 (25%) $93.00 7% offside — DCA 2. Target 60% = 6.0 units; 2.5 already open. Opens short 3.5 units at $93.00. 6.0 (60%) $92.16 Tranche 1 (entry $96.00) reaches 4% profit — its activation. Its stop is placed at $94.08 , 2% from its entry, locking in profit. It will never be pulled. 6.0 (60%) $90.00 10% offside — DCA 3. Target 70% = 7.0 units; 6.0 open. The 1.0-unit top-up clears the 0.5-unit minimum tranche. Opens short 1.0 unit at $90.00. 7.0 (70%) $89.40 The low of the move. Tranche 2 needed $89.28 to arm and missed it by twelve cents. Tranche 3 needed $86.40. Both are still Unprotected : 4.5 units, 45% of the main, riding with nothing under them. 7.0 (70%) The trail never fired. Tranche 1's stop sat at $94.08 and the deepest price got was $89.40 — a gap of about 5%, half of the 10% trigger. The trail is a big-move tool; this was not a big enough move. The market comes back Price What happens $94.08 Tranche 1's stop fires. It banks 2.5 × ($96.00 − $94.08) = $4.80 of real, realised cash. That money is yours whatever happens next. The safe zone now blocks any new tranche until price falls back below $93.70 . — Still open: 3.5 units at $93.00 and 1.0 unit at $90.00 — 4.5 units at a blended $92.33 . Neither ever armed, so neither has a stop; they can only be closed by the paired take-profit or by you. $108.58 The paired take-profit fires and closes everything. Main: 10 × $8.58 = +$85.80 . The two hedge riders: 4.5 × ($92.33 − $108.58) = −$73.10 . Banked earlier: +$4.80 . Combined: +$17.50 — 1.75% of the $1,000 main notional, the target. Main and both hedge legs close together at market. What that trade actually taught you Twelve cents cost about seven dollars a unit of exit price. Had the low been $89.28 rather than $89.40 , tranche 2 would have armed at $91.14 and banked 3.5 × $1.86 = $6.51 on the way up, leaving only 1.0 unit riding — and the combined target would have been met at $101.80 instead of $108.58. One tranche reaching its activation was the whole difference between exiting just above break-even and needing a further 8% rally. A hedge leg that never arms is a pure cost on a recovery. Those two riders were short from below the main's entry and lost money the whole way back, which is exactly why the pair could not exit at break-even. That is the real premium on the insurance, and why TP activation deserves more thought than any other field. The banked scalp is what makes the target reachable. $4.80 is small against a position $100 underwater, but it is permanent, and every scalp moves the finish line the right way. On a pair that chops around its low for a week, that is where hedging earns its keep. Coverage was never allowed to reach 100%. At 70% the combined result still moves with price, so the paired take-profit could be reached; at 100% it would barely have moved. Before you run this live: put your own average position size next to your own ladder and write out the units, in the same three columns as the table above. If the hedge at the deepest DCA is larger than you are comfortable holding, the ladder is too aggressive and no other setting will save you.

sections.title: ✋ The Manual Bot — your own trades, managed
sections.text: ✋ The Manual Bot — your own trades, managed You open a trade yourself on the exchange. The Manual Bot notices it, takes it over, and runs it like any other deal — a DCA ladder underneath, a take profit above, and a stop loss if you asked for one. That is the entire job. What it does, and what it will never do It never opens a trade. No signal, no entry price, no base order, no size of its own — if you never open one, it does nothing at all. It never changes your leverage. The position keeps whatever you opened it at, which is why the page has no leverage box. It manages one thing per pair. Once it has your position it owns the adds and the exits, and it will not open a second alongside. It is the only bot allowed to do this. No other bot ever touches a position it did not open itself — which is also why, with this bot off, your hand-opened trades are left completely alone. The three things it puts on your position A DCA ladder — limit orders beyond your entry, each bigger than the last, averaging the position as price moves against you. A take profit — a reduce-only limit resting on the exchange, a percentage from your average entry. One order, or a ladder of several. A stop loss — optional and off unless you switch it on. Unlike the take profit it does not rest on the exchange: the app watches price and sends a market close when the level is touched. If the position is too small for the venue, the take profit is watched rather than rested. A small hand-opened position can fall under the exchange's minimum order size — the same reason its DCA levels are refused — and then no reduce-only limit can be placed at all. That deal is switched to a monitored exit : price is watched and a market close is sent at your target, the way the stop loss already works. It only fires while this bot is running, so a restart leaves the position with no exit until it is back, and you get a TAKE PROFIT NOT RESTING notice saying so. It goes back to a real resting order by itself if the position grows past the minimum. Turning it on is a commitment to every trade you open from then on. It does not ask per position: any trade inside the direction and pair scope you set is taken over, including the quick scalp you meant to close yourself in ninety seconds. Narrow the scope before you enable it.

sections.title: 🤝 Being picked up — what happens, and how fast
sections.text: 🤝 Being picked up — what happens, and how fast "Picked up" (the app also says adopted ) means the app has taken responsibility for a position it did not open. Nothing on the exchange changes at that instant — not size, leverage or average entry. Only who manages it. How quickly About a second, normally. The exchange pushes a private message the moment your position appears; that message is only a doorbell, and the app answers by re-reading your whole account. Fifteen seconds at worst. Independently of the doorbell, the app re-reads every position every fifteen seconds — this is what picks your trade up if the private connection is down, asleep or not authorised. The orders come after the pickup, not with it. Taken over and protected are two separate moments, reported separately. The two messages, and why there are two First: "picked up the SOLUSDT long (5 @ 200) you opened yourself — it is placing the DCA ladder, take profit and stop loss now." That promises an attempt, and claims nothing is on the exchange yet, because nothing is. Then: "is now managing SOLUSDT — its take profit is resting on the exchange and the DCA ladder is in place." Checked, not assumed: the app has read back the order the venue accepted. Or instead: an UNPROTECTED alarm, if about half a minute passes with the position taken over and no take profit resting on the venue. It names the cause — the exchange would not accept the order, or there is no live price for that symbol. The practical rule: picked up is not protected . Wait for the second message; if it does not arrive, look at the venue. What being picked up changes for you The position appears on the Deals screen and in the Managing now panel, with its average entry and how many ladder levels have filled. Its ladder, take profit and stop are placed, tagged LQ90- on the exchange so you can tell them from your own orders. The pair is now owned : no other bot will take a position on it while this deal is alive. Its profit and loss is booked under the Manual Bot. Adopting is this deal's "open". Percentage-based DCA sizing is converted to fixed dollars at that instant and frozen for the deal's life — see the DCA card below. ATR-based DCAs need candles, and a fresh pair may not have them yet. An entry is refused in that case; an adoption is not — refusing here would leave real money with no ladder, no take profit and no stop. So the position is picked up with those DCAs dropped and you are told which and how many. They are not lost : as soon as that pair has candles the bot prices them, re-places the resting orders to match, and tells you it has. Static and timed DCAs are never affected. It also notices when you leave. Close the position yourself and the leftover DCA limits and resting take profit are cancelled, normally within a second, because the fill message rings the same doorbell. Without that stream, two consecutive fifteen-second reads must agree the position is gone first — deliberate, since cancelling a live deal's ladder on one bad read is far worse than waiting thirty seconds.

sections.title: 🔐 Who owns a position — the rules you will actually see
sections.text: 🔐 Who owns a position — the rules you will actually see A pair has one manager at a time, so before taking anything the Manual Bot works out whether the position already belongs to something. Most support questions about this bot are really questions about this paragraph. 1 · Another bot already has it — it is skipped, quietly A pair held by the Liq Scalper , an Optimized Liquidation Bot or a TV Signal bot is left entirely alone. This happens on every pass of a healthy install, so it goes to the app's log rather than Activity, where one line per deal per pass would bury everything that matters. You see it as an absence : the position sits on the Deals screen under the bot that opened it and is not in Managing now . That is correct and there is nothing to fix. The log names the holder — "the Liq Scalper already manages it", "a TV Signal / Optimized Liquidation bot already manages it", "another market on this account". 2 · A claim that is only pending blocks it just as hard A bot that has just sent an entry order and is awaiting confirmation already counts as the owner. It has to: for a second or two the position exists on the venue before the bot books it, and without this rule the Manual Bot would step in front and both would manage the same money. The same applies to an order whose outcome the app could not read — a timeout, a garbled reply, a restart mid-submit. That claim survives retries and restarts until the app can prove what happened, logged as "the Liq Scalper's unresolved order" or "another bot's unresolved order". This is the one that surprises people: the Deals screen may show nothing on that pair and the Manual Bot still will not touch it, because nothing is proven. Give it a moment. If the app cannot read its own record of unfinished order submissions, adoption stops for that whole market — not one pair, everything. It logs the fact and keeps managing what it holds, but picks nothing new up until the record is readable. Guessing would mean placing a ladder against somebody else's position. 3 · A Hedge Bot attachment does not block it The Hedge Bot is an add-on , not a manager: it runs an opposing leg and never owns the main position's ladder or exits. Example: open a long by hand and attach the Hedge Bot, and the Manual Bot still adopts your long and still places its ladder, take profit and stop. One position under the Manual Bot plus a hedge attachment on the same pair is the intended picture, not a conflict. The opposite leg is never adopted. The short opened against your long belongs to the Hedge Bot, and the log says "the Hedge Bot's opposing leg". While a hedge is open, the main position's take profit is pulled off the book and the stop is suspended, with the hedge's paired exit covering both sides. Both come back automatically when the hedge closes. 4 · Both sides open, and nothing tracking either A pair with a long and a short open and neither managed is left alone entirely — adopting one as the main would put a ladder and a take profit straight into the other's face. The log says "both sides open and neither tracked". Close one leg, or attach the Hedge Bot deliberately, and the picture is readable again. 5 · "Our own records say a bot here opened it" The app keeps a record of every order it has sent. A record of one of your bots placing an opening order on that pair while this position was alive makes it the app's own, and it is not adopted. Only orders that can create or grow a position count as evidence. A close, a take profit or a stop never does — the order that ended a bot's previous trade there is proof the bot is gone . The safety net: if that record is the only claim and no bot is actually managing the position, the Manual Bot waits at least three checks and forty-five seconds — long enough for a restarting bot to reload its book — then takes it over anyway, loudly: "is on the exchange, an order record says a bot here opened it, and NO bot is managing it — the Manual Bot is taking it over so it is protected." A live position with no take profit and no stop is worth breaking a rule for. The exception to the exception: if the app cannot read its order records at all, it hands nothing over on that basis. "I cannot tell" must never become "take it". 6 · Things it cannot manage Dated futures (an expiry date in the contract name) are untouched — there is no live price feed for them here, so a ladder would be flying blind. Spot balances are not positions and are never picked up. Perpetuals are the whole scope: USDT, USDC and coin-settled, including inverse contracts.

sections.title: ⚙️ Every setting on the page
sections.text: ⚙️ Every setting on the page Everything on the Manual Bot's page, in order. There is no entry section and no leverage, because it has no entry to make. Save & enable saves, creates the bot if needed, and starts it. The two scope settings are live instantly — the next position obeys them with no restart. The ladder and exit settings govern positions picked up from then on ; to change a running deal, edit it on the Deals screen. What it ships with, if you save without changing anything: First DCA 10, Deviation 8%, Orders 3, Volume scale 2, Step scale 2, Orders on exchange 3, Take profit 0.7%, Stop loss 0 (off), measured from the initial entry price. Direction Both, Pairs All. What it picks up Direction — Long, Short or Both (default): which way your trade must point to be taken on. Example: set to Long, a short you open by hand is left alone — no ladder, no take profit, no stop. Get it wrong: narrow it to one side and forget, and the other side's trades sit unmanaged while the bot shows as running. Pairs — All pairs (default) or Only these . "All pairs" genuinely means all, including ones the exchange lists next month. Get it wrong: "Only these" is silent about everything you left out — a trade on an unlisted pair is simply never managed. Pairs it may take on — the search-and-pick list, shown only under "Only these". Type part of a symbol to add, ✕ on a chip to remove, with a count above the chips. Get it wrong: empty is refused at save — an empty allowlist is a bot that looks alive and adopts nothing. Neither of these can abandon a position — they decide only what the bot takes on . Narrow the direction to shorts while it holds a long, or drop a pair it holds off the list, and that deal carries on unchanged until it closes. DCA ladder DCA size type — Dollar (default), % of balance or % of entry , setting what "First DCA" means. "% of entry" is the natural one here, because "the entry" is your position as picked up — its exchange size times its average entry — so 100% makes the first step the size of the trade you opened. Percentages convert to fixed dollars once, at pickup, frozen for the deal's life. Get it wrong: "% of balance" at 100 makes the first ladder step alone your entire wallet. First DCA — the first step's size in that unit; every later step is this multiplied by the volume scale, once per level. Get it wrong: too big and the later steps, being multiples of it, dwarf the position you meant to take. Deviation — how far, as a percentage, the first step sits from your position's average entry at pickup. Get it wrong: too tight and the ladder is spent on ordinary noise, leaving nothing for the move that needed it. DCA style: Static / Scaled ATR · the tab above Deviation — this bot has the same DCA-style tab the Liq Scalper does. Static uses the Deviation above on every pair; Scaled ATR replaces it with each pair's own volatility (ATR multiplier × ATR ÷ price, held between a minimum and maximum you set), worked out once when the deal opens and frozen for that deal. Get it wrong: on Scaled ATR, a pair whose ATR cannot be worked out is not opened at all — there is no fall back to Deviation — so a stalled candle feed is a bot that quietly stops trading. It tells you: the pair's row says refused with the reason, and an alert fires if nothing at all can be priced. On a position this bot did not open , “when the deal opens” means when the position opened, not when the bot picked it up, so the same position gets the same ladder whether it is adopted now or after a restart. Where the exchange publishes no open time — Bybit and Aster do not — the ATR is dated from the takeover and the bot says so. It never substitutes your Static distances. The full explanation is under Dollar Cost Averaging Orders in the Liq Scalper section above. Orders — how many ladder steps exist. 0 means no DCA at all , so the bot manages only the exits. Get it wrong: at the default volume scale of 2, each extra step roughly doubles what the ladder can spend. Volume scale — the size multiplier between steps: 1 keeps every step equal, 2 doubles each, so step 4 is 8× step 1 and step 8 is 128×. Get it wrong: this is the number that turns a small ladder into a liquidation, and nothing in the app caps it. Step scale — the multiplier on the distance between steps, accumulating: deviation 8 with step scale 2 gives 8%, 24%, 56%; step scale 1 spaces them evenly at 8%, 16%, 24%. Get it wrong: below 1 is treated as 1 — the ladder can never fold back on itself. Orders on exchange — how many unfilled steps rest on the venue at once, default 3, minimum 1, with deeper ones placed as shallower fill. Get it wrong: at 1 a fast move travels through several levels before their orders exist, so those steps are placed afterwards at whatever the market gives.

sections.title: ⚙️ Every setting — the take profit and stop loss half
sections.text: ⚙️ Every setting — the take profit and stop loss half The rest of the Manual Bot form: what it does to close a position it has adopted, and the ladder editor that appears when you ask for more than one target. Take profit & stop loss Take profit type — Percentage from average price (one exit for the whole position) or Ladder (multiple TPs) (several exits taking it off in slices). Ladder hides the single box and reveals the ladder editor. Get it wrong: the two are configured in completely different places, so half-finished switching leaves the wrong one in force. Take profit — single mode only: the percentage from your average entry at which the reduce-only limit rests on the exchange. 0 turns it off entirely and clears any resting order. Get it wrong: 0 means the position has no exit at all unless you also set a stop. Stop loss — the stop percentage, or 0 for no stop , which is the default. The next setting says what it is measured against. Get it wrong: a stop inside your own ladder fires before the ladder has finished its job. SL offset from — Initial entry price (default): a fixed price worked out once from the average at pickup, never moving. Current entry price (avg) : from the live average, so the stop walks down as the ladder pulls the average — unreachable by drift, but the money at risk keeps growing. Account balance : name a percentage of your wallet and the app solves for the price where the loss is exactly that. Get it wrong: "Current entry price" is picked expecting safety and gives the opposite — an unreachable stop on a position that keeps growing. Account-balance mode fails open, not closed. The stop price comes from your live wallet balance, so if that cannot be read — or position size or average entry reads as zero — no stop level is produced and nothing fires on that pass . You will never see it on a healthy connection. Plan for the day you do. The take-profit ladder editor · only when Take profit type is Ladder Profit % — one per step, closing part of the deal at that profit from the average entry. Between 2 and 10 steps, each strictly higher than the one above. + Add step adds a row, ✕ removes one, never below two. Get it wrong: a step that does not increase is refused at save, with the offending step named. Close % of deal — how much each step takes off; these must total 100 , and the running Σ under the table turns green when they do while the form refuses to save when they do not. Even split fills them equally. Get it wrong: the form catches it only at save — watch the Σ readout while editing. Ladder SL — an on/off chip, off by default. On, the stop walks as take-profit steps fill and owns the stop from then on, rather than the plain percentage above; switching it on reveals the three settings below. Get it wrong: off, a retrace after a partial take profit runs straight back into the DCA ladder instead of stopping at breakeven. SL mode — Level based trails a fixed number of steps behind the last filled take profit; Average entry jumps to breakeven when the arming step fills and stays. A one-line explanation prints under the control. Get it wrong: "Average entry" never trails, so a deal that runs a long way gives it all back to breakeven. Arm after — how many take-profit steps must fill before the walking stop starts; 1 to 10, default 1. Get it wrong: set high and it never arms on a deal that only reaches step one, so you silently have no walking stop. SL buffer — how far past breakeven, toward profit , "breakeven" actually means. Default 0. Get it wrong: at 0 a stop-out after a partial take profit is a small loss once fees count, not the flat result it looks like. Every ladder step rests as its own reduce-only limit order anchored to the average entry. A partial close books its slice of profit and removes its share of cost basis — it does not move your average entry. Steps below the exchange's minimum order size merge forward into the nearest earlier step, so the whole position is always covered.

sections.title: 📉 The DCA ladder it puts under your position
sections.text: 📉 The DCA ladder it puts under your position The ladder is what the bot adds with. It is worked out once, from your position as it stood at pickup, and never re-planned — and it treats a position you opened exactly as one a bot opened. How the prices are worked out The anchor is the average entry your position had at pickup — not a price the bot chose, and not the moving average afterwards. A step at 24% stays 24% from that starting average for the deal's whole life; a fill above it does not drag the ones below closer. Distances accumulate, multiplied by the step scale. Example: deviation 5% and step scale 2 over three orders gives 5%, then 5+10 = 15%, then 15+20 = 35%. Sizes multiply by the volume scale. Example: First DCA 100 at volume scale 2 over three orders gives 100, 200, 400 — 700 USDT of ladder. Percentage sizing is frozen at pickup. Example: "% of entry" at 50% on a 1,000 USDT position fixes the first step at 500 USDT for the deal's life, even if the position later grows. How they fill On touch — no bounce required, no minimum time between fills, no cooldown. One fast wick can fill the entire ladder in a single candle. They are resting limit orders on the exchange, up to the "Orders on exchange" count, so they can fill while the app is not running — which is exposure, not protection. Every fill re-anchors the take profit : the old exit is cancelled and re-placed at the new average for the new quantity. In ladder mode the whole ladder is torn down and re-placed, already-filled steps included, which re-arm. A partial fill is booked immediately but does not use the step up; the step is consumed only when its order completes. When the deal closes, every surviving ladder order is cancelled. If a cancellation cannot be confirmed the app keeps the pair and says CLEANUP BLOCKED rather than releasing it — a leftover order filling behind a closed deal would open a position nothing is watching. If the exchange refuses a level — below its minimum size, say — the bot records it, tells you, and waits thirty seconds before retrying that level. There is no cap on any of this. Nothing in the app clips a DCA order: the total committed to one position is your entry plus every ladder step, and the ladder you configured is the only ceiling. Volume scale 2 over 8 orders makes the last step alone 128× the first. Your exchange's margin and liquidation price are the real limit, and they are not gentle. When a position has no ladder, the card says why A position can legitimately be held with no DCA ladder, and the deal now names the reason instead of printing 0/0 . There are four different reasons and they used to look identical. “DCA pending — resolving ATR” is the normal one on a Scaled ATR bot: your position is picked up, protected and fully managed, and only the averaging half waits while this pair’s candles arrive — the card counts them out for you (“3/15 1h candles”). “DCA pending — ATR DCAs owed” is the builder’s version of the same wait. “No DCA ladder” is not a wait at all: DCA is switched on but the distances you saved can never rest away from the entry, so nothing will ever average this position — fix it on the bot’s form. “DCA not placed — refused” means the exchange turned the ladder down, and Details prints its exact words. A bot with DCA simply switched off says nothing, because that is not a fault. Retry DCA ladder · in Details, only while one of those is showing — asks the bot to try again now rather than on its own thirty-second timer, which is what you want after fixing whatever the exchange objected to. It cannot double your orders however many times you press it : the bot cancels every resting DCA and proves the cancellations before it places anything, so a ladder is never half-moved and old orders are never left beside new ones. It answers in words every time — the ladder moved, or it is still waiting and why.

sections.title: 🎯 Take profit and stop loss on an adopted position
sections.text: 🎯 Take profit and stop loss on an adopted position The take profit lives on the exchange; the stop loss lives in the app. That difference decides what still protects you if the server stops. Take profit — a real order on the venue A reduce-only limit resting the percentage you set from your average entry, for the full position size. It re-anchors after every add — a ladder fill, a partial fill, or a hand add on the exchange all cancel and re-place it at the new price and the new quantity. Both matter: a hand add can move your size a lot without moving the average much, and a take profit at the right price for the wrong amount closes only part of the deal. It survives the app dying , because the order is on the exchange. If something cancels it outside the app , the next check notices and puts it back. Setting it to 0 turns it off and clears any resting one, leaving nothing to catch you but the stop, if you set one. This describes Fixed %. Its own exit does not follow price up — it moves only because your average moved. Trailing and ladder mode's own optional trailing last step are the two alternatives that do follow price, at the cost of resting nothing on the exchange (see Exit orders ): pick Take-profit source before typing the rest. A live hedge suspends it : the take profit comes off the book and the hedge's paired exit owns both sides, restored when the hedge closes. Stop loss — a watcher, not an order Nothing rests on the exchange. The app watches price and sends a plain market close when the level is touched, which appears on the venue as an ordinary close, not a stop. So it needs the app running and a live price. If the server is off, there is no stop. That is the most important sentence on this card. Touch is inclusive , with a small tolerance for floating-point noise, so a stop at exactly 110.00 fires at 110.00. A live hedge suspends it too , and it re-arms when the hedge closes. 0 means no stop , and that is the shipped default — a fresh Manual Bot has a take profit and no stop until you give it one. Which "offset from" to choose — with numbers A long picked up at an average of 200.00, 5 units, stop loss set to 20%, wallet 5,000 USDT. After the first ladder step fills, the position is 5.5263 units at an average of 199.05. Initial entry price — 200.00 × 0.80 = 160.00 , before and after the fill. A fixed price that does nothing surprising. Current entry price (avg) — 160.00 at first, then 199.05 × 0.80 = 159.24 after the fill. The stop walks down as the ladder pulls the average down, so the deal can never reach it by drifting — and the loss it books keeps growing, because the position does. Account balance at 2% of a 5,000 wallet = 100 USDT of risk. Before the fill, 100 ÷ 5 units = 20.00 away, so the stop is 180.00 ; after, 100 ÷ 5.5263 = 18.10 from 199.05, so 180.95 . The price moves; the money at risk stays 100 USDT. If you set one risk control, this is the honest one. Editing one deal’s exits, in Details The boxes under “Edit this deal” are that deal’s OWN numbers, not the bot’s. A deal freezes its take profit, stop, on-book count and TP ladder when it opens, so a bot you have edited since is running different settings from a deal you opened last week — and this drawer shows the deal’s . Nothing here reads your bot’s form. If a deal cannot report its own settings the boxes are disabled and say so, rather than showing you a number this position has never traded on. Apply sends only what you changed, and changing nothing sends nothing. Opening Details and pressing Apply without touching a box does not write to the deal at all — it tells you so instead. That matters because this really is a live edit: it re-anchors the take profit and cancels and re-places the resting DCA orders, so there is no such thing as a harmless save here. Clearing a box is refused by name rather than ignored, because a per-deal edit can change a value and cannot unset one. After it saves, the app re-reads the deal and quotes back the setting it now holds and the price the exchange is working — if the two disagree it says so rather than showing a tick.

sections.title: 🔎 "Why has it not picked up my trade?"
sections.text: 🔎 "Why has it not picked up my trade?" Sorted by how often each turns out to be the answer, with what to check for each. It is not created, or it is paused — by far the most common answer. Confirm: My Bots. For adoption, a paused card and no card are the same thing. Fix: create it, or resume it. Your trade is on a different market from the bot. Every bot belongs to the market it was created on, and its card is simply not shown on the others — a Manual Bot on USDT will never adopt a USDC position. Confirm: the market selector in the header, then look for the bot's card. Fix: create a Manual Bot on that market too. Your own scope excludes it. Direction set to Long only and you opened a short; or Pairs set to "Only these" and this pair is not on the list. Confirm: the Activity log shows a row for that symbol reading "Left alone — the Manual Bot is set to pick up long positions only…" or "…is not on the Manual Bot's pair list…". It appears once, when the answer changes, not on every pass. Fix: widen the scope on the bot's page and save — it takes effect on the next check. Another bot in the app already holds that pair , so the Manual Bot stands off. Confirm: the Deals screen lists the position under whichever bot opened it. Normal; nothing to fix. Another bot has an unfinished order on that pair — an entry sent and unconfirmed, or one whose outcome could not be read — which holds the pair even with no deal showing. Confirm: the app's log names it — "the Liq Scalper's unresolved order", "another bot's unresolved order". Fix: usually nothing; wait. It is the opposing leg of a Hedge Bot attachment , which belongs to the Hedge Bot and is never adopted. Your main position on the pair is not blocked and should have been picked up. Confirm: the Deals screen shows the main under the Manual Bot with a hedge attached. If the main was also skipped, the reason is elsewhere on this list. The app's own order records say a bot here opened it. Confirm: the log says "this app's own order records say a bot here opened it, so it is not a position you opened yourself". If no bot is genuinely managing it, wait — after about forty-five seconds it is handed over anyway, with an "UNMANAGED POSITION ADOPTED" message. Both sides of the pair are open and neither is tracked. Neither leg is taken. Confirm: the log says "both sides open and neither tracked". Fix: close one leg on the venue. The app cannot read its record of unfinished order submissions. Adoption is blocked for the entire market until that is repaired — deliberately, rather than guessing. Confirm: the log carries a line saying adoption is blocked on that market and names the file it could not read. It is not something this bot can manage. A dated future, or a spot wallet balance rather than a derivatives position. Confirm: the log says "not a managed perpetual". There is no fix — manage it yourself. It was picked up, and the orders did not land. Different problem, and the app shouts about it. Confirm: an UNPROTECTED alarm naming the symbol. If it says there is no live price for that symbol, nothing can be managed on it at all; if it says no take profit is resting, check your take-profit settings and the venue's minimum order size. Where to look, in one line each. My Bots — is it created and running, and on this market? The Manual Bot's page — the "Managing now" panel is the honest answer to "is it holding anything". Activity — decisions your settings caused. The server log — decisions ownership caused, which are deliberately kept out of Activity so they do not bury everything else.

sections.title: ⏸️ Turning it off — what actually happens
sections.text: ⏸️ Turning it off — what actually happens Off does not mean abandoned. Pausing stops it taking on anything new ; everything it already manages is managed through to the exit. That is the opposite of what most people expect, so read both lists. What stops Adoption. All of it. Nothing new is picked up on any pair in any direction, so a position you open by hand while paused gets no ladder, no take profit and no stop — and no other bot steps in, because positions opened outside the app are left entirely alone. Paused and never created are the same state. There is no partial mode. What carries on, for positions it already holds The DCA ladder keeps working — steps rest, fills are booked, and the next step rolls onto the book behind them. The take profit keeps being re-anchored after every fill, and re-placed if something cancels it. The stop loss keeps watching and will still fire. Closing the position on the venue is still noticed , and leftover ladder orders and the take profit are still cancelled — a paused bot that stopped watching would leave live limit orders behind a dead deal, one fill from reopening a position nothing manages. The protection check keeps running , so an adopted position that loses its take profit still raises the UNPROTECTED alarm while paused. Deleting it Refused while it still holds anything. Close those positions on the venue first, or leave the bot paused. Once it holds nothing, deleting really does stop it — the engine is shut down rather than left idling. Moving it to another market has the same shape: an instance still holding a deal on the old market manages it to its exit and accepts nothing new. If the app finds unmanaged positions at start-up, it asks rather than assuming.
